name: Alaska Beacon
title: Juneau neighborhoods spared major damage in glacial outburst flood
authors: Alix Soliman, KTOO, Clarise Larson, KTOO, Corinne Smith
description: Mendenhall Valley residents in the flood zone celebrated Thursday afternoon as the Mendenhall River crested at a level well below initial predictions. The event was much less destructive than disastrous floods that struck over the past three years. The flood crested at 14.7 feet on the Mendenhall Lake gauge at 2:15 p.m., according to the […]
text:
The Mendenhall River as it crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)Mendenhall Valley residents in the flood zone celebrated Thursday afternoon as the Mendenhall River crested at a level well below initial predictions. The event was much less destructive than disastrous floods that struck over the past three years.
The flood crested at 14.7 feet on the Mendenhall Lake gauge at 2:15 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. As floodwaters started to recede Thursday afternoon, only a handful of residents reported damage.
“We have crested officially, and we are now on the way back down — we did it, Juneau,” said Zoe Kaplan, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, during a livestream just before 3 p.m.

Ann Lind lives in the flood zone on Marion Drive. She said she had been anxiously waiting for the flood all spring and summer. Last year, her home flooded when drainage pipes failed and water leaked through the floodwall.
“For months it was like this slow-moving bullet coming straight at me, and didn’t know if it was going to be a hit or a miss,” she said. “And today, it’s a miss.”
Lind said the water didn’t even touch the HESCO barriers that make up the flood wall in her backyard.
“This flood this year is the scenario we all wanted — we all hoped for,” she said.

A pump pipes water over the flood wall on Killewich Drive as the flood crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)
A couple of riverfront homeowners on Killewich Drive said their crawl spaces flooded this year due to seepage, but they were able to pump out the water.
 
Riverfront homeowners on Killewich Drive pump water out of their crawl spaces on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)    

View Drive residents saw the worst flooding, as they have every year. This is the second year in a row they were left without the protection of the flood wall constructed by the City and Borough of Juneau and the Army Corps.
Mandy Mallott lives at the end of the street. Last year, she and her neighbors set up their own flood wall made of HESCO barriers and an earthen berm in an attempt to protect their homes. She said her home was spared, but there was still a lot of damage throughout the neighborhood.
On Thursday afternoon, she said she and others who put up barriers on the street didn’t see flooding in their homes.
A man walks across the top of HESCO barriers as the Mendenhall River rises on Thursday morning, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)
“The emotions that are running through us are a big sense of relief and thankfulness to our friends and our neighbors that we got through the night and this gorgeous day together,” Mallott said.
Malachi Thorington also lives on View Drive, where he said his house and his next-door neighbors’ flooded this year, but not as badly as in the past.
Downstream on Meadow Lane, near Juneau International Airport and the mouth of the river, Bob Jacobson watched the flood from his son’s deck overlooking the river.
He described watching a tree strike the barriers across the river — just minutes before — to two U.S. Army Corps officials who had just arrived at the barrier.

Army Corps crews chainsaw a log that struck a HESCO barrier across from Meadown Lane on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
Within minutes, Army Corps crews chainsawed the log away from the barrier. Pumps were stationed along Meadow Lane but did not need to be turned on as the flood peaked.
The HESCO barriers below Brotherhood Bridge are new. There was some seepage, but neighbors said it was nothing compared to last year when water rose up the bank and into yards and some driveways, just feet from homes.
 
An industrial-sized pump pipes water over the flood wall on Meander Way as the flood crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)    

Jeff Garmon is the meteorologist in charge at the Weather Service in Juneau, and he lives on Meander Way — a street that’s been hit hard by flooding in the past. As the flood peaked, he had minor pooling in his backyard, which was piped back over the HESCO flood wall by pumps provided by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.

Jeff Garmon walks to his backyard, where an industrial-sized pump pipes water over the flood wall on Meander Way as the flood crests on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (Photo by Clarise Larson/KTOO)
“We’re fortunate this year we didn’t have an atmospheric river going into this,” Garmon said. “I think that was our saving grace.”
Garmon said he’s proud of how the city, Army Corps, U.S. Geological Survey, University of Alaska Southeast researchers, the Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska, flood advocacy groups and countless others worked collaboratively to support residents in the flood zone.
“It’s something Juneau should be proud of — that as a community we came together,” he said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama carries out first execution of 2026
description: The state of Alabama Thursday executed Jeremy Williams, 41, for his role in the sexual assault and murder of a 5-year-old girl in 2021. Williams, who waived his appeals, was executed by lethal injection. “I want to thank God for forgiving me for my sins so I can meet him in peace,” Williams said before […]
text:
Jeremy Williams, 41, was executed by the state of Alabama Thursday after being convicted of the assault and murder of a five-year-old child in Russell County in 2021. (Alabama Department of Corrections)The state of Alabama Thursday executed Jeremy Williams, 41, for his role in the sexual assault and murder of a 5-year-old girl in 2021.
Williams, who waived his appeals, was executed by lethal injection.
“I want to thank God for forgiving me for my sins so I can meet him in peace,” Williams said before his execution, according to media witnesses. “Goodnight.”
Media witnesses reported that he blinked his eyes and moved his head from side to side during the execution. Williams also moved his lips and witnesses said he appeared to be speaking or singing to himself. At the same time witnesses reported that he smiled to himself. His body convulsed slightly and he closed his eyes. At some point later, he started taking deep breaths before he stopped breathing altogether.
The time of death was at 6:16 pm.
“There are few words to adequately describe the depth and depravity of Jeremy Williams’ evil act,” Ivey said in a statement after the execution. “The unspeakable nature of this crime is exactly why we have the death penalty statute in the state of Alabama.”
The Russell County Sheriff’s Office and the District Attorney’s Office hosted a news conference following the execution. Alabama state forbids them from witnessing the execution.
“The baby didn’t die in peace,” said Rick Chancey, district attorney for Russell County. “She didn’t close her eyes and say, ‘I can meet my maker in peace.’ That baby was brutally killed. I am glad that Jeremy died in peace because that baby didn’t.”
Alabama has put 13 people to death since 2023, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Of those, seven were executed by nitrogen gas.
The state executed five people in 2025, tied with Texas and South Carolina, for the second highest total. Florida had the highest total with 19 executions for the year.
Williams’ execution was the first in the state since Anthony Boyd was put to death in November 2025. Charles “Sonny” Burton was scheduled to be executed by nitrogen gas in March. Burton was sentenced to death for participating in the robbery of a Talladega AutoZone in 1991, during which customer Doug Battle was killed. Burton did not kill Battle and was not present when he was killed; Derrick DeBruce, the man responsible, later had his death sentence commuted to life in prison and died in 2020.
Amid criticism, Ivey in March commuted Burton’s sentence to life in prison.
Death row inmate Jeffery Lee, sentenced to death for killing two people during an Orrville pawn shop robbery 1998, was scheduled to be executed by nitrogen gas in June. But a federal court ruled days before the execution that Alabama’s nitrogen gas protocol constituted cruel and unusual punishment.
Lee is set to be executed by lethal injection in September.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Toned-down Amendment 3 ballot language ready for another judicial review
description: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has submitted for judicial review a rewritten version of the title and ballot summary for Amendment 3. Circuit Judge David Frank in  Leon County ordered the AG’s office to rewrite the far-reaching property tax amendment’s ballot language after ruling the original title, “Save our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes,” w[...]
text:
Attorney General James Uthmeier's office submitted new Amendment 3 title and ballot summary language for judicial review. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has submitted for judicial review a rewritten version of the title and ballot summary for Amendment 3.
Circuit Judge David Frank in  Leon County ordered the AG’s office to rewrite the far-reaching property tax amendment’s ballot language after ruling the original title, “Save our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes,” was “akin to a political slogan” in violation of state law.
Under a 2011 law, the office had 10 days from the ruling, or until Aug. 14 — Friday — to submit new language for the judge to review. 
Former State Sen. Jeff Brandes, one of the named plaintiffs in the legal challenge, seemed satisfied with the new language submitted by Uthmeier.
“Finally, the practicing attorneys took control of the language. The text is honest about what the amendment does,” Brandes said in a text to the Phoenix. “I hope Florida voters will dig deeper, ask hard questions, and understand the consequences before they decide the outcome.”
If passed, Amendment 3 would constitute one of the most significant changes to property taxes in the state in more than a generation. Its projected financial impact could reach up to $12 billion annually beginning in 2031.
The new title and ballot summary language come days before the Aug. 18 primaries, after which the local supervisors of elections will start preparing ballots for the general election.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the new version, the title “Save our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes” has been replaced by, “Increased Homestead exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non Homestead Property Assessment.”
The ballot summary would now make clear the measure would increase the homestead exemption for all non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 and adjust for inflation thereafter.
The amendment reduces the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%.
The summary makes clear the Legislature would write a law laying out a “uniform procedure” for counties and municipalities (and special districts, subject to referendum approval) to follow that would “increase the homestead exemption to the full assessed property value.”
The new ballot summary also makes clear counties and cities would be required to use property taxes solely for public safety, education and schools, infrastructure, natural resources, bond debt service, retirement benefits for employees, and operations and administration.
With a projected $12 billion annual loss in revenue, those interests will compete for a smaller amount of available revenue, which is why the amendment has drawn opposition from groups representing law enforcement, local government officials from both political parties, as well as the Florida Democratic Party.
And while Gov. Ron DeSantis says he supports Amendment 3, he isn’t investing his political energy into helping get it passed because, he says, it wasn’t his original plan. His proposal would included school taxes in the cuts, which was a step too far for the Florida Legislature.
Edie Ausley, a spokesperson for the “Vote No on 3” campaign, issued a statement saying Frank’s ruling along with the the new language “confirm what we’ve long known — this amendment is a wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
She said the Amendment is not tax relief but a tax shift.
“The proposal doesn’t eliminate the cost of local services — it shifts more of the burden onto renters, businesses, and other property owners while leaving communities to make up the difference.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Amid widespread opposition, Alaska governor’s gasline compromise bill appears dead on arrival
description: Leading members of the Alaska House and Senate said this week that they will not meet to discuss Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s latest attempt to provide a tax break for the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline. The bill, said Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon and Senate President Gary Stevens, lacks the support to advance in […]
text:
The chambers of the Alaska House of Representatives stand empty on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (James Brooks photo / Alaska Beacon)Leading members of the Alaska House and Senate said this week that they will not meet to discuss Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s latest attempt to provide a tax break for the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline.
The bill, said Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon and Senate President Gary Stevens, lacks the support to advance in either body.
“The caucus is really not at this point, really not interested in having to rush a bill,” Stevens said.
“The votes just aren’t there,” Edgmon said. “The Senate made it very clear that they need more time than what could be allotted.”
Glenfarne, the firm acting as the project’s lead developer, has said that a tax break is necessary to finance the pipeline. Glenfarne had said that it was planning to reach a final investment decision on the first phase of the project by the end of this year. 
It has already missed several self-imposed deadlines, and it isn’t clear whether it will again change its plans. The company did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

As proposed, the pipeline project would be built in two phases, with the first completed no sooner than 2029. The first phase would deliver gas from the North Slope to Southcentral Alaska for in-state use. The second phase would allow international exports. 
Official estimates state that the total project will cost as much as $54.5 billion, making it one of the largest natural gas projects in the world. Unofficial estimates are significantly higher. 
The governor released his proposal 17 days into a 30-day special session about pipeline taxes. This is the third special session of 2026 devoted to the issue; the second special session ended in July after the state House voted down a compromise bill.
The governor’s new bill appears similar to that failed compromise. It would replace the state’s petroleum property tax with a tax on gas shipped through the pipeline, a change that would help the project pencil out financially, and it would cap the cost of gas for in-state use and shield the state from cost overruns.
It also includes a 2% corporate income tax on certain privately owned oil and gas companies that don’t pay the state’s existing corporate income tax. That’s a little over a fifth of the size of a similar tax proposed by the Senate.
The so-called “pass-through entities” tax was a key condition of skeptical state Senators and helped last month’s compromise bill pass the Senate.
But business-friendly trade groups and legislators opposed the tax increase, causing it to fail in the House, and Dunleavy said before the House vote that he would veto the Senate’s version if it reached his desk.
Dunleavy’s proposed tax rate is lower than the one approved by the Senate, but it nonetheless represented a major concession. The governor had said in June that the tax was “a line in the sand.”
On Wednesday, he had a different perspective.
“This bill is a compromise that removes a significant barrier to moving the gas line forward,” he said in a written statement.
But the compromise appears to have satisfied no one. 
A coalition of trade groups and the Alaska Chamber of Commerce issued a letter opposing it, and Stevens said by phone on Thursday that lawmakers will need to review the governor’s changes.
In a Tuesday news conference with reporters, Stevens said 2% is “not very much. … We need to do a careful analysis of that. I think the intention of the Senate was a higher tax than that.”
The 35th Alaska State Legislature is scheduled to convene in January, after this fall’s election. Incumbent Gov. Mike Dunleavy is term-limited and will leave office in January. The Legislature will have new leaders, too. Stevens is retiring and Edgmon is running for Senate. 
“I think we’ve reached the point, honestly, where we need to turn it over to the new governor, whoever that would be, and a new legislature,” Stevens said.
Glenfarne, the development firm that owns 75% of the pipeline project, did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday about the governor’s latest proposal and did not answer a question asking what it thinks about the potential for there to be no bill this year.
Earlier this year, Glenfarne officials said the tax break is necessary for the project to obtain financing.
Some state legislators say Glenfarne supported a prior compromise bill but subsequently withdrew its support under pressure from the oil and gas company Hilcorp. 
Hilcorp killed Alaska LNG bill, some legislators say, but governor calls the claim ‘bulls**t’

In response to a request for comment about the latest bill, Hilcorp spokesman Matt Shuckerow said the company doesn’t support the governor’s proposal.
“The underlying issues with this structurally incomplete and insufficiently developed income tax language remain unchanged and unresolved,” he said by email. “Hilcorp supports the Alaska LNG Project, but legislation intended to improve the project’s commercial viability should not impose a new tax that increases the cost of producing its gas, further complicates long-term investment and commercial negotiations, and challenges Cook Inlet development at a time when continued investment is critical to maintaining reliable natural gas supplies.”
Hilcorp offered a longer statement about its position on July 23, shortly after the failure of the prior compromise proposal.
Late Wednesday, the leaders of the 21-person coalition in charge of the state House issued a statement declaring that “intractable differences have emerged on the Governor’s bill relating to property tax relief for the gas line. The proposed HB 4001 does not appear to have the support needed to pass the Alaska House, with opposition being expressed by both Majority and Minority members.”
The 19-person, all-Republican House minority caucus responded with a letter asking the Majority to call the House back to Juneau anyway in order to continue talking about the gas pipeline.
House Minority Leader DeLena Johnson, R-Palmer, said the letter doesn’t mean that all members of the minority support the governor’s bill, just that they want to continue talking about the issue and trying to find a path forward.
But Edgmon said that doesn’t make sense.
“It costs a lot of money to reconvene the Legislature,” he said. “It doesn’t make fiscal sense to just go down and talk about something with no resolution at hand, or no means to achieving a resolution, and so here we are.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Idaho community fund helps farmworkers fight heat, wildfire smoke
description: On the morning of July 31, Idaho Organization of Resource Councils members Samantha Guerrero and Julia Santiago met at a Nampa Home Depot. Their cars, parked right next to each other, trunks open, were prepared for a distribution of aid to local farmworkers impacted by wildfire smoke and high summer temperatures. They carried crates of […]
text:
Farmworkers form a line behind a white SUV, awaiting a supply distribution by the Idaho Organization of Resource Councils on July 31, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)On the morning of July 31, Idaho Organization of Resource Councils members Samantha Guerrero and Julia Santiago met at a Nampa Home Depot. Their cars, parked right next to each other, trunks open, were prepared for a distribution of aid to local farmworkers impacted by wildfire smoke and high summer temperatures.
They carried crates of Gatorade, N95 masks, protective gloves, eyewear – basic supplies needed by farmworkers to carry out rough, often unforgiving agricultural work across the state.
Soon, they would be driving 20 minutes away to a group of farmworkers combing through a corn cob field. Santiago and Guerrero said their mission, as well as that of the Idaho Organization of Resource Councils as an organization, is to provide rural immigrant workers with supplies needed for their day-to-day activities.

To donate to the 2026 JJ Saldaña Heat and Smoke Relief Fund, go to https://givebutter.com/2026hsf.

“Samantha and other members of Idaho Organization of Resource Councils noticed that there was a need for essential supplies, because there was essentially no organization that goes out to the fields and delivers gloves, masks, bandanas and water,” Santiago said in an interview with the Idaho Capital Sun. “One way they realized that they could help farmworkers was being able to purchase these items for them. That way, it is not coming from their paychecks.”
The organization channels aid through the JJ Saldaña Heat and Smoke fund, a community-based program that collects donations, supplies and other items for distribution to farmworkers exposed to smoke and heat.
The fund, which turned almost six years old, began during 2020 in an effort to help farmworkers with COVID-19 related expenses. During that time, undocumented workers could not receive stipends for medical or other necessities, so the fund stepped in to help, according to Guerrero.
“It’s an injustice to have the people who help feed us not always be able to provide food for themselves, and that is definitely something we saw during the pandemic,” Guerrero said. “People who didn’t have access to food or couldn’t leave their house, or they lived in rural areas and couldn’t go out to get healthy food at the grocery store … It really made us aware of so many injustices that our farmworker community faces.”
Since then, Santiago said they have “continued to do this fund to help farmworkers.”
 Delivering supplies to Idaho farmworkers

Arriving at the first distribution site, Santiago parked her SUV on the side of the road, agricultural fields spanning wide on both sides.
She opened the trunk, pulled out a Gatorade freezer and set up other items inside the car, preparing a makeshift assembly line where farmworkers could pick up supplies.
Nearby, a foreman tasked with directing work and communicating with the Idaho Organization of Resource Councils for the supply drop approached. In a few minutes, and after the foreman had called a “quebrada” – Spanish slang for break – close to 10 farmworkers previously detassling corn in the fields formed a straight line behind the SUV.
One after the other, they grabbed drinks, a meal bar, protective gloves and masks for the smoke.
“(Aid) is very important, especially here in Idaho,” Santiago said of supply distributions. “In other states like Oregon and Washington, there are stricter regulations when it comes to workers getting breaks. But here in Idaho, there is not, and we want to support farmworkers as much as possible.”
Among the main threats facing farmworkers over the summer months is smoke and heat, Guerrero said, which in addition to long workdays, often insufficient pay and out-of-pocket expenses for basic gear can make work dangerous.
Wildfire smoke, like that lingering across much of Idaho, can create a myriad of health conditions from headaches, nausea and respiratory tract irritation, to more long-lasting problems like worsened asthma, according to the EPA.
Over the past months, the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality has issued multiple advisories warning of unhealthy air conditions in the state, as previously reported by the Sun.
Information about the effects of smoke exposure, however, went unnoticed by many farmworkers, according to Guerrero.
“We saw that the smoke health advisories have been that people should stay indoors, that it’s very unhealthy,” she said. “We were in Weiser, where there was a fire ongoing, and people had no idea about these advisories. They were just like ‘it’s hot,’ or they were feeling sick and they were thinking there was something else, but the symptoms correlate with the smoke.”
Through the fund, Guerrero said the Idaho Organization of Resource Councils aims to fill those gaps, bringing awareness and supplies that may not be available to farmworkers in Idaho.
Like Santiago, she gave the comparative example of Oregon, a state which she said provides more heat-related regulations around “equipment and standards for life: take rest breaks, shade, more water, and here we don’t really see that.”
Oregon’s Occupational Safety and Health Division announced in 2022 that it would establish permanent rules protecting farmworkers against heat and wildfire smoke.
The administrative orders established basic principles that employers must follow, such as providing shade in high-heat areas, cool drinking water and, in case of exposure to wildfire smoke, approved filtering respirators like N95 masks.
Idaho Administrative Code also maintains that employers should provide basic safety equipment to employees, but it does not make any particular mention of heat or smoke related protections. Available shade or water are not included.
“So for us, it’s important to be out in the fields reminding the farmworkers to … ‘drink water,’” Guerrero said.
“Today’s supposed to be 101 degrees; next week there’s going to be days (where) there’s going to be 105 degrees,” Santiago remarked. “And the smoke acts like another stressor for them.”
In these conditions, she said farmworkers “shouldn’t be buying stuff out of their pockets.”
 Community involvement, crowdsourcing

Aid and supplies come primarily from community donors, which Santiago said the Idaho Organization of Resource Councils relies on for distribution.
“This is all mutual aid,” she said. “We accept both monetary donations and physical items with our fund … and then we also partner up with different businesses where we set up bins, and (people) can go to these places to drop off a case of water or a pack of Gatorades, whatever they can purchase for our farmworkers.”
Their main sought-after items include bottled water, bandanas for the heat, safety glasses, work gloves, coolers and other objects to stave off the heat, as broadcasted in an Instagram post.
During the July 31 supply distribution, one farmworker approached Santiago with his old set of gloves, a bright-green pair discolored around the fingers and palm after months of work.
Santiago said she believed the man might have gotten his old pair from them in a previous supply drop, but that over time, the gloves had deteriorated.
The event, and others like it, embodied what Santiago said the fund aimed to accomplish: give visibility to farmworkers.
“We just want to let farmworkers know that they’re not alone,” she said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Attorney general decision could boot GOP primary winners from ballot
description: Montana House Majority Leader Steve Fitzpatrick said Thursday he’s going to have to file a lawsuit to stay on the ballot after a decision from Attorney General Austin Knudsen this week affected how term limits are calculated. Fitzpatrick, who ran unopposed for re-election in the Republican primary, called the decision from the attorney general a […]
text:
House Majority Leader Steve Fitzpatrick (R - Great Falls) speaks during a press conference on MEPA legislation on Feb. 12, 2025. (Nathaniel Bailey for the Daily Montanan)Montana House Majority Leader Steve Fitzpatrick said Thursday he’s going to have to file a lawsuit to stay on the ballot after a decision from Attorney General Austin Knudsen this week affected how term limits are calculated.
Fitzpatrick, who ran unopposed for re-election in the Republican primary, called the decision from the attorney general a “total affront to the electoral process” and an “affront to democracy.”
The decision by Knudsen, also a Republican, affects how term limits are calculated, requiring candidates to wait a full cycle between chambers of the legislature. The law limits lawmakers to eight consecutive years in any one chamber, but previous attorneys general had taken the position that the law allows lawmakers to switch without waiting a year in between.
The change potentially means the Secretary of State’s Office will remove at least two candidates who won primaries from the ballot.
Ballots for the general election need to be certified by Aug. 20. A spokesperson for the Secretary of State’s Office did not respond to a request for comment. 
Knudsen’s office also did not respond to a request for comment.Thursday in Kalispell, Gov. Greg Gianforte said the conflict will likely be decided by the courts.
He declined to answer whether his office would be involved in any legal action but offered strong words for fellow Republicans.
“I think Republicans ought to start getting along with each other because there’s too much important work we have to do for the people of Montana,” Gianforte said.
The decision highlights the rift in the Montana Republican party between ultraconservatives and GOP legislators who call themselves “grassroots” Republicans.
The opinion came at the behest of Republican Senate President Matt Regier, part of the hard right wing of the party.
In a letter, Regier asked Knudsen to determine if Rep. Llew Jones, a Conrad Republican and one of the biggest foes of the ultraconservatives, was eligible to run for state Senate.
Regier, of Kalispell, did not immediately return a request for comment.
Knudsen’s opinion overturns a 2012 decision by then-Attorney General and Democrat Steve Bullock, later the state’s governor. Bullock interpreted the term limits statute as allowing candidates to run for election if they had eight years out of their previous chamber by the start of the next term. 
In practice, Bullock’s interpretation has allowed legislators to switch between the state House and state Senate every eight years should they so choose and be elected. They can switch chambers immediately — they don’t have to wait an election cycle.
But Knudsen’s opinion states if a candidate has served for eight of the last 16 years in a chamber, they cannot appear on the ballot. The opinion, sent to the Secretary of State’s Office, would require those legislators to wait an extra year should they run into the term limit law.
The decision says Regier requested his opinion after Jones won as to whether he is constitutionally eligible to appear on the ballot as the Republican nominee for Montana State Senate District 9 in the November 2026 general election.
In a statement Wednesday to MTN News, which first reported the change, Jones said that Regier and the Freedom Caucus Political Action Committee “spent unprecedented amounts trying to beat me at the ballot box” and lost to him.
Jones, chairman of the powerful House Appropriations Committee and an architect of the state budget, beat Rep. Zach Wirth in the Republican primary by about 200 votes.
Jones could not be reached for comment Thursday by the Daily Montanan.
Fitzpatrick said Thursday the new opinion was a continuation of a long-running rift in the state Republican party that led to a coalition of Democrats and more moderate Republicans working as an acting majority in the Senate in 2025. It’s been an “immense” distraction for the Republican party, he said.
“We haven’t been able to advance our objectives because Regier is busy fighting and bickering with everybody instead of doing the job,” Fitzpatrick said. “In the middle of an election cycle, I could be out campaigning. Instead, I’m sitting here with my attorneys concocting a lawsuit in order to stay on the ballot.”
Fitzpatrick, an attorney himself, served three sessions in the state House before moving over to the state Senate for two terms. He was reelected and served in the state House last session.
He’s facing Democrat Pam Carroll in the general election.
Fitzpatrick, along with his father, also a legislator, Jones and numerous other Republicans were targeted by their own party in primaries across the state with mixed results. The Montana Republican Party also disavowed some Republicans and its bylaws are currently the subject of a lawsuit in Lewis and Clark District Court in Helena.
Micah Drew contributed to this report.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Why no trawl backlash to Dan Sullivan’s proposed bycatch bill?
description: In May 2024, when then-Congresswoman Mary Peltola introduced a Bycatch Reduction and Mitigation Act and Bottom Trawl Clarity Act, the bills drew immediate backlash.  Peltola, a Democrat, received a letter signed by 53 trawl interests and nationwide fishery stakeholders urging her to withdraw the proposed legislation saying, “These new federal mandates and ti[...]
text:
Trawl-caught pollock harvested during an Alaska research survey. (Photo by David Csepp/National Marine Fisheries Service)In May 2024, when then-Congresswoman Mary Peltola introduced a Bycatch Reduction and Mitigation Act and Bottom Trawl Clarity Act, the bills drew immediate backlash. 
Peltola, a Democrat, received a letter signed by 53 trawl interests and nationwide fishery stakeholders urging her to withdraw the proposed legislation saying, “These new federal mandates and timelines are utterly unworkable.” 
Fast forward to 2026.
In her current campaign to unseat 12-year incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, Peltola introduced a similar “Fighting for Alaska Fisheries” platform to no reaction from the trawl sector. Sullivan quickly followed by proposing a Bycatch Reduction Act,  a revamped version of a 2022 Alaska Salmon Research Task Force bill that produced a report recommending more research. Again, no trawler reaction.
What’s the difference?  
This time around, Peltola’s push is a campaign policy platform, not a proposed congressional bill. While Sullivan’s Act fits that description, the trawl sector apparently views him as its strategic shield against Peltola. If they aggressively attack his bill, they could politically weaken their strongest ally in Washington. 
There are fundamental differences between the two bills.
Peltola’s approach leans toward statutory restrictions that would force the government to draw hard lines on where trawling is allowed — the goal is to stop “multi-species collapse.” It would make changes to language loopholes in the outdated Magnuson-Stevens Act, such as “minimizing bycatch to the extent practicable.” Her proposal would remove “to the extent practicable”  as it is widely regarded as the phrase that allows trawlers to declare under the law that they “are doing the best they can” to reduce bycatch. It has been included in management decisions for decades as a way for the trawl sector to avoid more stringent bycatch rules. Peltola’s approach calls for restructuring the North Pacific Fishery Management Council to dilute trawler influence, and adding seats for subsistence and small-boat fishermen. It calls for investment in Alaska seafood processing innovation, fish by-product utilization and seaweed and shellfish mariculture.
Sullivan’s bill offers industrialized trawlers a heavily subsidized pathway to compliance rather than an eviction notice. It requires stricter operational rules like mandatory salmon excluders — devices built into trawl nets that can allow salmon to escape — and tougher seafloor contact accountability. It focuses heavily on using advanced data, real-time technology and gear innovations to mitigate bycatch and ecosystem impacts without adding regulatory burdens. Crucially, it includes massive federal carrots: funding for a flume tank, electronic monitoring upgrades and streamlined Exempted Fishing Permits that allow vessels to conduct experimental fishing activities that would otherwise be prohibited.
Instead of resorting to angry rebuttals, the trawl sector has outsourced its messaging to new advocacy fronts like The Truth Alaska, Sustaining Alaska’s Future and the Alaska Pollock Fishery Alliance. One originates in Texas; the others are fronted by former state directors for Republican Congressional delegates Sen. Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich III. 
This strategy lets the trawl sector counter anti-trawl sentiment without making it look like they are fighting a sitting US Senator. They reframe the debate as “supporting science and Alaska jobs,” allowing Sullivan to position himself as the reasonable middle ground.
During his tenure, Sullivan has been one of Big Trawl’s top recipients of campaign contributions. He obfuscates the fact that those cash cows all are homeported in Seattle or Oregon. 
In recent social media ads, for example, he calls for reining in chum salmon bycatch by “holding foreign fleets accountable,” knowing full well that foreign fleets have been banned from Alaska waters out to 200 miles since the mid-1970s. 
Sullivan dismisses the fact that each year 75% of the value of all groundfish taken from Alaska waters by industrialized trawlers leaves the state; for pollock, it’s 82%.  
It looks like Sullivan’s prime objective is maintaining the reliable donor flow from the Outside trawl sector. His sudden campaign year concern about reducing trawl bycatch and protecting Alaska’s marine ecosystem has as much staying power as a fish out of water.

Acc[...]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.A Libby clinic that focused on patients with asbestos-related diseases abruptly shuttered on Monday, two weeks earlier than its planned wind-down.
The Libby Center for Asbestos Related Disease has since 2000 offered screening and resources for patients with asbestos-related diseases due to exposure to vermiculite mined in the region throughout the 1900s.
According to a post on the clinic’s Facebook page, “unforeseen circumstances beyond CARD’s control, including circumstances relating to grant funding,” prevented the clinic from staying open through the end of the month.
The clinic was largely funded through federal grants, but has been at the heart of several legal battles in recent years with the BNSF Railway, which sued the clinic, arguing it had defrauded the federal government by falsely diagnosing patients and helping them receive Medicare benefits.
The clinic filed for bankruptcy in 2023, citing the lawsuit, and further funding cuts from the federal government led to the decision to shutter it on Aug. 31.
The clinic director and members of the board could not be reached for comment on Thursday.
In its Facebook post, the clinic said its “ability to process and respond to medical records requests is currently limited,” but that clinic staff are consulting with government agencies and legal counsel to determine “the appropriate process for handling medical records requests during this transition.”

name: VTDigger
title: Local police aid in Border Patrol’s deportation efforts raises questions on statewide compliance to policies on immigration enforcement
description:
“Vermont’s existing framework for keeping local police out of the deportation business clearly needs to be stronger, and there must be accountability when local officials violate that policy,” ACLU told VTDigger. “Vermont should not be complicit in ICE and Border Patrol abuse.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Local police aid in Border Patrol’s deportatio[...]
text:
A U.S. Border Patrol vehicle patrolling the area near Richford, Vermont in August 2025. CBP file photo by Jerry Glaser/Wikimedia Commons

Moments after a Chittenden County sheriff’s deputy pulled over a Chevrolet Spark on a back road in Berkshire last month, the officer picked up his personal cellphone and texted a group of Border Patrol agents. 
“Need one of you,” the text said.
Within the hour, a farmworker was in federal custody. He was later deported.
The act has led observers to question the act in lieu of Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy, which bars local officers from aiding federal immigration enforcement. 
So why was a Chittenden County deputy making a stop in Franklin County — more than 50 miles from home?
The answer lies in a federally funded program that has for years pulled the Chittenden department and others into Border Patrol’s orbit.
Operation Stonegarden, a program run by the U.S. Homeland Security, provides overtime and equipment to local and state police for northern border enforcement. While the program is overseen by Border Patrol, the local officers continue to work in their cruisers and wear local uniforms, acting as state officers. 
Executive Director of the Vermont Criminal Justice Council Christopher Brickell said that while patrolling the border, local police are still held accountable to everything that they would be required to do as a Vermont certified law enforcement officer.
“All statewide policies still remain in effect, regardless of what it is that they’re doing with Border Patrol,” he said. “If they’re acting as a Vermont law enforcement officer, then all of the statewide policies still remain in full effect.” 
While Vermont’s original Fair and Impartial Policing Policy expressly exempted Operation Stonegarden and similar programs from its restrictions on local immigration enforcement, the state’s current policy no longer shows that exemption.
The change in policy raised questions about whether Operation Stonegarden’s federally mandated coordination with Border Patrol can be reconciled with Vermont rules that generally bar local officers from investigating unlawful entry, facilitating civil immigration detention or sharing a person’s location with federal immigration authorities.
Those questions gained urgency after the Chittenden County sheriff’s deputy, Sgt. Scott Costella, was on Stonegarden patrol last month and summoned Border Patrol to a traffic stop, helping the agents detain the farmworker.
Records obtained by Migrant Justice and shared with news organizations show that Costella’s explanation for calling Border Patrol changed after the county’s internal legal review. Costella’s initial account cited the remote location of the stop, the impending tow of the vehicle and his uncertainty about its occupants. 
The final version described Border Patrol as “officer safety backup” and added that Costella was “unsure how they would react,” apparently referring to the occupants of the stopped vehicle.
“He doesn’t even try to contact state and local authorities, so even if he thought his physical safety was in danger, then the proper protocol would be to radio dispatch and see who is your closest backup,” said Will Lambek at Migrant Justice. “He didn’t do that. Those are not the actions of somebody who believes that they are at risk of physical injury.” 
Chittenden County Sheriff Dan Gamelin said this was the first time he could remember in the 15 years the police department had been participating in the program of an incident like this one occurring with his officers or deputies.  
“Our main duties when we work that program up there is criminal interdiction,” he said in reference to Chittenden’s participation in Operation Stonegarden. 
However, in 2023, the sheriff’s office paid a $25,000 settlement to an immigrant farmworker after another deputy called Border Patrol during a 2019 traffic stop that resulted in his deportation. At the time, Operation Stonewall was exempted from the Fair and Impartial Policing Policy. 
“We cannot be involved in any immigration status or anything to do with immigration. We can’t ask questions about immigration,” Gamelin added. “We are all aware about the Fair and Impartial Policing Policy when we’re working up there.” 
Recent updates by the council under the Vermont Attorney General narrowed local collaboration parameters and instead placed general prohibitions against warrantless detention or inquiring about immigration status without safety justifications.
“The only thing we focus on is the criminal activity that occurs on the border, including drug trafficking and gun trafficking and human trafficking,” Gamelin said, “We do not focus on immigration status.” 
According to Costella’s statement, his action to call on Border Patrol for backup was not based on race or gender. He said police dispatch had informed him — and he later confirmed by phone — that the vehicle registration had expired.
Despite the restrictions on local police executing civil immigration duties, local and county agencies in Vermont, such as Chittenden County police, have continued to navigate overlapping federal border grant funds through Operation Stonegarden.  
While the Vermont Attorney General’s Office helped in constructing the policy, the office acts merely as a consultant for the state criminal justice council, said Haley Sommer, senior advisor to Vermont’s Attorney General. 
Sommer said the Attorney General’s Office did not have any role in investigating or settling allegations that individual officers have violated their agencies’ Fair and Impartial Policing Policy. 
“The people of Vermont have been very clear that they do not want state resources aiding or abetting ICE and Border Patrol,” James Duff Lyall, executive director of Vermont’s American Civil Liberties Union, said in a statement to VTDigger. “Still, we are still seeing examples of local police colluding with these lawless federal agencies as they continue to terrorize communities across the state.”
An internal review is being conducted into determining if Costella’s actions were in line with the policing policy, Gamelin said in a complaint filed with the Vermont Criminal Justice Council.

name: WyoFile
title: Gift card giveaways, Freedom Caucus bashing, promoting public land: US House hopefuls strive to stand out
description:
A crowded field of nine GOP contenders are going to attention-grabbing lengths to pull ahead, but it remains unclear if anybody has broken free from the pack. 
The post Gift card giveaways, Freedom Caucus bashing, promoting public land: US House hopefuls strive to stand out appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Steve Friess’ campaign staff have been promoting a clear incentive for coming to hear the U.S. House candidate’s spiel: The stop could yield money.  
The campaign is giving away gift cards — they’ve slid into pockets in Gillette, Casper, Cheyenne and Rock Springs — and the value isn’t trivial. Although the Friess campaign website states that the bait is a “massive $1,000 Sportsman’s Warehouse gift certificate,” in practice four attendees at some campaign stops have been walking away with more open-ended $250 Visa gift cards, according to Elishah McAvoy, Friess’ campaign manager.
“We’re thrilled with the gift card giveaways,” McAvoy said, “and being able to provide a little extra something to people.”
Recipients of the gift cards aren’t required to vote for Friess, and their names are drawn out of a hat, she said. 
“It comes with absolutely no strings attached,” McAvoy said. 
For Friess, the son of late financier, GOP megadonor and philanthropist Foster Friess, the campaign tactic is perhaps flitting. The largely self-funded candidate from Teton County has loaned himself $3 million, tops among the nine Republican candidates competing in next week’s primary election to represent Wyoming in the U.S. House.
Republican primary candidate for U.S. House of Representatives Steve Friess talks during a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
The gift card tactic is also controversial. In July, the Wisconsin Elections Commission found that Elon Musk “likely broke the law” when he gave $1 million checks to voters before the 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election, the Wisconsin Examiner reported.
Gift card giveaways at campaign stops might legally fly in Wyoming, said retired University of Wyoming law and political science professor Stephen Feldman. 
“As far as I know, this is not illegal,” Feldman told WyoFile. “But from an ethical standpoint, it seems somewhat questionable.” 
It’s unclear where the Wyoming Secretary of State’s office, which oversees statewide elections, falls on the issue. The office’s chief policy officer and general counsel, Joe Rubino, did not respond to an interview request. 
Rubino works for Secretary of State Chuck Gray, who’s one of nine GOP candidates vying for the U.S. House seat being vacated by Harriet Hageman, who’s running for Senate. Other candidates include former Superintendent of Public Instruction Jillian Balow, Wyoming Senate President Bo Biteman, retired Bureau of Land Management employee Kevin Christensen, actor and singer Richard Dodson, former Army Ranger David Giralt, Casper resident Keith Goodenough and Casper businessman Reid Rasner. (There were 10, but Jackson Hole resident Frank Chapman dropped out after he and the Fighting for Wyoming PAC spent roughly $3 million on his campaign.)
None of the candidates is the clear frontrunner. Although Donald Trump endorsed Hageman for the same seat in her high-profile contest against foe Liz Cheney in 2022, the president has not stated a preference for Wyoming’s next congressman. (He has weighed in on this year’s gubernatorial and U.S. Senate contests, endorsing Megan Degenfelder and Hageman, respectively.)

Secretary of State Chuck Gray listens to testimony at the House Corporations, Elections and Political Subdivisions Committee on Jan. 15, 2025. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

There hasn’t been independent polling data on Wyoming’s U.S. House race that has been made public, but the Friess campaign has claimed its internal polls found it’s a two-man race, between Gray and himself. Gray, meanwhile, has claimed that he’s neck and neck, but with another candidate. 
“We just got some new polling numbers. This race has turned into a two-man race between myself and Christensen,” Gray said in a Facebook video following a candidate forum in Sheridan hosted by Wyoming Public Television (PBS). 
Gray’s another big spender, loaning his campaign $1.38 million and securing another $519,000 in support from a super PAC that’s funded by his father, Jan Gray. He did not respond to WyoFile’s request to discuss or share the polling that he says showed him atop the field with Christensen. 
With less than a week to go before Tuesday’s primary, candidates are trying to grab attention and differentiate themselves. This week, Rasner’s campaign staff sought out and succeeded in securing headlines about his distaste for the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, a faction of the GOP that’s been on the upswing in the statehouse. During the 2026 election season, the caucus seeks to win majority control of the Wyoming Senate and bolster its existing majority in the Wyoming House into a supermajority. 
Rasner, who raised his national profile in a failed bid to buy TikTok, leads all candidates in soliciting individual contributions, which total over $450,000. But he’s invested much more from his own fortune, loaning his campaign $1.87 million.  

Republican primary candidate for U.S. House of Representatives Reid Rasner talks during a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

The Rasner campaign has also used that campaign war chest to buy media attention. This week the Wyoming Tribune Eagle published two sponsored stories, one touting the campaign’s grassroot contributions and another promising $1 billion for Wyoming as a result of a proposed change to the state’s share of federal mineral revenues.
Like Gray and Friess, Rasner has touted favorable internal polling. The results have his campaign feeling “comfortable,” he told WyoFile. When asked, he did not divulge any specifics. 
Other candidates are campaigning in the home stretch with an altogether different strategy. Biteman, the Wyoming Senate president, has eschewed costly mailers and is running with a much tighter budget: He raised nearly $115,000 in individual contributions and didn’t loan himself anything.
“Many of the candidates are just burning through cash, pushing out mailers and text blasts attacking the rest of the field,” Joey Correnti, Biteman’s campaign associate, wrote in a text message. “As a coalition builder and fixer of problems, Bo prefers to meet people where they are at and have real conversations and make real connections, regardless of ideology.” 
Bo Biteman takes a snap of the audience before the start of a forum for U.S. House of Representatives Republican candidates on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College.(Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Biteman’s not the only candidate taking the more traditional approach to campaigning in Wyoming. Just this week, Gov. Mark Gordon called for a return to decorum in the state’s elections. 
“This election, similar to the one two years ago, has amplified the sorts of big city, big money, nasty half-truths and flat-out lies or falsehoods that have become all too common in other states,” the governor wrote in an opinion piece. “It’s not the Wyoming I know.”
Many contenders for the House seat have refrained from attack ads and mudslinging, and their pitch to voters is instead focused on issues. In the wake of a western public lands sale being axed from the federal budget bill, political rhetoric about keeping the federal estate intact has been on the rise. During a July 23 candidate forum in Casper, the crowded pool of GOP candidates were unanimously opposed to disposing of federal lands.
Some candidates have made their public lands positions a feature of their campaigns. 
Christensen, the former BLM employee, was the only candidate at the Casper forum who called for the Trump administration and Congress to retain the 2001 Roadless Rule. And he’s also called for the repeal of the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act. In a written response he provided to WyoFile, he proclaimed that he’s “passionate about public lands in Wyoming.” 

Republican primary candidate for U.S. House of Representatives Kevin Christensen talks during a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

“In my time in the BLM, I expanded public land access by 80,000 acres,” Christensen wrote, “and ensured that oil and gas, coal, grazing, and recreation powered our economy while preserving the beauty and productivity of the land for future generations.” 
For more information about the nine candidates vying for Wyoming’s seat in the U.S. House, see WyoFile’s 2026 election guide. Videos of candidate forums on July 23 in Casper and Aug. 4 in Sheridan are also available online. 
Wyoming’s primary election is Tuesday. Early voting is underway.
For more information about candidates in Wyoming’s federal, state and legislative races, check out WyoFile’s 2026 Election Guide.

title: WA state House hopeful arrested for alleged impaired driving
description: Tacoma police arrested a progressive candidate for the state Legislature on suspicion of impaired driving this week.  Krista Perez was reportedly booked into jail in Pierce County just past 7:30 a.m. Tuesday on a charge of driving while intoxicated, a gross misdemeanor. She was released six hours later, according to jail records. Efforts to immediately […]
text:
Tacoma police reportedly arrested Krista Perez on Tuesday for suspicion of driving while intoxicated. She's running for Washington state House in the 29th District. (Photo courtesy of the Krista Perez campaign)Tacoma police arrested a progressive candidate for the state Legislature on suspicion of impaired driving this week. 
Krista Perez was reportedly booked into jail in Pierce County just past 7:30 a.m. Tuesday on a charge of driving while intoxicated, a gross misdemeanor. She was released six hours later, according to jail records.
Efforts to immediately obtain the police report on the arrest were unsuccessful. 
The arrest came just a week after Perez made a strong showing in the primary race for a House seat in the 29th Legislative District. She leads incumbent state Rep. Melanie Morgan, D-Parkland, by over two percentage points, or nearly 400 votes. 
As they’re the only two candidates running, both automatically advance to the November general election. The race is seen as a test of whether a progressive challenger can unseat a more moderate Democrat. The district covers most of south and east Tacoma, Parkland, Spanaway, and parts of Lakewood.
Perez did not respond to requests for comment Thursday.
She may comment at some point in the future “regarding an investigation pertaining to an uncharged case,” attorney Bryan G. Hershman said in a statement issued by officials at Argo Strategies, Perez’s campaign consultant.
Tuesday’s arrest isn’t deterring Perez’s pursuit of a legislative seat, he noted. 
She “chooses, instead, to focus on the important issues that matter most to the families of this community” and is “incredibly grateful” for the support she’s received, said Hershman, a Tacoma-based defense attorney. He didn’t immediately respond to requests for further information about Perez’s case.
Perez, who is a strategic partnerships manager for the state Department of Commerce, was reportedly working Wednesday and Thursday. Her responsibilities include the Community Reinvestment Program. 
She published a book in 2022 explaining how marginalized groups can implement “transformative and healing practices within their communities.”
Last year, she ran for Tacoma City Council, but didn’t advance past the primary.
In this year’s primary, Perez led Morgan 48.9% to 46.6% as of Thursday.
Perez, who is backed by the Service Employees International Union and the Washington Federation of State Employees, two powerful statewide unions, has attacked Morgan for the incumbent’s vote against the state’s new high-earners income tax. 
Morgan, whose endorsers include Gov. Bob Ferguson, could not be immediately reached for comment.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia board adds certain HIV diagnoses to conditions that can bypass Medicaid work requirements
description: Georgia health officials moved to include low-income people living with certain HIV diagnoses among those considered “medically frail,” meaning they would not have to satisfy work requirements to qualify for Medicaid coverage.  HIV had initially been left off the list, which sparked concern from advocates who said they were puzzled by the decision.  At a […]
text:
At a Tuesday meeting, the Georgia Board of Community Health revised its list of conditions that would make a person too "medically frail" to comply with Medicaid work requirements. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderGeorgia health officials moved to include low-income people living with certain HIV diagnoses among those considered “medically frail,” meaning they would not have to satisfy work requirements to qualify for Medicaid coverage. 
HIV had initially been left off the list, which sparked concern from advocates who said they were puzzled by the decision. 
At a Tuesday meeting, the Board of Community Health revised the list before unanimously approving it. The policy is aimed at aligning Georgia’s Pathways to Coverage, a partial Medicaid-expansion with work requirement components, with new federal changes to Medicaid eligibility that were included in President Donald Trump’s tax break and spending cuts package that passed last year.
Under the policy approved Thursday, patients living with HIV that leads to malignant cancer would be automatically granted an exemption to work requirements. People living with general or asymptomatic HIV, as well as the rarely occurring HIV Type 2, could be exempt from work requirements on a case-by-case basis.
Under Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance released in June, able-bodied adults must complete 80 hours of work, community service or education per month to keep their healthcare coverage, something that is already required in Georgia’s Pathways to Coverage program. In that federal guidance, HIV/AIDS alongside cancer, end-stage renal disease and sickle cell disease were listed as potential examples of medical conditions that states could consider including. 
Georgia is the state with the highest rate of new HIV infections in the nation, with about 2,400 newly diagnosed HIV cases in 2024.

title: Colorado issues public health order over tuberculosis case at Aurora ICE facility
description: The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued a public health order on Thursday afternoon ordering The GEO Group to provide information about a recent tuberculosis case in an Aurora immigration detention center. It comes nearly two months after the Adams County Health Department issued an order on the same issue. GEO, the private […]
text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Aurora, operated by private prison firm GEO Group, is pictured on Jan. 30, 2025. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued a public health order on Thursday afternoon ordering The GEO Group to provide information about a recent tuberculosis case in an Aurora immigration detention center.
It comes nearly two months after the Adams County Health Department issued an order on the same issue. GEO, the private company that operates the detention center for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has not complied with that order.
“CDPHE’s priority is protecting everyone connected to the facility, including detained people, employees, contractors, visitors, and the broader community,” CDPHE Executive Director Jill Hunsaker Ryan said in a statement. “We sought to complete this routine investigation collaboratively, just as we would with any other facility in Colorado. Because repeated requests and the county’s public health order have not produced the necessary information, we are taking this additional step to obtain the information needed to protect public health.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The order seeks access to the facility and information about the confirmed TB case in order to complete a public health investigation. GEO and ICE have provided general information that the infected person was isolated, treated and removed from the country, but state and local public health officials are unable to independently verify that without the requested access.
They want specific information about infected people’s test results, treatment and current location, as well as information for contact tracing. The order does not demand that public health workers physically go inside the facility. Federal officials have repeatedly said there are not active cases in the detention center.
“GEO’s denial of access to the detention facility, the individual with confirmed tuberculosis, the individual’s medical information, and other potentially exposed individuals is impeding public health’s ability to conduct a needed disease control investigation to ensure that infection control measures are sufficient to prevent further spread of disease,” the order states.
If GEO does not comply with CDPHE’s order by Aug. 17, the state can take legal action against the private company.
Adams County officials first learned of a laboratory-confirmed active TB case in late June, then issued a county-level public health order. It has been state law for decades that public health officials investigate any active cases of TB. An oversight report from U.S. Rep. Jason Crow’s office then found that 61 people were exposed to the sick person and isolated.
After GEO did not address Adams County’s order, Ryan formally requested clinical information from GEO. Since then, the governor’s office has reached out twice. GEO has not provided the requested underlying action or access. Advocates have been calling on the state to escalate the issue for weeks.
Representatives from GEO and ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC auditor’s office liaison invoked state GOP wishes in some county early voting plans
description: A staff member in the North Carolina auditor’s office used mentions of the wishes of his boss and the state Republican Party in an attempt to sway decisions on at least two counties’ early voting plans. Hundreds of pages produced as a result of public records requests reveal the extent to which Dallas Woodhouse, a […]
text:
Text from former Boliek elections liaison Dallas Woodhouse to Cabarrus Co. elections chair Jay White. A staff member in the North Carolina auditor’s office used mentions of the wishes of his boss and the state Republican Party in an attempt to sway decisions on at least two counties’ early voting plans.
Hundreds of pages produced as a result of public records requests reveal the extent to which Dallas Woodhouse, a former elections liaison for state Auditor Dave Boliek, pushed for early voting sites in particular locations and against them in others.
Woodhouse recommended that counties eliminate Sunday voting hours, advised county chairs on bargaining tactics to reach unanimous approval for early voting plans that Democrats didn’t like, and told two county elections chairs what Republicans on the state Board of Elections would or wouldn’t approve and what the state Republican Party wanted.
Woodhouse also provided county chairs with a sample letter to the editor intended to counter a news story he didn’t like, communicated with the New Hanover county elections board chair about its former director, who was fired this year, and asked the state Republican Party general counsel to help find an early voting site in Cabarrus County.
“Why not?” Woodhouse said when asked about his request to the state GOP lawyer for help. “We ask all kinds of people, ‘Do you know of a place?” Woodhouse said in an interview.
Woodhouse is a political operative and former North Carolina Republican Party executive director whom Boliek hired last year to work with counties as his elections liaison, a newly created position under Boliek’s oversight of the board.
Woodhouse and others on Boliek’s staff, including Kelly Mann, monitored early voting site selection. The documents show Boliek also expressed preferences for particular locations. When Woodhouse wanted counties to delay votes on early voting plans, he used Boliek’s name.
Boliek’s office did not respond to an emailed question about its involvement in early voting plans.
Woodhouse said in an interview that there was never an interest in using early voting plans to tip the scales in Republicans’ favor. The auditor’s office did have a goal of establishing early voting sites in counties’ more rural stretches, he said.
Rather than limiting early voting, this year’s plans will result in expanded hours, Woodhouse said.
Woodhouse was reassigned from his elections liaison job after media reports about his involvement in early voting plans. County elections officials were told Mann would be their new point person in Boliek’s office. Woodhouse resigned from the auditor’s office last month, about a week after his reassignment.
NC auditor’s office in public records fight over Dallas Woodhouse’s work

A controversial 2024 law stripped Democratic Governor-elect Josh Stein of his power to appoint the state Board of Elections ,and gave that power to Boliek, a Republican. The state and county elections board flipped from Democratic to Republican majorities. Boliek appointed all county chairs.
The documents were obtained by American Oversight, a progressive nonprofit organization that specializes in obtaining public records.
American Oversight made several attempts to obtain records from the auditor’s office.
Mentions of GOP interests
Several email and text exchanges reveal an interest in establishing early voting sites in Republican areas or maintaining early voting hours for GOP voters.
In Anson County, Woodhouse cautioned against deep cuts in early voting hours. Anson had adopted a plan that cut early voting to the bare minimum, he said in an interview.
In a text exchange with Anson elections board Chair Kelly Cox Newton on June 10, Woodhouse said he would work on an early voting plan that would win state approval.
The text chain is a back-and-forth about Anson adding more early voting hours, with Woodhouse offering advice on how to convince Democrats on the Anson elections board to go along with a plan.

Woodhouse said in the interview that he was trying to cajole a Republican chair into considering a more robust early voting plan.
“I’m talking their language,” Woodhouse said. He wanted to emphasize that “Republicans vote, too.”
In a May 14 email, David Boone, Durham’s elections board chair, gave Woodhouse a rundown on Durham’s plan, lamenting that it did not add a location where there is “a considerable Republican presence.”

Boone said in an email to NC Newsline that county elections staff provided the density map, and finding early voting sites near Republican voters is required by state law.
“It is required in accordance with NCGS 163-166.35(a) that the State Board consider any disproportionate favoritism based on party, race, ethnic group, or candidacy,” Boone wrote. “As such, staff considers those factors when proposing plans to the Board.”
Boone also sent an email to Courtney Geels, a Republican who ran for Congress in 2022 from the 4th District, statistics on turnout and ages of voters at NC Central and Duke University polling sites for the 2022 general election.
In Wake County, Woodhouse mentioned in a May 19 exchange with Mann that state Board of Elections member Angela Hawkins, the former county chair, was continuing to work on early voting plans for Wake County.

Hawkins was appointed to the state Board of Elections in March. She did not respond to repeated emails or phone calls about her work on Wake’s early voting plan after her appointment to the state board.
The state board votes to approve early voting plans that win unanimous approval. The Wake elections board approved its plan unanimously.  The state board sets early voting plans only for counties where votes are not unanimous.
Rep. Michael Schietzelt, R-Wake, represents a district in northern Wake County. He said in an email he did not ask for a new early voting location.
Woodhouse said Schietzelt was mentioned because he is from the area.
Directions on early voting locations
The auditor’s office pushed Cabarrus County to open a fifth early voting site.
In texts with Cabarrus elections Chair Jay White, Woodhouse asked him to delay a vote on a fall early voting plan while they pursued a site in or around Midland, which is more Republican than the county as a whole.

White told Woodhouse it would be up for discussion.
At its April 27 meeting, White made a motion to table the early voting plan vote for 30 days to allow for time to look for a site in Midland, the board’s minutes show. Four members voted in favor. One was opposed.

Woodhouse also texted Fraley, the state Republican Party lawyer, about the attempt to delay a vote in Cabarrus over an additional site.
“We urge in the strongest possible terms” that they delay a vote on early voting plans, Woodhouse told Fraley in an April 23 text.
“I am on it!” Fraley replied.
The Cabarrus Board stuck with four sites. None are in Midland.
In Jackson County, the auditor’s office was trying to convince two Republicans on the board to reject an early voting site on the Western Carolina University campus.
Republicans said at a board meeting where the campus site was approved in a 3-1 vote that they received “pressure from Raleigh” not to approve the campus site. 
NC Local previously reported that Woodhouse told Jackson County elections chairman Bill Thompson the morning before the board voted in June, “Don’t let them have a vote.”
The recently released texts reveal that Woodhouse’s attempts to delay a vote started weeks before. Woodhouse looked to arrange conference calls with Boliek, Thompson, himself, and another member of the auditor’s staff, and the two Republican members of the Jackson board who wanted the campus early voting site.
It’s unclear whether Boliek participated in those calls. In a May text, Woodhouse said the vote was delayed and they had more time, so a call with Boliek was not necessary.

Thompson was the only member to vote against including the campus site.
In a text, Woodhouse had urged Thompson to “stand strong” if there was a vote. An alternative plan that Thompson voted for without the campus site would win approval from the state board, Woodhouse wrote. The state board would adopt an alternative, a recreation center, that had been used in previous elections, Woodhouse said.

Woodhouse said in a Thursday interview that critics just don’t like Republicans being involved in elections administration.
“They scandalize normal activity even when it serves the same interest they have,” he said.
A lawyer with Boliek’s office told American Oversight the office could not recover all relevant records because Woodhouse deleted some information from his phone even though he was told not to. That information could not be retrieved.
American Oversight denounced the destruction of public records.
“According to the State Auditor’s own general counsel, Dallas Woodhouse deleted public records after being explicitly instructed to preserve them, in direct violation of OSA policy. That is an extraordinary breach of the public trust, and Woodhouse should be held accountable, as should OSA for failing to secure these records sooner,” Chioma Chukwu, American Oversight executive director, said in a statement.
“The records that survived show why their destruction matters,” Chukwu said. “They reveal OSA officials, including Woodhouse, working behind the scenes to influence decisions about early voting, Sunday voting, and polling locations, while communicating with Republican Party officials about some of those decisions. The records also raise serious questions about the extent of Auditor Boliek’s involvement in these efforts.
“These are decisions that directly affect how North Carolinians exercise their right to vote. The public deserves to know the full extent of OSA involvement, what records were destroyed, and whether state officials entrusted with overseeing our elections were using their offices to advance partisan interests,” Chukwu said.
Asked in the interview why he deleted information from his phone, Woodhouse said, ”That assumes something I don’t think is true. I believe I turned over everything.”
