title: Colorado ethics panel begins hearing over Rep. Mandy Lindsay’s handling of caucus bank account
description: A panel of Colorado state representatives began questioning witnesses Thursday in response to an ethics complaint against Democratic Rep. Mandy Lindsay, who is alleged to have mismanaged the internal Democratic House caucus fund. The bipartisan House Ethics Committee in May found probable cause in the complaint, allowing further investigation. “Rep. Lindsay[...]
text:
Colorado state Rep. Mandy Lindsay, an Aurora Democrat, applauds on the floor of the Colorado House of Representatives on the final day of the 2026 legislative session on May 13, 2026, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)A panel of Colorado state representatives began questioning witnesses Thursday in response to an ethics complaint against Democratic Rep. Mandy Lindsay, who is alleged to have mismanaged the internal Democratic House caucus fund.
The bipartisan House Ethics Committee in May found probable cause in the complaint, allowing further investigation.
“Rep. Lindsay made a few mistakes and did not use best practices to manage the petty cash fund,” attorney Jerome DeHerrera said at the start of the meeting. “Rep. Lindsay has acknowledged those mistakes and she’s restored the petty cash fund.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Fellow Democratic Rep. Bob Marshall of Highlands Ranch filed the ethics complaint earlier this year, alleging that Lindsay improperly reimbursed herself thousands of dollars from the caucus fund and breached her fiduciary duty as caucus co-chair. Those reimbursements include over $6,000 for a November 2024 hotel charge that was already debited from the caucus account and $2,500 in dues. She also mistakenly used the caucus card for a motel room in March 2025.
In her response to the complaint, Lindsay wrote that she initially thought the hotel was going to charge her personal card on file, so she wrote a check to herself for reimbursement. She later realized the caucus card, not hers, was charged. She kept the check, however, as partial reimbursement for the “several thousands of dollars” she personally spent as caucus co-chair.
Before the evidentiary hearing, DeHerrera contended that it’s improper for the committee to act as a judicial body, since a court would need to determine if Lindsay was technically a fiduciary, and therefore if she breached that duty. The committee continued with the hearing.
Asked to resign
House Speaker Julie McCluskie, a Dillon Democrat, told lawmakers that she thought the caucus account was “very poorly managed,” and was concerned with Lindsay’s persistent use of personal money for caucus expenses, her poor communication about the account’s low balance, and irregularities with her explanation of the $6,000 check. McCluskie organized the effort to have Will Quinn, compliance director with the state’s Democratic Party, reconcile the account in spring 2025. Quinn ultimately found that the fund had been used for its intended purpose but that basic accounting principles weren’t followed. On Thursday, he said he was less confident in that conclusion, but that the majority of expenses seem in line with caucus purposes.
McCluskie said that after learning about inconsistencies with the caucus fund, she asked Lindsay multiple times to resign as caucus chair. Lindsay did not. McCluskie also said it was difficult to obtain requested receipts and records from Lindsay for that account reconciliation.
“I find some of the explanations and behaviors unusual and concerning,” she said, adding that she didn’t think any of it was criminal.
“Her stepping down (as caucus chair) would have resolved any concerns with the caucus,” she said.
Jaclyn Davison, who served as Lindsay’s aide in 2024, testified on Thursday that she doesn’t remember specific instructions about how to store and track caucus-related receipts. She also said that some caucus food orders were placed on her personal DoorDash account, though not on her personal card.
The committee also heard testimony on Thursday from Quinn, former Lindsay aide Kate Ehrlich and Rep. Brianna Titone, an Arvada Democrat who previously served as caucus co-chair with Lindsay. The committee will continue with the evidentiary hearing on Friday and hear from Marshall, Lindsay and Rep. Junie Joseph, the current caucus co-chair.
When that process is complete, the committee can decide to dismiss the complaint or make recommendations to House leadership about penalties.
Lindsay will not return to the Legislature next year. She lost her district’s Democratic primary to Sarah Woodson.

title: Most of New Mexico’s oil-related water contamination in area around Chaco, advocate tells lawmakers
description: The majority of water contamination linked to oil and gas spills in New Mexico happens in a county that includes much of Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a culturally and spiritually significant site for many Pueblos and tribes that the Trump administration is proposing to open up to more oil and gas operations, an environmental advocate told state la[...]
text:
Pueblo Bonito, constructed by Ancestral Pueblo People a millennia ago, as seen from the air on Sept. 14, 2025. It is the most significant site at Chaco Canyon National Historical Park, which Pueblos and advocates say remains under threat from continued oil and gas development, and worry protections could be scaled back by the new administration. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The majority of water contamination linked to oil and gas spills in New Mexico happens in a county that includes much of Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a culturally and spiritually significant site for many Pueblos and tribes that the Trump administration is proposing to open up to more oil and gas operations, an environmental advocate told state lawmakers on Thursday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Melissa Troutman, a climate and health advocate with WildEarth Guardians, spoke before legislators on the interim Radioactive and Hazardous Materials Committee in Los Alamos. In a presentation, she said that the oil and gas industry reported spills that impacted 15 waterways across the state in 2025. The vast majority of them — 12 — were in San Juan County, which includes Farmington, the Four Corners region and Chaco Culture National Historical Park.
“This is where the majority of water contamination from oil and gas spills is happening in New Mexico, in the place where many rural residents already struggle with access to fresh drinking water,” Troutman told the committee.
The Bureau of Land Management last month opened a two-week window for members of the public to weigh in on its proposal to eliminate or shrink the 10-mile buffer zone that protects Chaco from mining operations.
Native leaders in New Mexico and every member of the state’s federal delegation have sharply criticized the proposal.
New Mexicans protest outside BLM office over proposal to undo Chaco Canyon mining protections

Troutman told lawmakers that produced water — a term that refers to wastewater left over from fracking operations — is the most common liquid spilled by oil and gas operators and that public lands, in particular, are the most affected.
Lea, Eddy, Chaves, San Juan and Rio Arriba counties are the most-polluted in the state, she said, before recommending several legislative solutions, including aggressively enforcing civil penalties and focusing on stopping pollution at the source rather than mitigating it.
“Put down the mop and turn down the tap,” Troutman said. “We’re leaving the tap wide open and we’re relying on more and more mops to help clean up the pollution that’s ongoing.”
How to handle produced water in New Mexico is currently up for debate. The state Water Quality Control Commission earlier this year voted to restart the lengthy rule-making process on whether and how to use the water, which often contains radioactive material and other proprietary chemicals used by oil and gas operators. Officials recently said they hope to begin those hearings in 2027.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New report says federal cuts provide an opportunity — not a crisis — for New Mexico’s nonprofits
description: Federal funding cuts have pitted many of New Mexico’s 8,000 nonprofit organizations against each other in a fight for private foundation funding, but a recent report from a New Mexico consulting firm says that pressure actually presents an opportunity to transform the sector statewide.
text:
Leaders of Prospera Partners, a local consulting firm, told Source NM on Aug. 12, 2026, that federal funding cuts affecting many of the state’s 8,000 nonprofit organizations actually represents an “opportunity for change.” Above: A 2024 performance funded by the Paseo Project, a Taos-based arts nonprofit that received a notice of federal funding cuts in early 2025. (Provided photo)Federal funding cuts have pitted many of New Mexico’s 8,000 nonprofit organizations against each other in a fight for private foundation funding, but a recent report from a New Mexico consulting firm says that pressure actually presents an opportunity to transform the sector statewide. 
New Mexico’s nonprofits employ more than 50,000 people and indirectly contribute roughly $1.4 billion annually to the state’s economy. But spending cuts early in 2025, along with federal requirements aimed at defunding “diversity, equity and inclusion” initiatives, have deprived more than one-third of the state’s nonprofits of much of $300 million in annual federal funding, according to a report publicized Aug. 9 from Prospera Partners, a New Mexico consulting firm for nonprofits and small businesses. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’ve had clients from everything from the food economy, regenerative agriculture, sustainability, climate change, education, gender issues, everything — cut, cut, cut, cut,” Prospera Partners CEO Vicki Pozzebon told Source NM. 
The cuts, including to organizations like the New Mexico Humanities Council, have affected all of the state’s nonprofits, even those that don’t receive any federal funding. That’s because roughly a dozen major foundations in the state are left inundated with requests.
The report, called “A New Way for New Mexico Nonprofits,” draws on years of research as well as a series of interviews with nonprofit leaders. It argues nonprofits can survive the financial hit by coordinating better to reduce overlaps with fellow organizations and reducing the size and influence of their boards, “which often exert unbalanced power over making decisions that affect staff in the everyday,” the report says. 
One major recommendation is that nonprofits need to focus more on implementing solutions instead of talking about them, including through values lists or mission statements that don’t often provide a clear path forward. Report author Eileen Everett told Source NM on Wednesday that nonprofits need to focus on what values like “honesty” and “compassion” mean for an organization’s operations. 
“What does that really look like in action? Because until we have those conversations, nothing can change, because then we don’t know what we’re aiming to do,” she said. 
The report also calls on private foundations to help organizations plan for the future by offering multi-year grants and simplifying application processes. Removing restrictions on what funding can be used for within a nonprofit would also allow organizations to make a bigger impact, the report recommends. 
NM Humanities Council will have to close its doors following latest Trump cuts, director says

The report identified national foundations including Kellogg and McArthur as the main funding sources remaining for statewide nonprofits, as well as the local Santa Fe, Taos, Albuquerque and Los Alamos National Laboratory community foundations, among others. 
Despite the federal cuts and other challenges, Everett said the report offers a path forward for a more sustainable future for a sector in which roughly one in 13 New Mexicans work. 
“There is just such an opportunity for change. It’s maybe our best opportunity we’ve ever had,” she said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota lawmaker wants clemency for men who killed 2 federal agents
description: A North Dakota lawmaker is proposing legislation to ask President Donald Trump to grant clemency for two men convicted in connection with the infamous 1983 Medina shootout that left two federal officers dead. Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, said he plans to present a resolution to a key legislative panel on Monday regarding convicted killers Scott […]
text:
Deputy U.S. Marshal Robert Cheshire Jr., left, and Marshal Kenneth Muir were killed in 1983 while trying to make an arrest in Medina, N.D. (Photos courtesy of State Historical Society of North Dakota)A North Dakota lawmaker is proposing legislation to ask President Donald Trump to grant clemency for two men convicted in connection with the infamous 1983 Medina shootout that left two federal officers dead.
Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, said he plans to present a resolution to a key legislative panel on Monday regarding convicted killers Scott Faul and Yorie Kahl.
Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton. (Photo provided by the North Dakota Legislative Assembly)
The measure states that Faul and Kahl “have remained incarcerated for more than 40 years and their length of imprisonment warrants consideration for executive clemency.”
Clemency encompasses a pardon and a commutation. The measure does not specify a pardon, which wipes away a conviction, or a commutation, which ends a prison sentence early but doesn’t remove a conviction.
“It will be controversial, and I expect it to be,” Magrum told the North Dakota Monitor Thursday. “But I’m committed to doing what’s right.”
Legislative Management, a powerful committee of lawmakers who guide the Legislature’s decisions between sessions, will decide whether to advance Magrum’s measure along with others for a special session starting Sept. 2. Gov. Kelly Armstrong called the special session to restrict kratom and related products.
Magrum said Faul reached out to him after seeing he was one of the state’s three presidential electors during the 2024 election and asked if Magrum had any access to Trump. Magrum told Faul he did not.
North Dakota casts 3 electoral votes for President-elect Donald Trump

“I thought, why don’t I try a resolution and see what the Legislature thinks, and I’m hoping to get sponsorships from legislators in that area,” Magrum said.
Kahl is the son of Gordon Kahl, who was a leader of a group known as Posse Comitatus and was wanted in connection with refusing to pay federal income taxes. On Feb. 13, 1983, the Kahls and others including Faul left a meeting in Medina and encountered law enforcement at a roadblock near town, where the deadly shootout unfolded.
U.S. Marshal Kenneth Muir and Deputy Marshal Robert S. Cheshire Jr. were shot and killed. Three other officers were wounded. Yorie Kahl was shot in the stomach.
Gordon Kahl and the others fled the scene, but his wife and son were arrested shortly afterward. Faul surrendered. Gordon Kahl was killed in June 1983 in a shootout with law enforcement in Arkansas.
A jury convicted Faul and Yorie Kahl of second-degree murder, assaulting marshals and other law enforcement officers and other charges, according to court documents. They were sentenced to two concurrent life sentences and received lesser sentences for the other offenses.
“It’s a tragedy no matter whose side you are on,” Magrum said.
The shooting shocked people around North Dakota for its violence and the deaths of two federal officers in a quiet, sparsely populated state. Medina today is a town of 260 people along a slope of Interstate 94 and a gateway to Chase Lake National Wildlife Refuge.
North Dakota Attorney General Drew Wrigley, who was twice North Dakota’s top federal prosecutor, said the two men “are convicted, rightfully so, of cold-blooded murder of law enforcement officials in an unprovoked, vicious attack.” 
“I would welcome the opportunity to share the actual facts of these vicious crimes with any legislator who is forced to consider this matter,” Wrigley told the Monitor. Faul and Kahl “should die behind bars,” he said.
House Judiciary Chairman Larry Klemin, R-Bismarck, said he does not agree with Magrum’s measure. 
Gov. Armstrong announces special session, emergency actions to ban kratom in North Dakota

“They were criminals and they killed two marshals in a gunfight,” Klemin said. Lawmakers are unlikely to take up such a measure in a special session with limited time, he said.
In a statement, former U.S. Attorney Tim Purdon, who served from 2010-2015, said most North Dakotans remember the shock they felt the day of the shooting and the deaths of the two federal officers
“The idea that their own elected officials would now be seeking to have their murderers released from Federal Prison will be an absolute punch to the stomach,” he said via email.
The resolution says Faul and Kahl’s requests for parole were denied in 2023 and 2025.
Being eligible for parole does not guarantee an inmate will be paroled, Klemin said.
Magrum said he’s spoken to the family members of Faul and Kahl who have expressed exhaustion in waiting for them to be released.
“I know there are victims on the other side, and I’m very sympathetic to them too,” Magrum said. “I just feel that justice is not being served in this case.”
Faul, 73, is held at a federal prison in Michigan. Kahl, 67, is at a federal prison in North Carolina.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com
Reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lawsuit: Six Iowa nursing homes owe a total of $2.1 million in unpaid back rent
description: A group of six Iowa nursing homes owes more than $2.1 million in back rent, two of the homes’ former landlords allege. Summit Healthcare Operating Partnership of California and Fantasia Investment of the Cayman Islands is suing six Iowa nursing homes that operate under the common ownership of Accura Healthcare, an Oklahoma company with offices […]
text:
The corporate headquarters of the West Des Moines nursing home chain Accura Healthcare. (Photo via Google Earth)A group of six Iowa nursing homes owes more than $2.1 million in back rent, two of the homes’ former landlords allege.
Summit Healthcare Operating Partnership of California and Fantasia Investment of the Cayman Islands is suing six Iowa nursing homes that operate under the common ownership of Accura Healthcare, an Oklahoma company with offices in West Des Moines.
Named as co-defendants in the lawsuit are six of Accura’s 27 Iowa facilities, located in Bancroft, Carroll, Cresco, Marshalltown, Milford and Spirit Lake.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Summit and Fantasia allege that in late 2022 and 2023, each of the six care facilities began to fall behind on their rent payments. The plaintiffs allege that instead of pursuing foreclosure they restructured the debt, with the facilities agreeing to pay the back rent over 18 months, beginning in January 2024 and ending in June 2025.
The plaintiffs claim the facilities didn’t make good on that pledge and now owe $2,105,617 in base rent. Rather than pay that debt, the plaintiffs allege, the facilities “have decided to take a shot at escaping their obligations via sophistry.”
Summit and Fantasia say they sold their interest in the group that owned and rented the facilities to Accura in August 2025. As part of that deal, Summit and Fantasia were assigned an interest in the unpaid back rent that was in proportion to their previous stake in the group.
Accura, the plaintiffs alleged, has now taken the position that because the deal between the owners relates to the collection of back rent, they have a right to enforce the terms of that agreement — which, Accura claims, calls for another 18-month repayment plan that would begin in January 2027.
In their lawsuit, Summit and Fantasia argue Accura’s “position makes no sense and is completely unsupported under Iowa law.” They claim the “plain text of the contract” with the ownership group does not obligate them to offer the extended repayment plan and instead merely allows Summit and Fantasia to offer Accura such a deal if they choose to do so.
Given the size of their former stake in the ownership group, Summit argues it has the right to demand immediate payment of 10% of the owed rent or $240,484, and Fantasia has the right to demand payment of 8.5% or $204,412.
The lawsuit seeks monetary judgments in those amounts as well as a court declaration stating that Accura has no rights under the contract between Summit, Fantasia and the ownership group.
Accura: No impact on resident care
In response to the lawsuit, Accura Healthcare said in a written statement the issue is “isolated to a small handful of our Iowa facilities.” The company said that while it “does not comment on specific details of pending litigation, we take all legal obligations seriously and remain fully compliant with our governing contractual agreements. We are actively reviewing the filing with legal counsel and intend to vigorously defend our position through the court system.”
The statement added that the lawsuit will have “no impact whatsoever on our day-to-day operations, our broader network of locations or our financial stability. Our highest priority remains unchanged: providing continuous, high-quality care to our residents and fully supporting our dedicated care teams across every community we serve.”
Some Accura facilities cited for insufficient staffing
In recent years, some Accura facilities have been cited by the state for insufficient staffing levels, which is believed to be one of the biggest contributors to poor quality care. Last year, self-reported staffing data that was analyzed by the nonprofit Long Term Care Community Coalition showed Accura Healthcare of Marshalltown was staffed at 43.5% below expected levels given the residents’ needs there.
On March 12, 2026, the Marshalltown home was cited by the state for insufficient staffing due to a failure to have a registered nurse in the building for at least eight consecutive hours every day. According to the inspectors, the facility failed to meet that standard on 19 separate days between Dec. 1, 2025, and March 8, 2026.
Accura Healthcare of Carroll was cited on April 2, 2026, for insufficient staffing, with inspectors noting that residents had complained of inadequate staffing and long waits of up to two hours for a response to their call lights.
State records indicate that while some of the Accura facilities have struggled to meet federal standards, the company’s CEO, Ted LeNeave, has continued to contribute significant amounts of money to political campaigns and to the industry’s primary political action committee, Iowa HealthPAC.
Campaign finance reports show that since June 2025, LeNeave has made at least $88,500 in political contributions, including $25,000 for the gubernatorial campaign of Randy Feenstra, who in June 2026 lost to Zach Lahn in the Republican primary. During that same period, Accura’s president, Lisa Toti, contributed $17,500.
Accura Healthcare operates more than 40 long-term care and senior housing communities across Iowa, Minnesota, South Dakota and Nebraska.

title: Leader of Nebraska’s embattled Medicaid program resigns
description: LINCOLN — The director of the Nebraska program that oversees Medicaid and long-term care has resigned after less than two years in his position and as Nebraska became the first state to implement more aggressive work requirements for program participants. Drew Gonshorowski, director of the division of Medicaid and Long-Term Care in the Nebraska Department of[...]
text:
DHHS CEO Steve Corsi, left, and Drew Gonshorowski, the state agency’s Medicaid and Long-Term Care director during a news conference in July, 2025. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The director of the Nebraska program that oversees Medicaid and long-term care has resigned after less than two years in his position and as Nebraska became the first state to implement more aggressive work requirements for program participants.
Drew Gonshorowski, director of the division of Medicaid and Long-Term Care in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, plans to pursue opportunities on the East Coast while being closer to family, according to a statement Thursday by Gov. Jim Pillen’s office.
Drew Gonshorowski was appointed in late 2024 to direct Medicaid and Long-Term Care for the Nebraska DHHS. (Photo courtesy of Paragon Health Institute)
Pillen said Gonshorowski understood the fundamentals of strong health care policy and “how best to implement programs that benefit the greatest number of people.”
“His leadership has allowed Nebraska to be first in implementing work requirements and eligibility checks as required through the One Big Beautiful Bill,” the governor said.
States are required to implement those changes by Jan. 1, 2027, but Nebraska began requiring new enrollees to comply on May 1, eight months early. Starting Aug. 1 in Nebraska, the rules also applied to existing enrollees — translating into a likely loss of coverage for some current participants. Gonshorowski had estimated that about 200 Nebraskans will lose Medicaid coverage starting in August under the new rules. 
Health advocates have raised alarms about what they have called Nebraska’s “rushed” implementation. 
The governor’s statement said a search for Gonshorowski’s replacement will begin, and the governor has appointed Jeremy Brunssen, deputy director of finance and program integrity for Medicaid & Long-Term Care, to serve as the division’s interim director.
 According to the statement, Brunssen has been with DHHS for nearly a decade and served as interim director for the same division in 2020.
DHHS CEO Steve Corsi said Gonshorowski has been a tremendous asset to the state.
Gonshorowski began serving as director of Medicaid and Long-Term Care in December 2024. He previously was a policy analyst for Paragon Health Institute and before that with the Heritage Foundation.
In the statement released by Pillen’s office, Gonshorowski said it has been a “privilege and an honor to serve alongside some of the most dedicated workers within MLTC Division.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: ACLU sues State of Iowa over The Satanic Temple’s access to the Capitol rotunda
description: On behalf of The Satanic Temple, the ACLU of Iowa filed a federal lawsuit Thursday alleging the state has blocked the temple’s rights to free speech, nondiscrimination and religious exercise. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, stems from the state’s repeated refusal to grant permission for the […]
text:
A coloring book used as part of The Satanic Temple's winter festivals. (Photo illustration based on image provided by the ACLU of Iowa.)   On behalf of The Satanic Temple, the ACLU of Iowa filed a federal lawsuit Thursday alleging the state has blocked the temple’s rights to free speech, nondiscrimination and religious exercise.
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, stems from the state’s repeated refusal to grant permission for the group to stage what the ACLU of Iowa calls “a family-friendly winter holiday event” in the Iowa Capitol rotunda in the manner of other religious and civic groups.
Named as defendants are the director of the Iowa Department of Administrative Services, Mark Campbell; the department’s former director, Adam Steen; and the department itself.
The lawsuit asks the court to declare that state officials’ denials have violated The Satanic Temple’s constitutional rights under the First and 14th Amendments as well as their rights under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and Iowa Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
It seeks a court order requiring the Iowa Department of Administrative Services to specifically to allow The Satanic Temple to host a holiday event at the Capitol this December, as well as unspecified damages for alleged past violations.
The State of Iowa has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.
In December 2023, The Satanic Temple was permitted to hold a holiday display in the rotunda, alongside other holiday displays such as a Christian nativity scene. Beginning in 2024 and continuing through 2026, the state denied The Satanic Temple’s applications, the lawsuit alleges.
Matt Kezhaya, general counsel for The Satanic Temple, said in a press release Thursday that “the Constitution protects unpopular viewpoints from political power, not the other way around… The First Amendment does not allow government officials to pick and choose which religions may participate in public life.”
Shefali Aurora, ACLU of Iowa staff attorney, said that “when the state makes the public space in the Iowa Capitol Rotunda available for religious holiday events — for example, a Christmas or Hanukkah event — it cannot then deny the same right to other religious groups it disfavors.”

title: Another pipeline parts company accuses Summit of backing out of contract
description: The company planning to build a carbon sequestration pipeline through Iowa is being sued by a second pipeline parts company, this time for $6.6 million.  SCS Carbon Transport LLC, an affiliate of Summit Carbon Solutions, is being sued by Patton Myhre Sourcing, a Texas-based company that Summit allegedly contracted with to purchase custom valves.  Patton […]
text:
A pipeline company in Iowa is being sued for backing out of a contract to purchase parts for its pipeline. (Photo via Getty Images)The company planning to build a carbon sequestration pipeline through Iowa is being sued by a second pipeline parts company, this time for $6.6 million. 
SCS Carbon Transport LLC, an affiliate of Summit Carbon Solutions, is being sued by Patton Myhre Sourcing, a Texas-based company that Summit allegedly contracted with to purchase custom valves. 
Patton Myhre Sourcing alleges Summit is in breach of its purchase contract and now owes more than $6.6 million for the valves it agreed to purchase in 2022 for the pipeline that, at the time of the contract, would have transported sequestered carbon dioxide from biorefineries in Iowa and surrounding states to underground storage in North Dakota. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Summit’s project has faced a number of delays since, including a ban on the use of eminent domain for carbon sequestration pipelines in South Dakota, and attempts to pass a similar law in Iowa. 
In May, the company announced it was changing its route to instead go through Nebraska and end in Wyoming. 
According to the lawsuit, Summit requested a series of payment delays and accommodations as the carbon sequestration pipeline project “stalled.” In 2025, the petition alleges, Summit said it “was electing not to pursue the project and no longer wanted the valves.” 
“Summit simply chose not to pay,” Patton Myhre Sourcing alleges in the lawsuit. 
The lawsuit alleges Summit agreed to pay more than $7.3 million to Patton Myhre for 251 “specialized” valves. Patton Myhre is requesting $6.6 million in damages which comprise the $2.3 million it alleges Summit still owes for the valves themselves, $3.6 million in storage costs and more in interest and freight costs. 
“Summit’s delinquency caused significant financial strain on Patton Myhre, which had already incurred substantial costs to manufacture and store the valves,” the filed complaint reads. 
The lawsuit alleges that more than a year after Summit paused its payments and relationship with Patton Myhre, “nothing has changed for the better.” 
The lawsuit said Summit has not given an indication of “un-pausing” payment obligations and “in fact” the company’s plan to use the pipeline for enhanced oil recovery, rather than carbon storage, represents “a different use for which the valves were not designed.” 
This is the second pipeline parts company that has sued Summit for failing to uphold a purchase agreement. 
In 2024, the Arkansas pipe manufacturer Welspun Tubular sued Summit for $15 million after the company canceled its agreement with the pipe maker. The companies failed to reach a settlement, leading the case to be tried in June in a Delaware court. A decision on the case has not been issued. 
The most recent case against Summit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Summit Carbon Solutions did not respond to a request for comment and as of Thursday, it had not filed a response to the petition from Patton Myhre.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: As voters cast ballots, advocates push to open the state’s closed primary system
description: More than 1 million people have already voted ahead of Florida’s Aug. 18 primaries but, in the marquee races for governor and senator, millions registered as No Party Affiliation (NPA) won’t be able to participate because of the state’s closed primary election system. And that’s not right, says Villa Johnson of the League of Women […]
text:
Hired security personnel wait for voters outside the Leon County Supervisor of Elections office on Nov. 3, 2020, in Tallahassee. (Photo by Mark Wallheiser/Getty Images)More than 1 million people have already voted ahead of Florida’s Aug. 18 primaries but, in the marquee races for governor and senator, millions registered as No Party Affiliation (NPA) won’t be able to participate because of the state’s closed primary election system.
And that’s not right, says Villa Johnson of the League of Women Voters of Sarasota County.
“This year our closed system will shut out 4 million voters that are not registered with the party or with a minority party,” she said in a Zoom conference call Thursday. “That’s 28% of the electorate, but even that number doesn’t tell the whole story. Many thousands of voters register with a party they don’t support just so they have a voice in the election.”
Thursday’s virtual press conference was organized by Open Primaries, a national advocacy group working to promote open and nonpartisan primary systems that let all voters participate. The group has active lawsuits in Pennsylvania, Oregon, and Maryland challenging use of public funds for “private elections,” said John Opdycke, president of Open Primaries.
The organization is contemplating filing such a lawsuit in Florida, he added.
The Sunshine State is one of only 10 with completely closed primary systems, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission.
Facing a more than a 1.5 million voter registration gap with Republicans, Florida Democratic Party (FDP) Chair Nikki Fried announced a year ago that the party was considering opening its primary election system.
“As soon as this election cycle is over, then we’ll continue a conversation  to decide on where the party is,” Fried told the Phoenix last weekend in Tampa. “Every single day, more and more people are registering as independents. I think a real conversation needs to happen within our party.”
Opdycke says that 10,000 Americans change their voter registration from either the Republican or Democratic parties to independent every week. “As the number of independents rise, the fact that they’re shut out of voting in so many states has become more and more controversial,” he said.
John Marvin is state coordinator for Florida Open Primaries. After the FDP discussed the idea last year of opening its primaries, his organization conducted an online survey of Democratic and independent voters, receiving more than 600 responses from each of those groups, he said. Some 90% of both Democrats and independents said Florida should adopt open primaries and more than 80% of each group said Democrats should unilaterally open its primaries if that were the only choice.
Fried sees “some gray area” in Florida statute as to whether a political party could change to an open primary.
“The Republicans have already said that they will sue us, and so we would be prepared for a legal challenge to overturn that statute as being unconstitutional,” she said.
Open Primaries is looking for a legislative sponsor for an open primaries bill in the Florida Legislature next year, Opdycke said, although he wasn’t certain exactly what it would say.
However, given the Republican Party of Florida’s vow to challenge any such proposal, it’s difficult to see how far such a bill would advance in the GOP-controlled Florida Legislature.

name: VTDigger
title: A quilt project in Brattleboro aims to sew connection across prison walls
description:
“Fractured, Not Broken,” a collaboration between residents and incarcerated people, combines quilting and music as a means of restorative justice.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A quilt project in Brattleboro aims to sew connection across prison walls.
text:
Brattleboro locals participated in a community stitch event, adding stitches and messages for the incarcerated people at Springfield prison. Courtesy photo by Katie Kohnfelder/Community News Service.

This story by Emily Rodin was first published in the Community News Service on Aug. 6, 2026.
Via Community News Service, a University of Vermont journalism internship, and Report for America
A quilt stitched by incarcerated Vermonters and Brattleboro community members will go on display in September after nearly a year of collaborative work designed to build connections across prison walls.
From September 2025 to April 2026, seven incarcerated quilters participated in a workshop led by Marie-Pierre Py, a restorative justice practitioner with Interaction: Youth Services & Restorative Justice. The workshop encouraged participants to design and piece together a quilt that incorporates personal experiences and stories. 
The colorful quilt measuring 7 feet, 5 inches by 8 feet, 6 inches features cyanotypes of flowers and leaves that weave through each individual quilter’s block. Its border is made up of the score for “Quilted Forest,” a piece of music composed by Alli Cooper-Ellis, a University of Vermont student who helped conduct research on life in the prison. 
Incarcerated people who participated in the project weren’t made available for interviews. But one quilter’s artist statement said he chose symbols that illustrate his experience behind bars. 
“From the very beginning, I knew I wanted to depict a ship coming home from a long, hard voyage. I’m ready to go home. And ready to find peace,” the statement says. 
Py has been conducting support groups at Southern State Correctional Facility in Springfield for about three years. She realized that many men were interested in participating but felt intimidated by the idea of being vulnerable in a talking circle. 
As a quilter herself, Py thought an art project would be the perfect way for the men to nonverbally express themselves. 
“Working with your hands and making art is therapeutic. It’s a way to allow things to start moving, even if you don’t have words for them yet,” Py said. 
Called “Fractured, Not Broken,” the quilt project is a partnership with the Prison Research and Innovation Network, which is collecting data on safety, transparency and accountability at the Springfield prison. 
As part of the project, researchers at the University of Vermont have been conducting prison climate surveys. The results showed that approximately 85% of incarcerated people said they do not feel prepared for release, according to Abigail Crocker, director of UVM’s Justice Research Center. 
“If you think about conditions people need to thrive, feeling like you’re part of community and the sense of belonging is one of them,” Crocker said. 
Data points from the survey’s findings are stitched onto the back of the quilt along with cyanotype of a Margaret Wheatley poem called “Turning to One Another,” Crocker said. 
Last month, Brattleboro locals participated in community stitch events where they added stitches and wrote messages in the quilt for the incarcerated men. 
Py said this part of the project aims to build awareness and relationships between people inside and outside prison walls. 
Interaction volunteer Suzanne Ruse participated in the community stitch at July’s Gallery Walk and was especially moved when the mother of one of the incarcerated quilters “sat right down and started stitching,” she said.
“It was incredible. It was folks of every age there. And everybody sitting around this beautiful quilt and adding their piece to it,” Ruse said. 
Katie Allaway, a longtime volunteer for Circles of Support and Accountability, a support program for formerly incarcerated people, also attended the event. She said she stitched hearts onto the quilt as a symbol of love and support for the incarcerated quilters. 
“I think for a very long time, our society in the United States has thought that healing injustice is something you do on your own,” Allaway said. “Participating in healing needs to be a community process.”
The completed quilt will be featured in an exhibit at the Brattleboro Museum & Art Center from Sept. 9 through Nov. 1, with a celebration planned Oct. 15. 
The exhibit will also feature audio components, including Cooper-Ellis’ song and “Redemption Road,” written by an incarcerated quilter whose refrain is featured on the quilt. The latter song was first performed at the prison in April by participants in a weekly music class. 
Another performance was recorded at Brattleboro’s Community Bible Chapel and performed by Mel Dawson of the Greater Falls Community Justice Center, the Rev. Matt Miller and members of a peer-led COSA group in Brattleboro.
James Cashatt and Bob Havens, who are both on the Vermont sex offender registry and served time at Springfield prison, are part of the COSA group that helped record “Redemption Road” at the chapel. Havens accompanied the song with guitar. 
Both Cashatt and Havens said they felt a strong connection with the song’s plaintive melody as well as the lyrics. 
“I have regret about things that I did and questions about redemption, and that’s kind of what the song is about,” Havens said. 
While the quilt project is meant to showcase the shared humanity between incarcerated people and the rest of society, both Cashatt and Havens acknowledged that some may struggle with that concept due to the nature of their crimes. But they said they hope the message comes through in the music.
“I pray that it does make us appear to be just as we are: human beings who are doing everything they can to become better than who they were,” Cashatt said. 
After the exhibit at the Brattleboro Museum & Art Center, Py hopes the quilt will be displayed at more venues and ultimately return to the prison’s visitor center. 
Emily Rodin is an intern for UVM’s Community News Service through Report for America’s Local News Internship Program.

name: VTDigger
title: Long-vacant ‘pit’ in downtown Newport nears new chapter with purchase plan
authors: K. Fiegenbaum and Alan J. Keays
description:
Caught up in scandal, the city block known as “the pit” has been empty for a decade. Now it’s slated for purchase by the Northeastern Vermont Development Association, which plans to transfer the property to the city or a development partner. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Long-vacant ‘pit’ in downtown Newport nears new chapter with purchase plan.
text:
An undeveloped vacant lot in downtown Newport in March 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
On a recent summer afternoon in downtown Newport, portions of Main Street were bustling: Vendors were setting up for the Wednesdays on the Waterfront concert series, neighbors chatted at a cafe, and visitors were enjoying the town’s flower displays and sweeping views of Lake Memphremagog.
However, one part of downtown — “the pit” — sat quiet and empty, as it has for over a decade. The razed city block, tied to the EB-5 visa scandal, is surrounded by a tall chain-link fence, its concrete foundations taken over by nature with stands of poplar trees and sumac.
Now, a path forward for the site — also known as “the Hole” — has emerged in an announcement Thursday: The Northeastern Vermont Development Association plans to purchase the property for $1.1 million, pending approval by a federal judge. The group’s goal is to transfer the property to the city of Newport or another development partner.
“We are thrilled,” said Newport Mayor Rick Ufford-Chase late Thursday afternoon. “This is the first step of many that will have to take place to actually make something constructive happen on that property, but nothing could happen until we gained control of the pit and put it in the hands of folks locally to make decisions.”
The NVDA expects to complete the purchase of the property in October and immediately begin assessing the site’s current state and work needed to remediate it. According to Thursday’s press release, the city will conduct a market study to inform a future use for the large property consistent with its master plan. The area will now be known as the “Newport Development Block.”
According to Ufford-Chase, the master plan calls for the centerpiece of Newport’s downtown development efforts to be housing. The plan calls for 400-plus units to be built in the downtown core over the next 15 years, along with a hotel, commercial space and a recreation center for the community. 
“I expect this block will be the heart of that redevelopment strategy,” he said, adding that the master plan aims to make the city’s downtown “livable and walkable, so that people could live downtown and find what they need right here.”
According to a fact sheet from the NVDA, the organization hopes construction could begin as early as 2028.
“This is just the beginning of a new future for the City of Newport” and the Northeast Kingdom, said Ufford-Chase in the press release. “This news, together with the $3 million dollar grant we were awarded by the Northern Border Regional Commission to redevelop our infrastructure on Main Street, lays the necessary groundwork for the next steps. While the City focuses on making those improvements, our team will turn its attention to seeking developers to build out the property.”
To purchase the property, the NVDA received a $1 million Rural Industry Development Program grant from the state’s Department of Economic Development, also announced Thursday. The NVDA will supplement the state grant to cover the property’s purchase and carrying costs and has grant money from the Environmental Protection Agency to complete an environmental study and site clean-up efforts, according to the fact sheet.
A lot of state agencies, organizations and officials had to cooperate to make the sale a reality, Ufford-Chase said.
Michael Goldberg, a court-appointed receiver overseeing the Main Street property in Newport for the past 10 years, submitted a court filing Thursday in support of the sale.
“The Receiver has been marketing this land for years,” Goldberg wrote. “The Receiver has been in discussions with the Northeastern Vermont Development Association, Inc. for over a year and this is the only legitimate purchase offer for the land.”
The proceeds of the sale will go to investors who put money into a development that was announced for the site over a decade ago and were defrauded in the EB-5 visa scheme, as well as to other creditors, Goldberg added.
“Further,” the receiver wrote in the filing, “as this is the last piece of property in the receivership estate to be sold, this will now allow the Receiver to finalize and close the case.”
The Main Street property in Newport was among several properties put into receivership in 2016 when federal and state regulators started enforcement actions against the developers who were accused of misusing tens of millions of dollars from foreign investors in the state’s largest investment fraud scandal.
The developers had raised hundreds of millions of dollars for the various projects through the federal EB-5 visa program over several years. That visa initiative allows foreign investors to obtain green cards, or permanent U.S. residency, in exchange for putting money into rural development projects.
However, due to the fraud many investors were out both their money and their chance of obtaining green cards.

‘The pit’ in Newport on July 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger.

The Newport city block was razed more than 10 years ago as part of a plan to redevelop the site, then known as the Spates block. At that time, developers proposed turning the city block into a four-story development with retail and office spaces along with a hotel and restaurant.
Some of the series of projects proposed by the developers did take place. However, the proposed redevelopment of the Main Street property in Newport never materialized as regulators halted what they termed a “Ponzi-like” scheme.
Goldberg has since sold all the other properties off, including two ski resorts in the Northeast Kingdom: Jay Peak Resort and Burke Mountain Resort. 
Goldberg wrote in the filing Thursday that the sale of the 1.31-acre property in Newport would be “AS IS.” According to the receiver, the closing will be on or before Oct. 12.  
Goldberg’s filing was made in federal court in Miami, where the receivership case is pending. The case was brought in Florida because that was where Ariel Quiros, one of the developers, lived at the time. 
Quiros owned Jay Peak at the time. He, former resort President Bill Stenger and William Kelly, a Quiros adviser, later all reached plea deals to federal charges and were sentenced to prison for their roles in the scandal. They have all since been released. 
The Newport City Council will hold a hybrid informational meeting on the announcement at 6 p.m. Monday at the Gateway Center in Newport and online.
The meeting will “be about helping local folks to understand exactly where we are in the process and set expectations and answer their questions about how we got to this moment,” said Ufford-Chase.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: ‘Nuclear tariff’ on power bills would pay for utilities to explore small reactors
description: State regulators will decide next month whether to add a small fee to monthly electricity bills from Louisiana’s three major utility companies. The Public Service Commission postponed a vote planned Wednesday on what they’ve labeled a nuclear tariff. It would add a 20-cent fee to the monthly bills of all Entergy Louisiana, Cleco and SWEPCO […]
text:
Steam rises from the cooling tower at Entergy's Grand Gulf Nuclear Station, located just south of Vicksburg, as it generates electricity for Mississippi, Louisiana and others on the MISO grid. (Photo courtesy of Entergy Corp.)State regulators will decide next month whether to add a small fee to monthly electricity bills from Louisiana’s three major utility companies.
The Public Service Commission postponed a vote planned Wednesday on what they’ve labeled a nuclear tariff. It would add a 20-cent fee to the monthly bills of all Entergy Louisiana, Cleco and SWEPCO customers.
The utility companies would use the money to pay for feasibility studies, potential site assessments, economic modeling and other early-stage work to determine if small modular nuclear reactors and microreactors are cost-effective in Louisiana.
Smaller-scale modular reactors, or SMRs, have up to 300 megawatts capacity, or about one-third of the output of a classic reactor. On average, one megawatt can power roughly 1,000 homes, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.
Microreactors can generate up to 20 megawatts of electricity. They are generally portable and used in remote locations or for facilities such as data centers. Most can operate independently of the public electric grid. 
Commissioner Eric Skrmetta, R-Metairie, who came up with the idea for the tariff, placed it on the commission’s agenda just days before Wednesday’s meeting, though it stems from a March proposal in which he directed PSC staff to look into ways utilities could embrace more nuclear power generation.
Meta can keep its data center details private, PSC decides

Nuclear power is on average the most expensive form of electricity in the U.S. even after factoring in federal tax subsidies, according to a 2026 analysis by the investment firm Lazard. That analysis is based on conventional nuclear power plants, not the much smaller, portable reactors into which investors are pouring research dollars. 
President Donald Trump has called on state leaders to promote nuclear energy, and Louisiana was one of a handful recently tapped to join a federal initiative to encourage industry investment. Skrmetta has co-chaired Trump’s campaign in Louisiana for the past three elections, and the president recently appointed him to a position with the U.S. Department of Energy.
The commissioners addressed Skrmetta’s proposal at the end of Wednesday’s meeting that saw contentious debate and a party-line vote to allow social media giant Meta maintain its veil of secrecy over its Hyperion data center project and the large number of new power plants Entergy Louisiana wants to build to power it. 
Commissioner Davante Lewis, D-Baton Rouge, asked to postpone the nuclear tariff proposal, saying he’s not opposed to studying it but feels utility companies should pay for their own research rather than sticking Louisiana ratepayers with the bill. 
Commissioner Jean-Paul Coussan, R-Lafayette, backed Lewis’ concern, saying he needed more time to look into the matter.
“There may be other funding sources that make this negligible and do not impact the ratepayer at the extent this does,” Coussan said.  
Commissioner Mike Francis, R-Crowley, then prodded Coussan about whether he will support the tariff if he can’t find other funding sources.
“I’m a strong ‘maybe,’” Coussan said, drawing laughter from the large crowd in attendance.
The commission plans to vote on the tariff proposal at its next regular meeting Sept. 16.

text:
Quanta Services crews building the Boardman to Hemingway transmission line repositioned their equipment to help crews fight wildfires along the Oregon-Idaho border. (Photo courtesy of Quanta Services)Crews building the Boardman to Hagerman transmission line recently repositioned their crews and heavy equipment to help the effort to fight wildfires along the Oregon-Idaho border, company officials said. 
Idaho governor, Forest Service chief say significant wildfires are stretching resources thin

Crews and companies with Quanta Services, MG Dyess, PJ Helicopters, Summit Line Construction and Probst Electric all contributed to the effort to help fight wildfires, officials with Quanta Services said in a news release issued Wednesday. 
Working in partnership with Idaho Power, the crews and companies cleared land and cut access roads for firefighters and used aircraft to move equipment into the field. 
“They showed up with four dozers, water trucks, road blading equipment,” said Angelique Rood, vice president of corporate services and communications at Idaho Power. “At Idaho Power, we pride ourselves on being good neighbors and helpful members of every community we serve. Quanta’s actions to help those neighbors and communities reflect our values.”
In several cases, personnel and crews from the companies volunteered to help out alongside several local community members. 
“I live in northeastern Oregon,” said Brett Beveridge, construction manager with Summit Line Construction. “This is my community.”
The response from the construction crews helped protect an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 acres of land. 
“Our longstanding partnership with Idaho Power reflects the value of working together to strengthen and support the communities we serve,” Karl Studer, president of electric power at Quanta Services, said in a written statement. “That partnership positioned our crews and equipment to respond quickly when help was needed. Our ability to step up and assist in moments like these is a reflection of the partnership and our shared commitment to the communities we serve.”
Earlier this month, U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz and Idaho Gov. Brad Little said firefighting resources are stretched thin due to several significant wildfires that are burning in the Western United States.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State says it spent nearly $900k on Tulsa, Oklahoma City homeless camp cleanups
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The state spent nearly $900,000 to clear homeless encampments in Oklahoma’s largest cities last year, according to letters sent by the state’s chief operating officer.  Nearly identical letters were sent Monday to the chiefs of the Oklahoma City and Tulsa police departments warning that the state spent over $375,000 and $523,000, respectively[...]
text:
Crews use a front loader to clean up a former homeless camp on state property in Tulsa. (Screenshot of Operation SAFE video footage)OKLAHOMA CITY — The state spent nearly $900,000 to clear homeless encampments in Oklahoma’s largest cities last year, according to letters sent by the state’s chief operating officer. 
Nearly identical letters were sent Monday to the chiefs of the Oklahoma City and Tulsa police departments warning that the state spent over $375,000 and $523,000, respectively, to clear a homeless encampment on state property in each city. The encampments were cleared as part of Operation SAFE, a program announced in September by Gov. Kevin Stitt to clear state property using state resources and troopers with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol. 
While the letters penned by Chief Operating Officer David Ostrowe don’t demand immediate payments, it warns the state will attempt to pass legislation to recover costs for any past, present or future homeless encampment cleanups conducted by the state.
Operation SAFE also conducted cleanup efforts in Norman, but a city spokesperson said they have not yet received a letter from the state. It was not immediately clear why Norman did not receive a letter or how much cleanup costs totaled there. 
The state coordinated with a nonprofit for the homeless encampment cleanup efforts in Oklahoma City, but not with the municipal governments. Officials said the state sometimes conducted its cleanup operations without warning, according to reporting by Oklahoma Watch. 
David Ostrowe is pictured. (Provided by the Oklahoma Governor’s Office)
Ostrowe’s office referred questions to the Governor’s Office. 
Tevis Hillis, a Stitt spokesperson, did not answer specific questions from Oklahoma Voice but said the state has shielded cities from the costs of providing mental health and social services. 
“The least the municipality can do is keep the streets clean and safe,” Hillis said in a statement. 
Ostrowe wrote in the letter that the state expenditures were necessary because local police failed to “enforce the law and address these encampments.” When the city fails to act, the cost is shifted to all taxpayers, he wrote. 
“The State has repeatedly stepped in to remove dangerous and unsanitary encampments, dispose of abandoned property and waste, restore public areas, and address conditions that Oklahoma City has allowed to persist,” Ostrowe wrote in one of the letters. “Each time the City refuses to act, the financial burden is shifted from Oklahoma City to taxpayers across all 77 counties. That arrangement cannot continue.”
Tulsa received the same letter except it was personalized to that city.
Tulsa Mayor Monroe Nichols in a statement said the city already dedicates resources to maintain state property and has spent about $300,000 annually to clean state highways. 
“This should not be a competition over who can send the other government the largest bill,” he said in a statement. 
He said Tulsa is actively doing its part to address homelessness and public safety and has been able to move hundreds of people out of homelessness and closed 10 encampments. 
“The State made a decision to conduct a large-scale cleanup of property that it owns and maintains,” Nichols said. “It is difficult to understand how the City of Tulsa then becomes financially responsible for that cleanup simply because the State wants to be reimbursed for their own expenses.”
The City of Tulsa has also expended resources to respond to the “consequences” of Operation SAFE, like locating displaced individuals and connecting them to resources for medication, identification and more. 
“If the State’s position is that governments should simply bill one another for work they believe the other should have done, then we are certainly capable of having that conversation – and we can start by sending the State the bill for the work the City is already doing on its property,” Nichols said.
A spokesperson for Oklahoma City and the Tulsa Police Department declined to comment Thursday. A spokesperson for the Oklahoma City Police Department did not immediately return a request for comment. 
Letter – Chief Ron C. Bacy

Before that, he was a policy adviser and communications director for Armstrong from 2020-2024, when Armstrong was […]
text:
Conner Swanson has been named commissioner of the North Dakota Department of Human Services. (Photo courtesy of the governor's office)Gov. Kelly Armstrong has appointed a longtime aide to lead the Department of Health and Human Services, North Dakota’s largest state agency.
Conner Swanson has been a senior adviser to Armstrong since he took office in December 2024. Before that, he was a policy adviser and communications director for Armstrong from 2020-2024, when Armstrong was North Dakota’s sole U.S. House member. His appointment takes effect Aug. 29.
Swanson will be tasked with leading an agency comprising a $5.7 billion two-year budget and more than 2,000 employees. The department in the last year has been busy managing measles cases, rolling out rafts of federal money aimed at improving rural health care and implementing federal changes to Medicaid and food assistance programs.
More than $50 million available in new rural health grants

Swanson succeeds Pat Traynor, who began as interim HHS commissioner in June 2025, and will return to his job as executive director of the Dakota Medical Foundation, from which he had taken a civil service leave.
Traynor’s annual salary was $250,000; Swanson will earn $225,000 annually, according to the Governor’s Office.
“From Capitol Hill to the State Capitol, Conner has navigated complex policy issues with skill and a depth of understanding that will serve North Dakotans well – a great example being his behind-the-scenes leadership on the Rural Health Transformation Program that is deploying hundreds of millions of dollars in federal grants to improve health outcomes across our state,” Armstrong said in a statement.  
Swanson also has served as a senior adviser to the U.S. House Budget Committee and in the U.S. Interior Department during the first Trump administration. He also was assistant to the North Dakota House Republican Majority Leader Al Carlson, in 2015. He has a master’s degree in natural resources management from North Dakota State University.
“Since December 2024, I’ve worked closely with the department through my role with the Governor’s Office,” Swanson said in a statement. “I have seen firsthand their commitment to the mission and the people we serve, and I am thrilled to join HHS and help build upon that energy and dedication.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts is second state to appoint heat resilience officer
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: Schlick will coordinate state government agencies and work with communities to "prepare for rising temperatures, protect public health and reduce the impacts of extreme heat," according to a press release from Gov. Maura Healey's office.
text:
AS MASSACHUSETTS COPES with the prolonged impacts of rising temperatures, the Healey administration on Thursday named Katie Schlick as the state’s first heat resilience officer.
Schlick will coordinate state government agencies and work with communities to “prepare for rising temperatures, protect public health and reduce the impacts of extreme heat,” according to a press release from Gov. Maura Healey’s office. She will report to state Climate Chief Melissa Hoffer and state Public Health Commissioner Dr. Robbie Goldstein.
“Amidst another record-breaking year of heat and smoke, Massachusetts is taking bold, coordinated action to protect and uplift our communities,” Schlick said in the press release.
July was the hottest month recorded in US history and extreme heat kills more Americans than the combined effect of hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, and other weather hazards, according to Hoffer. Impacts from rising heat include emergency department visits for heat-related illnesses, drought-induced crop losses, threats to water supplies, railways and runways, and stressed forest systems, with Hoffer calling these impacts “what climate change looks like.”
In 2024, Arizona became the first state to name chief heat officer.
“Extreme heat is becoming more common, more intense and more dangerous in Massachusetts,” Healey said in the press release. “We need to be ready for what that means for our families and communities. This new role will lead our work to prepare for extreme heat and make sure we’re doing everything we can to keep Massachusetts and our residents safe.” 
Most recently, Schlick was a federal and external affairs associate and resilience policy lead with the US Climate Alliance. Before that, Schlick was a special assistant to the White House National Climate Advisor from January 2023 to January 2025. 
The salary for the role is $90,000 and is fully funded by the Boston Foundation, according to Healey’s office.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Business and labor groups both backed Golden in 2024. Now they’re split over LePage v. Dunlap
description: With U.S. Rep. Jared Golden on his way out of Congress, the business and labor groups that united behind him are once again at odds in the 2nd District.  The U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsed Republican Paul LePage in the race Thursday. In contrast, Democrat Matt Dunlap has the backing of several major unions. It’s […]
text:
Former Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican nominee running for Maine's 2nd Congressional District, touted his business experience at a press conference in Fairfield Thursday. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)With U.S. Rep. Jared Golden on his way out of Congress, the business and labor groups that united behind him are once again at odds in the 2nd District. 
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsed Republican Paul LePage in the race Thursday. In contrast, Democrat Matt Dunlap has the backing of several major unions.
It’s another front where the two candidates are at odds in their approach — LePage emphasizing his business experience, while Dunlap focuses on labor.
Steve McAllister, vice president of the Eastern Region for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, said LePage was an “outstanding advocate” for business interests when he was governor.
“He led the way on major things that benefited the small business community, things like permitting reform — which is going to be one of the first things he’s going to work on when he’s in Congress, because that’s something that’s coming up here,” McAllister said. 
He said LePage is “exactly what we are looking for at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.” 
“Paul LePage is going to be ready on day one,” McAllister continued. “He knows exactly what the people of Maine need. He’s going to be a big force in Washington D.C. Helping our business community.”
The endorsement is not entirely out of line for the chamber. Although the organization endorsed Golden in 2024, in 2016 and 2018 the chamber endorsed Republican former U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin. 
In 2024, McAllister said Golden ​​”has been a relentless champion for job creators, Main Streets and the workforce” in the district. 
That year, Golden also got the endorsement of Maine AFL-CIO, Maine’s largest labor organization representing more than 200 local unions and 42,000 workers and retirees.
This year, the Maine AFL-CIO has endorsed Dunlap, pointing to his record of supporting workers. 
“Falling union density has been a direct cause of rising economic inequality over the past five decades,” Maine AFL-CIO President Cynthia Phinney said in a statement. “When unions are strong, they set wage standards for entire industries and occupations, turning bad jobs into good jobs.” 
Phinney said the union plans to work with Dunlap to push back on attacks on federal workers’ collective bargaining rights and address the affordability issues impacting Mainers. 
LePage touts pro-business record
At a press conference Thursday, LePage cited his experience in the private sector, ranging from manufacturing to food service. 
“I’ve worried about payrolls,” said LePage, who before being elected in 2010 was a business consultant and general manager of the Marden’s discount chain. “I’ve balanced budgets. I’ve hired people. I’ve fired people. It’s just part of what the world of business is all about.”
And like many other issues, he pointed to his two terms as governor as evidence of how he will act in Congress. 
“When I became governor, my goal was to make government smaller, not bigger,” LePage said. “It was to make Maine workers keep more money in their pockets, and businesses could expand and create new jobs and better jobs here in Maine.” 
“I wanted every small business to know one thing: Maine was open for business,” he added, referencing the slogan he added to the state’s welcome signs as governor.
He also pointed to the rollback in regulations and significant tax cuts passed under his watch as examples of his pro-business policies, though economists at the time said those cuts pushed the burden onto local property taxpayers and contributed to a two-year, $900 million budget shortfall.
In addition to his pro-business policies, as governor LePage also pushed for a so-called “Right to Work” policy, weakening the state workers’ union, and dramatically cut state worker pension payments.

Dunlap’s focus on workers
When asked about economic policy, Dunlap is quick to focus on his support for workers. 
“I was a proud union member for ten years, and my family is union through and through—so I know firsthand that unions are how working families get ahead,” Dunlap said in a statement accepting the Maine AFL-CIO endorsement.
“Matt Dunlap gets it,” Grant Provost, vice president of Maine AFL-CIO, said in a statement. “He knows it is wrong that the Trump administration is stripping away collective bargaining rights from federal workers. In Congress Matt will fight alongside Maine workers to build a country where all working people are treated fairly, with decent paychecks and benefits, safe jobs, dignity, and equal opportunities.” 
Dunlap has also won the backing of the National Nurses Association, the National Education Association and the North Atlantic States Regional Council of Carpenters.
Speaking at the Maine AFL-CIO committee on political education convention in June, Dunlap said if elected he will fight to protect workers and unions. 
“Over the last few decades, the entire economy has slowly gotten tilted against us because you don’t have an army of lobbyists in Washington working for you,” Dunlap said. “That’s what Congress is supposed to do, and that’s what I intend to do.”
Tariffs
At the Thursday press conference, LePage was asked a question about President Donald Trump’s tariff policy, which has already strained many Maine business owners ahead of a new 50% tax on many Canadian imports set to take effect next week.
LePage said tariffs are a good negotiating tool, but that Canada is “not negotiating.” LePage said during the first Trump administration, he was an intermediary in tariff discussions with Canada, and would look to bring that experience to Congress now.
“Do I want tariffs? I want them to go away as quick as possible,” LePage said. But, he continued, “both nations have to be able to trade fairly.”
In a statement Thursday, Dunlap characterized LePage’s position as being “‘all for the tariffs’ that are currently jacking up prices for working Mainers and making it impossible for small businesses to succeed.”
In an April primary debate, Dunlap said targeted tariffs to protect specific Maine industries have been useful in the past, but broad tariffs just raise prices for working families in Maine. 
“I think overall, it’s a 19th Century policy which has sort of lost its primacy in the 21st Century,” Dunlap said. “And we should really avoid tariffs, unless we need to use them for some limited period of time to protect a specific industry or specific product.”
