name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: ‘We can’t wait any longer’: Latest Pa. budget lacks home health nurse funding increase
description: The commonwealth needs more home health nurses, but industry lobbyists say that lagging state Medicaid reimbursements make recruiting and retention difficult.
text:
Scarlotte Sells plays with a toy in her Hanover home while Michele Werner, a regional director with Angels of Care, watches on July 31, 2026. The six-year-old has an extremely rare genetic disorder and requires round-the-clock care, but home health nurses are scarce in rural York County. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Like many other 6-year-old girls, Scarlotte Sell’s excited to start first grade and laughs easily. She loves digging outside for worms and bugs to feed her pet turtle, Carlos, and running in the yard with her dog, Rocky.
Scarlotte also has an extremely rare genetic disorder — one of three children in the world with her gene mutation — and requires round-the-clock care to check her gastrostomy tube and catheter. But getting medically trained caretakers when her dad, Brandon Sell, is away from their York County home hasn’t always been easy. 
“Hanover is just not a saturated area,” when it comes to skilled nursing, said Sell. “So it’s really hard to get (someone) … Nursing in this area is far and few between.”
Scarlotte Sells plays with a worm who will soon be turtle food outside her Hanover home on July 31, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Demand in this sector is only increasing. Direct Care Workers (DCWs) are “one of the largest-growing job industries that we have here in the nation, and it has been growing across every state,” said Mia Haney, the CEO of the Pennsylvania Homecare Association. 
As of 2024, DCWs cared for nearly 21,000 children, many like Scarlotte, and roughly 155,000 adults, Haney shared. That count includes adults who are disabled and those who are aging. 
“But in Pennsylvania, in particular, we’re really starting to see more and more stagnant rates of workers coming into this (field) because our rates are so low that it is actually worth it for them to jump the border,” said Haney. 
Medicaid reimbursement rates in every neighboring state, from New York to West Virginia, are higher than Pennsylvania, where the average hourly wage for personal assistance services is $20.63. That puts families like the Sells, who live less than ten miles from the Maryland border, in a bind.
The turnover of nurses is hard on Scarlotte, Sell said, because “she gets attached.” There was a four-month period when he couldn’t find another provider when he almost lost his house because he couldn’t work. 
“If the compensation isn’t fair, they’re not going to be attractive,” Sell said about home health nursing positions. “If (Scarlotte’s nurse)’s getting $25 an hour, she’s only going to do $25 an hour work.”
 Maintaining dignity

Industry lobbyists like Haney emphasize the importance of home health nurses in their communities — whether caring for children, disabled adults or seniors.
“When people think about home care, they often think about older adults, but home and community-based care serves people across every stage of life,” Haney said. “Without that support, many families reach a breaking point, and institutional care often becomes the only option — a far more costly and less preferred option.”
Skilled nursing allows someone to participate in their communities, Haney continued, enabling children to go to school or adults to keep a job without relying solely on family caregivers who are at risk of burning out.
Scarlotte Sells, center, plays with a toy in her Hanover home on July 31, 2026. Her dad Brandon Sells, at left, coordinates with a home health agency for Brianne McKinsey, an LPN sitting on the right, to monitor Scarlotte’s health during the day while he works as an HVAC technician. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
While other states build semi-regular increases for these workers into their system — similar to how pay for legislators increases annually — Pennsylvania requires legislative action. That comes roughly every five or so years, Haney estimated, but wasn’t included in this year’s budget despite outreach efforts.
“But it’s not consistent. It’s largely dependent on advocacy work, and it’s so dependent on our legislature,” said Haney. “When we talk to legislators, it’s always supportive … and then when pen gets to paper and we have to find the money for it, we get nothing.” 
Studies estimate that upwards of $800 million is needed to raise wages, but Haney warns that the number is growing.
“There’s not enough money, but we have this huge need, and so we just keep pushing this problem to the next year and it’s snowballing,” said Haney. “That $809 million that we calculated at the beginning of 2025 is likely a bigger number this year, because every year more and more people are using the program.” 
Children like Scarlotte make up only a portion of Pennsylvanians who need home health services. Most of those in need of home health services are aging adults, a population that is rapidly growing. 
Some clients can be violent, Haney shared, and agencies will distribute keychains to employees that make loud noises and have flashing lights for  patients who might be more inclined to attack someone. They’re used to startle them, in order to defuse the situation. Others hid their declining health for years, creating “hoarding situations” or neglecting their home upkeep. 
Sometimes, there are bedbugs in houses with no cleaning products, she continued. 
“And we’re going to pay you $13.50 to put yourself in that scenario,” Haney said. “How do you ask somebody to do that and maintain your own sense of dignity?” 
 Part of the community

Brianne McKinsey, a licensed practical nurse, has been Scarlotte’s home health nurse for roughly 18 months, providing much-needed consistency that gives Sell flexibility as an HVAC technician. When McKinsey misses a day, it triggers “a domino effect” and Sell then has to cancel his work commitments. 
“If I’m not here, he doesn’t work,” said McKinsey. “If it’s a school day, she just misses school.” 
To minimize disruptions, McKinsey consults a shared calendar displaying Scarlotte’s frequent doctor appointments before making her own appointments, scheduling it simultaneously so her commitments don’t inconvenience the Sells.
Direct Care Worker Brianne McKinsey checks 6-year-old Scarlotte Sell’s catheter and gastrostomy tube on July 31, 2026. McKinsey, an LPN, works for a home health agency, but industry lobbyists say Pennsylvania’s low Medicaid reimbursement rates makes it difficult to secure quality nurses. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Overnight, another nurse monitors her dialysis and feeding tubes.
The consistency is also important for Scarlotte, who’s “very big on routine,” shared McKinsey. 
McKinsey occasionally uses American Sign Language to communicate with Scarlotte, who uses both a traditional hearing aid and a cochlear implant. The young animal lover enjoys watching McKinsey’s livestream of her chicken coop, but is still learning not to hit or bite the people she loves.
They’re also working on introducing Scarlotte, who has her father’s kidney, to new foods after years of intense acid reflux and vomiting dampened her appetite. 
McKinsey — who’s studying to become a registered nurse, which comes with a pay increase — said a lot of her fellow graduates work in nursing homes that pay “exponentially more,” but she enjoys working with kids.
“”You go through the stress of nursing school, you get your license and it’s almost like a slap in the face that people who are fresh out of high school are working at a gas station making almost what you’re making,” McKinsey continued.
Haney said agencies leaving the state cited the law reimbursement rate as a key factor, but each departure makes the situation worse and worse.
“There will be more. There are more every single day, and this inaction really has a lot of people wondering if Pennsylvania will ever do what it needs to do,” she continued. “We can’t wait any longer.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Trump visa policy leads to fewer international students at US colleges, report concludes
description: A decline in international students at American universities is attributable, in part, to Trump administration immigration policies, according to a new analysis, and that loss could cost the U.S. more than $3 billion, including $23 million for Louisiana alone.   The Association of International Educators based its economic impact calculations on data college[...]
text:
Graduates stand during the May 16, 2025, commencement ceremony at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, held at the Cajundome. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)A decline in international students at American universities is attributable, in part, to Trump administration immigration policies, according to a new analysis, and that loss could cost the U.S. more than $3 billion, including $23 million for Louisiana alone.  
The Association of International Educators based its economic impact calculations on data colleges provided in response to an Institute of International Education survey. It estimates there are 111,000 fewer international students heading into this academic year than in 2024-25, before President Donald Trump began his second term in office. 
The analysis projects the count of international students for the 2026-27 could drop as low as 1.05 million, down from nearly 1.18 million enrolled in 2024-25.
“This downturn reflects the convergence of several headwinds: declining application volumes, persistent visa appointment bottlenecks and newly restrictive immigration policy changes,” the association said in its analysis. 
Specific policy the report mentions includes Trump’s executive order in December that banned travel to the U.S. for residents of 39 countries. It effectively stopped the issuance of visas to students and participants in work- and study-based exchanges from those countries, among them Iran and Nigeria. Both send large numbers of students to the United States.  
Visa access was also made more difficult ahead of this school year when the U.S. prioritized foreign ticketholders for the FIFA World Cup, which coincided with the peak period for student and exchange applicants, the analysis noted.  
It also highlighted reports of limited and delayed appointments for international students at consulates in India and China — the top two countries sending international students to the United States. The same issue occurred across Europe, where many requests for expedited appointments were denied. 
In addition to immigration, the Trump administration has also cut funding for academic research, which has resulted in fewer graduate student spots being available for international and American students. 
The analysis cited recent data from the Association of American Universities that show international applications to U.S. doctoral programs for this fall declined 21%. It contributed to a 15% reduction in overall doctoral program admissions linked to uncertainty over federal research funding.
The Association of International Educators recommends the Trump administration prioritize interviews and processing for all student, work-training and study/work-exchange visa applicants. It also suggested exempting applicants from countries under current travel ban as long as they remain subject to the standard background checks and vetting required as part of the visa process. 
The $3.4 billion in projected losses for the U.S. economy from fewer international students is based on their “direct contributions,” according to the analysis. It said the decline in international graduate students was the “primary driver” of the economic losses. 
Louisiana’s universities have seen a small but noticeable decline in international graduate student enrollment since Trump took office. The Southern University System count fell from 208 in fall 2024 to 113 in fall 2025, and the University of Louisiana System saw a drop from 924 to 916 in the same time period. LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom has not responded to a request for LSU’s data.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump nominates U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky from Arkansas to appeals court
description: President Donald Trump has nominated U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky of Arkansas, who has issued rulings narrowing the scope of the Voting Rights Act and in favor of a state ban on classroom “indoctrination,” to a federal appeals court post. Trump on Wednesday announced he was nominating Rudofsky, a judge in the Eastern District of […]
text:
The exterior of the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse in St. Louis, Missouri on Friday, June 5, 2026. The courthouse includes the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)President Donald Trump has nominated U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky of Arkansas, who has issued rulings narrowing the scope of the Voting Rights Act and in favor of a state ban on classroom “indoctrination,” to a federal appeals court post.
Trump on Wednesday announced he was nominating Rudofsky, a judge in the Eastern District of Arkansas, to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The 8th Circuit covers Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota.
“Lee will be a rock solid defender of the Constitution on the Eighth Circuit,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post announcing the nomination. 
Rudofsky was nominated to the bench by Trump and won Senate confirmation in 2019. Previously, he served as state solicitor general under Arkansas Attorney General Leslie Rutledge and was assistant general counsel for Walmart.
U.S. District Judge Lee P. Rudofsky (Courtesy photo)
Rudofsky in 2022 tossed out a redistricting lawsuit, ruling that private individuals did not have the right to sue to enforce a key provision of the Voting Rights Act. A three-judge panel of the 8th Circuit upheld the decision, which was criticized by civil rights groups who said it weakened the 1965 law.
Earlier this month, Rudofsky dismissed part of a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of an Arkansas law banning “indoctrination” in public schools. Rudofsky’s ruling ordered additional arguments over whether the 2023 law was unconstitutionally vague.
As the solicitor general, Rudofsky represented the state in lawsuits over abortion restrictions and efforts to resume executions.
Conservatives praised Rudofsky’s nomination for the court. 
Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill of Arkansas called the judge a “qualified and solid selection” for the appeals court in an X post. 
If confirmed, Rudofsky would succeed Judge Bobby Shepherd, who was nominated to the court by former President George W. Bush. Shepherd, the father of state Rep. Matthew Shepherd and U.S. District Judge Thomas Shepherd, announced earlier this year he was retiring from active service on the appeals court.
Ten of the 11 active judges on the appeals court were nominated by Republican presidents.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Justice Robyn Brody to become chief justice of Idaho Supreme Court
description: Idaho Supreme Court Justice Robyn Brody will become chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court effective Oct. 1, officials the Idaho Judicial Branch announced Thursday. Brody, who was first elected to the Idaho Supreme Court in 2016, succeeds Chief Justice G. Richard Bevan, who is retiring Oct. 30. The Idaho Supreme Court is the highest […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho Supreme Court Justice Robyn Brody will become chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court effective Oct. 1, officials the Idaho Judicial Branch announced Thursday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Brody, who was first elected to the Idaho Supreme Court in 2016, succeeds Chief Justice G. Richard Bevan, who is retiring Oct. 30.
The Idaho Supreme Court is the highest court in the state, and Brody is set to become the second woman to serve as chief justice in Idaho, Idaho Judicial Branch officials said. Retired Justice Linda Copple Trout became the first woman to serve as chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court in 1997.
Brody currently serves as vice chief of the Idaho Supreme Court. 
Idaho Supreme Court Justice Robyn Brody will become chief justice on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Judicial Branch)
“Idaho is a special place; the dedication and professionalism of our independent courts have helped make it so,” Brody said in a statement issued Thursday. “I am honored to serve our state in this way, and I am grateful for the trust of my fellow justices.”
Brody has been a lawyer in Idaho for almost 30 years, and she started her own law firm in Rupert in 2010 prior to being elected to the Idaho Supreme Court. Brody has also been an adjunct law professor at the University of Idaho’s College of Law. 
Brody is chair of Idaho’s Pro Bono Commission and the Idaho Supreme Court’s Language Access Committee. She is also a board member of the Idaho Law Foundation, which oversees the Idaho Volunteer Lawyers Program and civic education programs, such as mock trials. 
Under the Idaho Constitution, the chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court is selected via a majority vote of the Idaho Supreme Court. 
The chief justice is responsible for leading the court, judicial officials said. The Idaho Supreme Court’s chief justice is also the executive head of the state’s court system and works with other justices to manage that system. 
The chief justice also traditionally addresses the Idaho Legislature each year. 
Bevan has served as chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court since 2021. On Thursday, he issued a statement expressing support for Brody.
“Justice Brody has long worked to ensure that in a changing world, our courts remain accessible to all,” Bevan said. “Our Judicial Branch is in excellent hands.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado candidate says his positions have evolved. Voters might be skeptical.
description: In 2021, when he was a law student at Yale, Colorado state Rep. Manny Rutinel told an animal welfare panel at the school, “The factory farming of animals is one of the largest sources of suffering on the planet.” That statement is indisputably true. Cattle, chickens, pigs and other livestock are sentient beings that feel […]
text:
Manny Rutinel speaks at his election night watch party after winning the Democratic nomination for Colorado's 8th Congressional District on June 30, at Las Dos Americas in Commerce City. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)In 2021, when he was a law student at Yale, Colorado state Rep. Manny Rutinel told an animal welfare panel at the school, “The factory farming of animals is one of the largest sources of suffering on the planet.”
That statement is indisputably true. Cattle, chickens, pigs and other livestock are sentient beings that feel pain and can suffer. Widespread factory farming practices — in which animals are confined in small spaces, experience from birth to death nothing of the natural environment they evolved to inhabit, and are slaughtered young — by any measure inflict suffering. Billions of these animals are slaughtered every year in the U.S. alone.
It’s an enormous source of suffering with few parallels. That’s beyond question. The only question lies in how one responds.
Rutinel responded by fighting Big Ag. He was a passionate activist on behalf of animals. He campaigned admirably against factory farming, both to end its ghastly treatment of livestock and to curb its massive contribution to global warming.
Then he did a one-eighty. Why the change of heart? Rutinel says he has gained a new perspective, but it happened to coincide with his run for Congress in a district with one of the most active factory-farm economies in the country.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And it wasn’t Rutinel’s only flip-flop, which gives voters reason to be skeptical of his positions. All politicians must compromise, and people can change their mind on the basis of experience and new facts, but the reversals in Rutinel’s case suggest a calculated move for power over principles.
His animal rights and environmental agenda at one point was part of his identity. As a student at the University of Florida in 2016, Rutinel promoted veganism, shirtless, as part of activism in support of the Student Animal Alliance. As a law student at Yale, he was part of a select group of students who studied animal law. He co-founded Climate Refarm, which declared, “Shifting to a predominantly plant-based food system is critical for ecological and human health.” 
The organization’s website today contains no mention of Rutinel, but archived images of it do.
Rutinel once testified before state lawmakers in Connecticut that, “The globe must dramatically shift away from animal products and towards fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains and nuts.” 
During that 2021 panel, Rutinel asked listeners to consider what a pig on a factory farm experiences. Raised in a small cage, it’s “constantly impregnated,” treated as a “lifeless machine,” subjected to a “series of mutilations without anesthetics … before getting sent to slaughter.”
“The issue of animal welfare looks to be one of the most important issues of our time and its importance cannot be overstated,” he said.
Rutinel later worked as a lawyer for Earthjustice, the public interest environmental law group, before being appointed to a seat in the Colorado House. Shortly after that appointment, Rutinel told law students at the University of Denver that mistreatment of animals on farms was one of the reasons he got involved in politics, according to The Colorado Sun.
Nothing about Rutinel’s animal activism is shameful. Far from being scandalous, Rutinel showed courage in stating inconvenient ecological facts and highlighting society’s moral violations against animals, which increasingly offend Americans and someday could be found repugnant by mainstream voters.
But all that’s out the window now.



The activist Rutinel used to be wouldn’t have allowed for categories of good ranchers and bad ones, because his previous positions for years cast corporate farms, not just bad apples, as inherently objectionable. That’s not so much an evolution as it is a complete break.



Rutinel, a Democrat, announced his run for Congress early last year. The 31-year-old Commerce City resident won the Democratic primary election last month and will face incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans to represent Colorado’s 8th Congressional District. Of all districts in the country an anti-factory farm activist could choose to campaign in, the 8th might be the most hostile. It’s home to some of the country’s largest meat and dairy producers, including Five Rivers, reputedly the largest cattle feedlot in the world, and an enormous JBS meatpacking plant.
In an interview with Newsline, Rutinel said his perspective on factory farming has shifted as he has toured Colorado ranches, talked to producers and visited farmers markets. He has concluded that meat and dairy producers in Colorado are doing it the right way.
“I think that this is across the board. Colorado’s ranchers are engaging in the best practices across the world,” he said.
He contrasts the good methods practiced in Colorado with the bad methods used elsewhere, such as forms of extreme animal cruelty and deforestation abroad, which he says he remains opposed to. In Colorado, he said, “They’re grazing appropriately and they’re using sustainable watering practices and they’re sourcing their feed from sustainable sources.”
The practical realities of legislating are also a factor. He said the intense kind of protest he once engaged in was part of “the honored tradition of the college experience.”
“But now, you know, I’m an adult and serving Coloradans in the state House and hoping to do so in Congress,” he said. “I would argue that providing an evolved perspective like that is something that many politicians are failing to offer or acknowledge. And I think we’re needing folks who have wide perspectives and people in Congress who didn’t curate their entire lives to become a politician.”
Legislating involves incremental change and negotiation, he said, adding, “People aren’t looking for ideological politicians. They’re looking for people who get results, and that’s ultimately who I’ve always been.”
Fair enough. But the activist Rutinel used to be wouldn’t have allowed for categories of good ranchers and bad ones, because his previous positions for years cast corporate farms, not just bad apples, as inherently objectionable. That’s not so much an evolution as it is a complete break.
And it’s not just factory farms. A major feature of his campaign is questions about multiple past positions he has seemingly abandoned.
During a candidate debate before the primary, Kyle Clark of 9News asked Rutinel about his shapeshifting. It got awkward. Clark challenged Rutinel on his progressive-to-moderate transformation on such topics as fracking, single-payer health insurance, student debt and climate change. Rutinel was evasive.
It might be hard for voters to believe Rutinel so sweepingly changed his mind in the name of truth rather than his rhetoric in pursuit of power.
Evans has his own challenges with truth-telling, and he has been a stalwart MAGA supporter of President Donald Trump’s agenda, including mass deportations. Voters will decide whose offences are greater. But their ballots will bear the names of two candidates they might find untrustworthy.

title: Evergy urges Kansas regulators to be cautious about AI revealing confidential information
description: TOPEKA — Evergy filed a request with utility regulators to ensure its confidential data wasn’t uploaded to artificial intelligence platforms, highlighting a concern that the rapid growth and use of AI may release private information. In a July 30 filing, Evergy asked the Kansas Corporation Commission to amend its standard protective order filed in regulatory[...]
text:
Evergy officials encouraged the Kansas Corporation Commission to make sure that artificial intelligence tools don't put the company's confidential information in jeopardy. Many companies nationwide are limiting the use of AI tools or investing in closed systems that make sure their private data isn't exposed. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Evergy filed a request with utility regulators to ensure its confidential data wasn’t uploaded to artificial intelligence platforms, highlighting a concern that the rapid growth and use of AI may release private information.
In a July 30 filing, Evergy asked the Kansas Corporation Commission to amend its standard protective order filed in regulatory cases to include protections from improper use of AI with regard to private information.
Confidential information is regularly given to regulators to help stakeholders in the decision-making process, said Matt Lucht, Evergy spokesman. But the company must also protect business, customer and infrastructure-related information from being disclosed, he said.
“Evergy has asked the Kansas Corporation Commission for additional protections that prohibit the use of confidential case information in open AI tools while still allowing the use of secure, closed AI systems with appropriate safeguards,” Lucht said. “We want to ensure that we can continue to openly share information with our regulators and case intervenors while maintaining appropriate confidentiality.”
Evergy’s concerns aren’t unusual as AI platforms are proliferating. Artificial intelligence tools transcribe meeting notes, summarize emails or write better letters for the general public. But in business, the tools are developing strategic plans, helping attorneys write better court documents and assessing competition.
A Stanford University assessment found that “responsible AI is not keeping pace with AI capability, with safety benchmarks lagging and incidents rising sharply.”
Justin Grady, KCC director of utilities, said “the sky’s the limit” regarding how people could use confidential information with generative AI tools. Generative AI refers to AI that creates new content, drawing from large datasets of information and learning as it goes.
For instance, an individual with access to confidential regulatory documents could “dump all of their files into some new large language model and say what were the weaknesses or the deficiencies that were in this filing,” Grady said.
The situation isn’t unique to energy regulation. Courts nationwide are defining how AI can be used, which Evergy noted in its filing.
“Prompting these AI tools with confidential or business proprietary information creates a risk that the generative AI will ‘learn’ from the prompt, which may result in the corporate owner of that AI tool retaining access to the confidential information,” Evergy’s filing said. 
The American Bar Association adopted guidelines for the use of AI tools and cautioned against the use of AI tools unless an attorney ensures the client’s confidential information will be secure, Evergy said.
Murtaza Nasir, assistant professor at Wichita State University’s business school, said there have been cases where OpenAI says it doesn’t share information, but then someone’s chats became public.
“People share their chats with other people, and then they don’t realize that their links they created are public or they are being indexed by the search engines,” he said. “That data may be used by the company itself for some type of training, or just to understand the businesses themselves.”
In fact, Nasir said, some AI companies “pose a threat” in industries where they eventually become a competitor.
“These AI companies have a unique look into how all of these different industries work, what they’re doing, and they may come up with competing services or that sort of thing,” he said.
 
Security options
KCC created rules around AI use, with the primary goal to make sure no one puts confidential information into any AI platform, Grady said. But he recognizes the usefulness of the tools and expects to see KCC develop or purchase a closed AI system.
An AI system housed within the KCC would mean that it doesn’t feed any information outside of the contained system, such as into a cloud-based language learning model that’s pulling everything in to expand its datasets, Grady said.
“I wouldn’t say that there’s immediate plans for it, but I’d be shocked if in five years we’re not using something like that,” he said.
Grady is a fan of using AI to simplify time-consuming tasks, but he also said it isn’t quite up to par yet for helping in regulatory work. Webinars have shown examples of AI assessing regulatory filings, but the tools weren’t outstanding, he said. Instead, the insights were the same as he currently receives from experienced staff members.
However, AI can make repetitive work easier or search through a 5,000-page regulation to find specific information fast, Grady said.
Nasir said there is a push right now to develop private AI tools that stay within a business or organization to maintain privacy but offer employees the opportunity to use AI in a way that is becoming important in most work.
“You can run the AI locally, or some companies have special tiers, like for example, Claude or OpenAI, of their services for the government or for defense companies, where they guarantee that none of the data will ever be used for training or any other purposes like that,” Nasir said.
“How much do you trust them with that? Yeah, that is up to you.So that’s why open source models are a very important topic right now,” he added. “These are models that you can even run on your laptop or on your computer at home for simple tasks.”
It is important, Nasir said, to understand that AI models don’t use all conversations or input for training purposes, but most do save conversations, sometimes only for certain customers, such as those who have free accounts. 
“All of these companies have different ways of creating their datasets for training, and they don’t share how they create those datasets because that’s what gives them their competitive advantage,” he said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: A mugshot turns a Kentucky data center dispute personal between an activist and a developer
description: Diane Floyd said she was watching her husband’s music show earlier this month when she got a message over Facebook. It was from Brian Luftman, the founder of American Farm Investors, one of the companies trying to bring a hyperscale data center to Mercer County.  Luftman threatened to publish a picture of her 2023 mugshot […]
text:
A screenshot of the message that Brian Luftman sent Diane Floyd, shared by Floyd on Facebook. (Screenshot)Diane Floyd said she was watching her husband’s music show earlier this month when she got a message over Facebook. It was from Brian Luftman, the founder of American Farm Investors, one of the companies trying to bring a hyperscale data center to Mercer County. 
Luftman threatened to publish a picture of her 2023 mugshot to a Facebook group called “Lexington Foodies.” 
“The insinuation, at least, of a vague threat that he’s going to post my arrest picture of the most, or one of the most traumatic nights of my life,” Floyd told the Lantern. “It was like he was trying to attack me in a way he knew it would hurt.” 
Floyd has been one of a number of Mercer County residents involved in We Are Mercer County, a group of residents organizing around concerns about the potential impacts to the environment, land use and local resources that such a massive project could bring. Much of that debate has centered on the small Mercer County city of Burgin, where leadership at the city’s small school district have advocated for the project because of the enormous tax windfall it could bring.
Floyd’s arrest came from a domestic violence case in 2023 that was later dismissed. 
“I don’t have money. I don’t have connections, I don’t have infinite resources. I’m just a mom in Mercer County, and I happen to not think that AI data centers are the best thing for Mercer County for a lot of reasons,” Floyd said.
Luftman’s message included the phrase, “Should I post this to Lexington foodies?” It was a reference to a private Facebook group that Floyd had made a post in on August 4. Floyd wrote in that Lexington Foodies group, sharing an article about Luftman’s Never Say Die Bourbon brand, that he was “trying to force an AI data center in historic Mercer County” and that “when and where we spend our money is one of our strongest tools.”
The Lexington Herald-Leader has reported that Luftman is establishing the Never Say Die Bourbon at a microdistillery and English-style pub in downtown Lexington.
On August 7, Floyd posted on Facebook a screenshot of Luftman’s message and her response to him, saying “[t]his is what speaking out can look like when powerful interests don’t appreciate public scrutiny.” 
Floyd said she viewed Luftman bringing up her past arrest as a form of intimidation because of her advocacy against the proposed project, something she says that other Mercer County people advocating for the project have done. 
In a Thursday phone interview with the Lantern, Luftman said he had subsequently apologized to Floyd and that his intent “was not to intimidate.”
“It was to shed light that it doesn’t feel great to be slandered, and I did it privately to her. And I shouldn’t have done that,” Luftman said. “It was an absolute incorrect way for me to handle it, and I regret it.” 
When asked about the alleged slander against him, Luftman pointed to Facebook comments and posts that are “pretty rude” in groups including “No Kentucky Data Centers”. Members of that Facebook group have discussed and criticized Luftman’s involvement with the proposed Mercer County data center, in at least one instance sharing his contact information from emails he sent. Floyd said she hasn’t personally posted Luftman’s contact information on social media. 
Another member of the group in an August 3 post also referenced Luftman’s involvement with Never Say Die Bourbon, encouraging people “to leave an honest review of Mr. Luftman and his various business ventures to ensure the public knows who they are supporting.”
Luftman said it wasn’t fair for activists to speak out against other businesses of his that have nothing to do with the proposed data center development. 
“What changed was when they started calling for boycotts and on other businesses that are unrelated to mine, which in turn puts undue stress on other relationships and businesses that I have that have nothing to do with this development,” Luftman said. “It was taken too far.” 
As for the proposed data center project, Luftman said it has “been a propagandized topic nationwide” and mentioned the Burgin school district’s support for the project. 
A county’s data center moratorium doesn’t include a small city considering huge project

Floyd said she takes her advocacy questioning the Mercer County data center project seriously, saying she’s talked with other people who live near data centers and with experts on “environmental impacts and health impacts.” 
“I’ve been very conscious of sticking to the facts of the situation,” Floyd said.
“These are not inflated claims. These are things that I’ve learned.”

name: Delaware
title: Scouting Finds New Momentum in Delaware as Families Look Beyond the Screen
description: A century-old youth organization is attracting new interest as Delaware families seek outdoor adventure, leadership, service and more face-to-face experiences for their children. WILMINGTON, Del. — Scouting is finding renewed momentum in Delaware as families look for structured activities that get children outdoors, build confidence and create stronger face-[...]
text:
Image is from Scouting America. To learn more, visit www.beascout.org to find a nearby pack or troop, email the Del-Mar-Va Council at info@dmvc.org or call 302-622-3300.
A century-old youth organization is attracting new interest as Delaware families seek outdoor adventure, leadership, service and more face-to-face experiences for their children.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Scouting is finding renewed momentum in Delaware as families look for structured activities that get children outdoors, build confidence and create stronger face-to-face connections.
Ray Teat, Scout Executive for the Del-Mar-Va Council, said the organization is seeing families return to Scouting following the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
“The number of scouts, scouting units and families involved with Scouting is once again growing following a challenging time for the program coming out of COVID,” Teat said. “But the number of young people, both boys and girls, is growing.”
The growth comes after a period in which Scouting America experienced significant national membership losses, including a sharp decline following 2019. In Delaware, however, local leaders say the focus has shifted to renewed family interest and the reasons parents are taking another look at Scouting.
“We’re seeing strong interest across Delaware because families want exciting programs with hands-on experiences that promote life skills — from Cub Scouts through high-adventure crews — and plenty of chances for parents to get involved,” Teat said.
Parents are looking for connection
Tim Holly, Executive Board President of the Del-Mar-Va Council, said the renewed interest reflects broader changes affecting children and families.
After the isolation and disruption of the pandemic, Holly said many parents are deliberately looking for structured activities that put children together in person and give them opportunities to build friendships, confidence and independence.
“Parents are looking for ways to reconnect their children with other kids and with their communities,” Holly said. “They want them outside, interacting face to face, learning how to work with other people and building confidence through real experiences.”
That desire for connection comes as families continue to wrestle with concerns about youth mental health, social isolation and the amount of time children spend online.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that about 40% of U.S. high school students experienced persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness in 2023.
The statistic does not establish a direct connection between mental health concerns and Scouting enrollment, but it provides context for parents seeking activities that emphasize friendship, physical activity, adult mentorship, responsibility and belonging.
Holly said Scouting offers a setting where children can step away from some of the pressures of an increasingly digital childhood.
“Families are increasingly concerned about how much of childhood is happening on a screen,” Holly said. “Scouting gives young people a reason to put the phone down, go outside, solve a problem, make friends and discover that they can do things they may not have thought they could do.”
An old idea fits a new concern
That may be giving one of Scouting’s oldest ideas new relevance.
Scouts camp, hike, cook, build, navigate, volunteer and work together. As they get older, Scouts gradually take greater responsibility for planning activities, solving problems and leading other young people.
“Scouting has always been about learning by doing,” Holly said. “What has changed is that parents now see even more value in experiences where kids have to interact with one another, solve problems together and learn how to lead.”
Holly said parents also are attracted to the resilience that can develop when children are allowed to encounter manageable challenges.
“You learn something about yourself when the weather changes on a camping trip, when something doesn’t go according to plan or when your patrol has to figure out what to do next,” Holly said. “Those are small challenges, but they teach independence, perseverance and leadership.”
More than camping
Modern Scouting reaches well beyond the traditional image of tents, campfires and knots.
Scouts can pursue interests involving science, technology, robotics, environmental conservation, public safety, communications, fitness and dozens of other subjects.
Holly said that combination of traditional outdoor experiences and contemporary skills has broadened the program’s appeal.
“Families don’t have to choose between outdoor adventure and the skills young people will need in the future,” Holly said. “Scouting can expose a child to conservation, technology, engineering, leadership and public service while still getting them outside and away from a screen.”
That flexibility also allows young people with different interests to find their own paths through Scouting.
Delaware is well suited for Scouting
Delaware’s geography gives local Scouting programs another advantage.
Families in New Castle County are within easy reach of state parks, trails, waterways, historic sites and camping opportunities. Farther south, Scouts have access to forests, coastal environments and Scout reservations across the Delmarva Peninsula.
Holly said Delaware’s compact size makes those experiences unusually accessible.
“One of the strengths of Scouting in Delaware is that adventure is not very far away,” Holly said. “Families can live in Wilmington or Newark and still be on a trail, near the water or at a campsite without spending half the day getting there.”
That accessibility allows local units to combine outdoor recreation with conservation, history and community service.
A broader Scouting organization
Scouting also looks different than it did for many of today’s parents and grandparents, although boys and girls participating together is not new to several of its older-youth programs.
Girls began joining Cub Scout programs in 2018, followed by the expansion of Scouts BSA to girls in 2019.
Young women, however, had already participated in other Scouting programs for decades. Exploring and Sea Exploring, now Sea Scouts, began welcoming young women in 1971. Venturing has included both young men and young women since the program was created in 1998.
Those programs continue to offer different paths for older youth, including high-adventure activities, maritime programs and career-focused experiences.
“Families and society have changed over time and Scouting has evolved,” Holly said. “We are reaching more young people, including girls, while remaining steadfast in teaching the things that have always made Scouting valuable — things like leadership, service, outdoor adventure and character.”
The organization has also adopted the Scouting America name as part of an effort to better communicate its broader mission to today’s families.
New Castle County shows momentum
Some of the most visible growth has come in New Castle County, where local units have expanded recruitment and held Join Scouting Nights designed to introduce parents and children to nearby packs and troops.
Teat said the growth is giving the council reason for optimism and reinforcing the relevance of Scouting for today’s families.
The experience also suggests Scouting may be benefiting from a broader shift in what parents value.
For earlier generations, playing outside, exploring a neighborhood and spending long stretches of time away from a screen were ordinary parts of childhood.
Today, Holly said, parents may have to create those experiences more intentionally.
“The things Scouting provides are not really new,” Holly said. “What may be new is how much families value them today. Being outdoors, having real friendships, serving other people and learning to take responsibility have become increasingly important in a world where so much of life is virtual.”
More than a century in Delaware
Scouting has deep roots in the First State.
The Wilmington Council was founded in 1914, became the Wilmington Area Council in 1931 and was renamed the Del-Mar-Va Council in 1936.
More than a century later, Scouting has changed considerably, but much of its fundamental proposition remains familiar.
Young people still go outside. They learn skills. They work in teams. They serve their communities. And gradually, they are expected to assume more responsibility for themselves and others.
For Teat and Holly, that combination may help explain why a century-old youth organization is finding renewed momentum.
In a childhood increasingly filled with screens, schedules and virtual connections, Scouting offers something decidedly different: a chance to get outside, build friendships, overcome challenges and learn how to lead.

What: Scouting America programs in Delaware and throughout the Del-Mar-Va Council
Programs include: Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing, Sea Scouts and Exploring
Who can participate: Programs serve boys and girls, with opportunities based on age and interests. Several older-youth Scouting programs have been coed for decades.
What Scouts do: Camping, hiking, community service, leadership development, STEM activities, conservation, public safety programs and other hands-on experiences.
Local leadership: Ray Teat, Scout Executive of the Del-Mar-Va Council; Tim Holly, Executive Board President of the Del-Mar-Va Council
Where: Scout units operate throughout Delaware, with parks, waterways, historic sites and Scout camps providing opportunities for outdoor and educational programs.
How to learn more: Visit www.beascout.org to find a nearby pack or troop, email the Del-Mar-Va Council at info@dmvc.org or call 302-622-3300.

text:
Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez is sworn into his clemency hearing through a video call from Oklahoma State Penitentiary on July 14, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma County killer Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez was put to death Thursday at Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester.
He died by lethal injection for the 2003 shooting death of Olimpia Fisher, 43, the mother of two daughters.
The time of death was 10:13 a.m., said Kay Thompson, an Oklahoma Department of Corrections spokesperson.
Fisher was shot in both eyes during an altercation between her and Cuesta-Rodriguez at the Oklahoma City home they shared. 
Her pregnant daughter witnessed the first shot.
“We continue to honor and love her every day through our shared memories and raising our families to reflect the love and faith in God that she taught us,” said her daughters, Cinthya Allen and Catya Wallis, said in a statement. “Our faith in Jesus has allowed us to forgive.
“We hope this tragedy and loss reminds everyone of the importance of domestic violence awareness.”
Last month, the Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board voted 3-1 against recommending clemency to Gov. Kevin Stitt, who has the final word.
Cuesta-Rodriguez, 70, told the board he did not deserve nor want clemency, saying “It’s time for me to pay for what I did.” 
Defense attorneys said he came from a troubled upbringing in Cuba and suffered from PTSD, depression and other health issues not originally introduced at his trial. They said he was using alcohol and steroids at the time of the murder.
“Justice has been served for Olimpia Fisher whose life was tragically cut short,” said Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond. “I pray that her family finds some measure of peace after enduring 23 years of unimaginable grief.”
Tennessee and Alabama also scheduled executions for Thursday.

The 151,000-square-foot Magis Hall, intended exclusively for sophomores, will be home to 409 students living in four-person apartment-style suites. Each floor has lounges, study ro[...]
text:
Creighton University's Magis Hall opened this week as the school's latest development project helping to change the face of downtown Omaha. (Photo courtesy of Creighton University)OMAHA — A new $50 million Creighton University student residence hall opened this week, adding to the private university’s continued transformation of parts of Omaha’s urban core.
The 151,000-square-foot Magis Hall, intended exclusively for sophomores, will be home to 409 students living in four-person apartment-style suites. Each floor has lounges, study rooms and gathering spots. Fall classes start Aug. 18.
The dormitory features “The Aviary,” a wellness-focused retreat space where students can unwind and recharge amid earthy tones, natural light, plants and nature-inspired materials.
$300M Creighton donor-funded plan aims to reshape part of downtown Omaha

The Rev. Daniel Hendrickson, Creighton president, said Magis Hall along 21st between Cuming and Burt streets is named for the Jesuit value that seeks “the greater good” and service. 
Built between Creighton’s School of Dentistry and the new softball competition field, the newest dorm builds upon the aesthetic of nearby Graves Hall, university leaders said. That $37 million project for freshmen opened in 2023 and was the first residence hall constructed on the campus since 2006.
“Situated at the intersection of our new residential and recreational corridors, this dedicated sophomore residence fosters community, encourages personal growth and helps all who call it home thrive,” Hendrickson said.
A Creighton press release says Magis Hall is the first building on its downtown campus to incorporate geothermal technology, calling it another milestone in the university’s sustainability efforts. 
Beneath the building and the parking lot north of Cuming Street are 186 geothermal wells that help heat the building’s domestic hot water and provide energy exchange for heating and cooling. 
Complementing the geothermal system is a photovoltaic solar array shared by Magis Hall and the School of Dentistry that’s expected to generate roughly 500,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, supplying roughly one-third of Magis Hall’s yearly electrical needs. 
Creighton says the two systems are expected to reduce the building’s annual energy costs by approximately 50% compared to similarly sized residence halls using traditional utilities.
The Aviary, where students can unwind and recharge, is viewed as a signature element of the newly opened Magis Hall on Creighton University campus. (Photo courtesy of Creighton University)

title: Even as inflation eases slightly, North Carolina families still feel squeezed from all sides
description: Inflation cooled slightly in July thanks in part to a dip in gas prices, but many consumers aren’t feeling any relief. David McLennan, a veteran political scientist at Meredith College, told NC Newsline that there’s a disconnect between the data and the economic pain consumers are facing. “Economic perceptions are getting to the point where […]
text:
Congresswoman Deborah Ross, D-NC-02, listens to Elena Rumyantseva and other North Carolina mothers discuss the economic squeeze their families are facing during a August 12, 2026 roundtable. Rumyantseva said daycare and health insurance are unaffordable after losing a full-time job in biotech. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) Inflation cooled slightly in July thanks in part to a dip in gas prices, but many consumers aren’t feeling any relief.
David McLennan, a veteran political scientist at Meredith College, told NC Newsline that there’s a disconnect between the data and the economic pain consumers are facing.
“Economic perceptions are getting to the point where they’re locked in,” said McLennan. “Even if we get a few months of declining consumer price index or some other inflationary measure, most North Carolinians, as well as most people nationally, think it’s bad.”
On Wednesday morning, a group of mothers at a political event said the data did not reflect their lived experience.
Congresswoman Deborah Ross, D-N.C., joined a breakfast roundtable hosted by the advocacy group MomsRising to hear directly from Raleigh-area moms about the economic squeeze families are facing.
Elena Rumyantseva said she is a trained scientist who worked in biotech until she was laid off last October.
“I found another job in January that was part-time, but I could not afford daycare being part-time,” Rumyantseva said.
The average monthly cost of daycare in North Carolina exceeds $1,100, according to a 2025 study by N.C. State University’s Center for Urban Affairs & Community Services.
She’s also going without health insurance, once provided by her employer.
“I cannot afford it. Our family medical insurance would be $1,700 a month with a $12,000 annual deductible,” said Rumyantseva.
Rumyantseva said her family is now facing $9,000 in medical debt after an emergency sent her husband to the ER.
“He’s fine now, but we are going to have to deal with that debt,” she said.
Liz Chavez, a mother of three and a public school teacher, said the economy doesn’t feel better to her.
“It doesn’t feel better when it comes to going to the grocery store, going to get gas or paying for insurance premiums,” said Chavez.
Chavez said she’s been going to the same doctor for a decade and even with insurance, prices have been steadily rising.
Stocks are up, unemployment is down – so why is a leading NC economist raising a red flag?

She paid $1,400 out of pocket for a procedure for Crohn’s disease in November of 2025. Six months later, the same treatment with the same provider and the same insurance cost another $1,900 out of pocket.
“That’s a really big jump in just six months,” Chavez said.
And paychecks are not getting any larger for the veteran teacher.
“I’m going to be going into my 22nd year of teaching. The pay scale is frozen from year 15 to year 25. There’s no step increase,” she said
Cheryl Staccio was working behind the counter of the Groovy Duck Bakery where Wednesday’s event was held and was not a part of the program, but it hit close to home for her.
Co-workers at the Groovy Duck Bakery in Raleigh, NC comfort Cheryl Staccio, who said paying for basic necessities is increasingly difficult in this economy. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Staccio choked back tears as she explained to the women she was working but living paycheck to paycheck with two children.
“Doing small, fun things with my kids is no longer possible. We wait until grandma comes to town to go to the movies or go out to the restaurants,” Staccio said.
When times are tight, she uses Affirm to pay for groceries, allowing her to buy now and pay over time. But that convenience adds interest to the rising cost of food.
“I don’t even know what happened,” she said. “I’m just making it through. I’m doing my best.”
Staccio is not alone. A Catawba College–YouGov Survey released in July of more than 1,000 North Carolinians found 57% said they had difficulty affording regular monthly expenses.
McLennan said these everyday struggles may outweigh any positive economic data points that emerge this fall.
“It’s hard to know how the Iran war will go, and there was even one energy expert this morning that said that higher prices could last through 2027,” said McLennan. “And that’s what a lot of people base their feelings on.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Same arguments, new insults: McKee and Foulkes clash in first TV debate
description: Familiar arguments over opioids, infrastructure and who cares more about everyday Rhode Islanders dominated the first televised Democratic gubernatorial debate of the 2026 election cycle. Yet Gov. Dan McKee and his challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, still managed to infuse their usual talking points with fresh insults during the hourlong forum, organized b[...]
text:
Gov. Dan McKee, right, gestures while making a point in the first television debate with Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes in the lobby of the Providence Performing Arts Center Wednesday night, Aug. 12, 2026. (Screenshot/WJAR)Familiar arguments over opioids, infrastructure and who cares more about everyday Rhode Islanders dominated the first televised Democratic gubernatorial debate of the 2026 election cycle.
Yet Gov. Dan McKee and his challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, still managed to infuse their usual talking points with fresh insults during the hourlong forum, organized by NBC10 and Coastal ABC and taped at the Providence Performing Arts Center on Wednesday night
“Uninformed and unapologetic,” was how McKee painted his opponent, labeling her characterization of state economic growth under his administration as “nonsense,” and her tenure as former president at CVS pharmacy as “bad leadership.”
Foulkes, in turn, called McKee a “desperate man,” proclaiming his statistics on job creation under his administration a “lie.”
McKee and Foulkes clash on CVS, Washington Bridge and Pawtucket soccer stadium in WPRO debate

Little has changed in their campaign talking points since they first squared off in 2022 when McKee defeated Foulkes by 3 percentage points in a four-way Democratic primary.
McKee, 75, still positions himself as a salt-of-the-Earth governor, frequently citing his upbringing in the Cumberland clubhouse of the Boys and & Girls Clubs and his six-year record as governor. Foulkes, 62, presents herself as a change to an unsatisfactory status quo, drawing upon her business background to improve the state’s stagnant economy and affordability woes.
What’s different this time: Foulkes leads McKee by 20 percentage points in recent public polls, with four times more campaign cash and the backing of a majority of local Democratic leaders, including in McKee’s hometown of Cumberland — a snub she highlighted in her closing remarks.
“This is a governor who unfortunately has a level of mediocrity and complacency that is hurting the people of Rhode Island,” Foulkes said. 
She highlighted repeated criticisms of the governor’s handling of the Washington Bridge demolition and rebuild, calling the project a “poster child” of government inefficiency and cronyism. Foulkes made clear in her campaign launch that she would fire then-Rhode Island Department of Transportation Director Peter Alviti Jr. immediately. Alviti has since retired. 
Foulkes also seized upon CNBC’s 2026 business rankings, where Rhode Island placed 48th out of 50 states in business friendliness, as evidence of McKee’s inability to boost business growth. 
McKee dismissed the ranking, noting that Rhode Island fares better in other measures, including livability, education and quality of life, and even business environment according to other organizations’ criteria,
“Rankings are like polls, you pick the ones you like,” he said. “The notion that somehow we’re not in far better shape today than when I took office is just not true.”



Quotation







Rankings are like polls, you pick the ones you like. The notion that somehow we’re not in far better shape today than when I took office is just not true. 


– Gov Dan McKee


Throughout the debate, no matter the question posed by moderator Gene Valicenti, McKee returned focus to Foulkes’ record at CVS. The top state employer faces multiple lawsuits, including a Department of Justice investigation unsealed in late 2024, for perpetuating the opioid crisis by filling fake prescriptions. Foulkes headed the company’s retail pharmacy arm from 2014 to 2018 — within the timespan of the federal lawsuit — but is not named specifically in any court documents.
“It’s not about the company, it’s about the company my opponent keeps,” McKee said multiple times throughout the debate. 
Echoing an unanswered request for an apology in the Republican gubernatorial debate three hours earlier, McKee asked Foulkes if she would apologize to the families who have lost loved ones in the opioid epidemic, which he blamed on her “bad leadership.”
“You’re going to talk about bad leadership, you are the epitome of bad leadership,” Foulkes said, turning the critique back on McKee for denouncing one of the state’s largest employers.
While Foulkes has not been directly linked to the investigations against CVS, her own campaign’s defense about her work combating the opioid crisis also relies on inflated numbers or does not directly involve her, a Rhode Island Current investigation found. 



Quotation







You’re going to talk about bad leadership, you are the epitome of bad leadership. 


– Helena Buonanno Foulkes


The pair shared emphasis on affordability concerns, including on housing and energy costs. But where McKee touted his administration’s housing plan, including creation of the first-ever housing department and cabinet-level housing secretary, Foulkes suggested the state’s strategy was not generating the return on investment needed.
On energy, McKee reupped his fiscal 2027 budget proposal, which did not survive legislative cuts, to save ratepayers $1 billion over the next five years by weakening state renewable and energy efficiency programs that hike bill charges.
Foulkes said choosing between climate and cost was a “false choice,” and accused McKee of not pushing back hard enough against the state’s utility supplier, Rhode Island Energy.
On truck tolls, McKee remained committed to the plan underway to reactivate the gantries from former Gov. Gina Raimondo’s Rhode Works program, while Foulkes answered “no” on restarting the truck toll program until she could determine a way to exempt Rhode Island companies from paying the fee.
“She’s been running for the office for six years and she still doesn’t know what she should be doing on truck tolls,” McKee jumped in, setting off one of several periods in which the candidates talked over each other as Valicenti tried to reign them in. 
The pair will meet again on Tuesday night, Aug. 18, for their third and final debate before the primary, in an event at Rhode Island College hosted by WPRI-TV 12. The first debate, hosted on WPRO radio on Monday, Aug. 3, was marked by similar acrimony.
Early voting begins Aug. 20 ahead of the Sept. 9 primary.

title: Solomon hits airwaves with TV ad in Democratic attorney general primary
description: Democratic attorney general candidate Joe Solomon Jr. has released his campaign’s first television ad as part of a six-figure shopping spree across broadcast television, cable and digital platforms. The 30-second spot “Safer” launches a week before early voting begins for the Sept. 9 primary and makes Solomon the last of the four Democrats in the […]
text:
Rep. Joe Solomon Jr., a Democratic candidate running to be Rhode Island’s next attorney general, debuted his first ad of the primary on Aug. 12, 2026 (Screenshot/Joe Solomon Democrat for Attorney General)Democratic attorney general candidate Joe Solomon Jr. has released his campaign’s first television ad as part of a six-figure shopping spree across broadcast television, cable and digital platforms. 
The 30-second spot “Safer” launches a week before early voting begins for the Sept. 9 primary and makes Solomon the last of the four Democrats in the race to hit the airwaves. All are seeking to succeed term-limited Attorney General Peter Neronha. 
At least $26,295 of Solomon’s ad spend went toward 44 TV spots to air on local broadcast stations WJAR and WPRI between Aug. 12 and Aug. 18, Federal Communications Commission filings show. The WJAR buy totals $16,180 for 22 spots, while the campaign reserved another 22 spots on WPRI for $10,115.
Solomon frames himself in the ad in much the same way as he has in recent debates, noting how his experience cuts across both civil and criminal areas of law. The ad references Solomon’s work as a prosecutor in the office of the Warwick city solicitor and his decade as a bail commissioner. 
“For a safer Rhode Island, I stood up for victims, and prosecuted hundreds of cases,” Solomon says in the ad. “And served as bail commissioner, keeping violent criminals off our streets.”
Four Democratic AG candidates’ records go on trial in first TV debate

The ad emphasizes Solomon’s endorsements from law enforcement and emergency personnel, noting that the candidate is “the only Democrat in the race endorsed by state troopers, police officers, and firefighters.” 
Solomon’s endorsements over the past few months have included Rhode Island Deputy Sheriffs, the Rhode Island State Association of Fire Fighters, the Rhode Island State Fraternal Order of Police, the International Brotherhood of Police Officers and National Association of Government Employees, Rhode Island Troopers Association, and Rhode Island Brotherhood of Correctional Officers.
The ad’s conclusion poses Solomon as a shield against President Donald Trump. 
“I’ll stand up to the criminal-in-chief, and enforce the law to protect all of our families,” Solomon says as cool-toned footage of Trump nodding backgrounds his voiceover.
The ad highlights Solomon’s General Assembly experience, with the candidate claiming he “led the fight to protect seniors from scams and fraud.” The Warwick state representative was first elected in 2014 and has chaired the House Committee on Corporations. Earlier this year, Solomon introduced the House version of a bill that would have created a statewide elder advocacy office, focused on protecting the rights of older Rhode Islanders.
Solomon voted against Rhode Island’s ban on certain semiautomatic weapons, which was passed and signed into law in 2025. It was sponsored in the House by Rep. Jason Knight, a Barrington Democrat and Solomon’s rival in the AG race. Knight debuted his television campaign on Aug. 7.
Keith Hoffmann — who received the endorsement of U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren on Thursday — was the first candidate in the Democratic primary to advertise on TV, with his first 30-second spot airing July 21. His campaign said at the time that it had authorized more than $1 million in television, digital and other media for ads through primary election day. 
Hoffmann — Neronha’s former policy director and assistant attorney general and the current AG’s own pick for his successor — had spent $412,000 worth of ads across Rhode Island’s broadcast and cable TV networks as of Aug. 7.
Former Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission Chair Kim Ahern, a former prosecutor, aired her debut ad the week after Hoffmann. In addition to $104,000 spent on TV ads as of Aug. 7, Ahern’s campaign purchased 71 more spots for $34,000, according to FCC filings, with the ads set to air on WJAR and Coastal ABC between Aug. 12 and Aug. 18.
Early voting begins Aug. 20, ahead of the Sept. 9 primary. The Democratic nominee will face Republican Alan Gordon in the Nov. 3 general election.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• ‘Common’ Sense. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “State urges residents to ‘use common sense’ as severe storms hit Ohio.”
Government agencies are warning Ohioans to be cautious of “very dangerous” summer storms battering much of the state.
Aside from high winds and tornado warnings, the ongoing severe weather could leave days of floodwater behind, Gov. Mike DeWine said Tuesday afternoon, standing inside the Ohio Emergency Management Agency in Columbus.
The first storm bands Tuesday morning left one dead in Roseville, a village of 1,500 residents south of Zanesville. Since then, DeWine has activated the Ohio National Guard’s high water rescue unit and declared emergencies in Muskingum County and Perry County. Crooksville and Roseville were being evacuated.
• More attorneys?! The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford reports, “Ohio’s rural areas need more attorneys. A new initiative aims to build a pipeline.”
In many parts of Ohio, legal help is hard to come by.
Seventy-eight out of Ohio’s 88 counties do not have enough attorneys to meet their residents’ needs, according to the Ohio State Bar Association. In northwest Ohio, the situation could get even more severe as many practicing attorneys near retirement.
A coalition of legal organizations and law schools in the area are working to ensure justice is still accessible.
• Ohio public schools money trouble, part infinity. Ideastream’s Conor Morris reports, “Cleveland schools predicting more hard decisions on the way, even after consolidation.”
More cuts could be coming for the Cleveland Metropolitan School District in the coming years, even after closing schools, laying off staff and taking other cost-cutting measures in recent years.
The district’s new financial forecast, approved by the school board Tuesday, shows it running out of cash entirely, about $50 million in the red, in just four years’ time. Chief Financial Officer Kevin Stockdale said rising costs of healthcare and state funding remaining flat are causing challenges for the district as it looks ahead. A recent enrollment study conducted by the state also suggests CMSD, like many public schools, will continue to see declining enrollment over the next 10 years…
(D)ata compiled recently by Ohio State University education policy researcher Vladimir Kogan… suggests almost 20% of public schools in the state are projecting negative cash balances by 2029, the highest rate since 2012.
• Miller’s Crossing. Politico reports, “Republicans stay mum on whether they’ll return campaign cash from embattled Max Miller.”
The money — more than $70,000 in all — has largely been donated in increments of $1,000, $2,500 or $5,000. In a few cases, such as with Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), the PAC maxed out with $10,000 donations.
Of these 16 Republicans who received money from Miller this cycle contacted this week by POLITICO, only the campaign for Rep. Brad Finstad of Minnesota said it had already returned its $5,000 contribution.
• Fact check. CNN’s Daniel Dale reports, “Fact check: Trump makes numerous false and misleading claims about vaccines and autism.”
Trump has long pushed vaccine misinformation. He delivered his latest inaccurate remarks at a White House event during which he signed an executive order that recommends that US children receive fewer vaccinations over a longer period of time than they do today.
Trump again floated the idea that vaccines cause autism, though that notion has been thoroughly debunked by extensive research in multiple countries. He again baselessly impugned the safety of the combination vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, which has for decades proven highly safe and highly effective.
He again wildly overstated the size of the vaccine doses children receive, which are nowhere near “the size of a bottle of soda.” He again wildly understated the prevalence of autism 20 years ago. And he again exaggerated the number of injections children have been required to receive.

title: AES Indiana seeks no action in ratepayer advocate’s rate rehearing request, amid lawsuit
description: AES Indiana filed a motion Wednesday asking the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to hold off on a second look at a recent rate case during legal action over the firing of a commissioner by Gov. Mike Braun. Braun fired Andy Zay on Aug. 3 after he was one of three votes supporting a $71 million AES […]
text:
The AES Indiana Harding Street electrical station in July 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)AES Indiana filed a motion Wednesday asking the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to hold off on a second look at a recent rate case during legal action over the firing of a commissioner by Gov. Mike Braun.
Braun fired Andy Zay on Aug. 3 after he was one of three votes supporting a $71 million AES Indiana rate hike. Zay fired back Aug. 10 in a lawsuit against Braun, alleging the governor’s office improperly pressured him to deny the settlement and that he wasn’t fired “for cause.”
AES Indiana doesn’t want any action taken in a rehearing Braun sought of the AES Indiana case, with newly appointed commissioner Joshua Bain replacing Zay.
Zay has also asked a trial court judge to stop Bain from taking over the spot or exercising any commissioner powers until the lawsuit is settled. Ultimately, Zay wants his seat on the IURC back.
The rate reconsideration was sought by the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor and Citizens Action Coalition. A decision is expected by a Sept. 8 deadline.
“AES Indiana respectfully submits that the allegations in the Zay Complaint, if true, may well invalidate any attempted action by the Commission on the OUCC and CAC Petitions in which Mr. Bain participated as a member of the Commission and Mr. Zay did not,” the filing said.
State’s ratepayer advocate asks regulators to reconsider $71M AES rate hike

It went on to argue that any adverse action to AES Indiana “would necessarily have to be addressed in any judicial review proceeding then initiated by AES Indiana.”
The investor-owned utility also said that Zay’s allegations “merit particular consideration” since the IURC is, by law, an “impartial fact-finding body” in utility proceedings. The Commission is not supposed to advocate for the public or the utilities in its decisions.
Zay’s complaint alleges that Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources Suzanne Jaworowski called him on June 15 — two days before the AES decision — to tell him, “You know affordability is a big deal to this governor” — as well as the day of, to “conve(y) Governor Braun’s disappointment with the outcome.”
Other representatives of the governor’s office told Zay he had “let the governor down” and that they’d “told (him) not to do this” in a meeting he attended later on June 17, according to the complaint.
Zay was called into another meeting on June 18 — this time featuring Braun, Chief of Staff Joshua Kelley, Jaworowski and Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray, whose office represents ratepayers in IURC matters.
“During that meeting, after discussion concerning utility rates and the AES Rate Proceeding decision, Governor Braun asked Gray, ‘How are we going to fix this?’” Zay’s complaint alleges.
He excused himself from the meeting, believing discussions had crossed into banned “ex parte” communications — seeking to sway a decision-maker in a case without the other parties to the case present. He was fired after seeking guidance from the Office of Inspector General about his ex parte communications and impartiality concerns.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: How abuse in a Tennessee businessman’s juvenile prisons remained under wraps
description: This story was originally published by ProPublica. The video clip lasted less than two minutes, but Tonya Webb remembers every second as heartbreaking. The grainy surveillance footage, dated June 29, 2024, showed a teenager in an anti-suicide smock being dragged violently by other teens across the floor at Middle Tennessee Juvenile Detention Center.
