title: DOJ targets 3 more states in effort to axe in-state tuition for immigrants
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Justice has sued New York, Connecticut and Vermont over laws that allow immigrants in the country without permanent legal status to pay in-state college tuition in the states where they live.The suits, filed Aug. 10, are part of a larger push from the Trump administration to go after states with such policies, as the administration seeks to curb any benefits that could be extended to people without permanent legal status.  Since President Donald Trump re-took office, the DOJ has sued 17 states over laws that allow noncitizen students who meet certain requirements access to in-state tuition at public colleges and universities, regardless of their immigration status. In five of those lawsuits the DOJ filed — targeting Texas, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Illinois — courts have already struck down the laws. All of those states, except for Illinois, had joined with the federal government rather than defend their laws. Beyond New York, Connecticut and Vermont, lawsuits are also pending in California, Colorado, Kansas, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Virginia.The lawsuits argue that the policies allow students without permanent legal status to pay drastically lower tuition for public education than U.S. citizens from other states.“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the DOJ’s Civil Division said in a statement regarding the New York, Connecticut and Vermont lawsuits. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country,” Shumate said.  Landscape of state lawsAt least 20 states and Washington, D.C., offer in-state tuition to “the states’ undocumented students,” according to the Higher Ed Immigration Portal, a project of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a nonprofit and nonpartisan organization. Roughly 525,000 “undocumented students” are enrolled in colleges and universities across the U.S., according to the Portal. An estimated 129,900 “undocumented students” are eligible for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. DACA is intended to help people brought into the country without legal documentation as children. The program, created by the Obama administration in 2012, protects participants from deportation and allows them to receive work permits and obtain driver’s licenses. Five states, Arkansas, Idaho, Maine, Ohio and Texas, limit in-state tuition access to DACA recipients, according to the Portal.Ongoing court battles threaten DACA recipients in Texas with the possibility of losing their ability to obtain a work permit. ‘Unprecedented’Diego Sánchez, vice president of policy and strategy at the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said the DOJ’s efforts to pursue states that offer in-state tuition benefits to students without permanent legal status is “unprecedented.”“It’s a coordinated federal effort to dismantle state tuition equity policies that have existed for decades,” Sánchez told States Newsroom.Sánchez added that the policies “do not provide free college or special tuition discounts — they generally allow students who attended and graduated from high school in the state and meet additional state requirements to pay the same in-state tuition rate as the classmates they grew up with.” The students “still have to apply, they still have to be admitted, pay tuition and meet the same academic requirements as everyone else,” he said. “The state has already invested in these students ... these are benefits that don’t only apply (to) undocumented students.” DOJ goes after Texas firstThe DOJ’s lawsuits came after Trump signed an executive order in April 2025 that calls on the U.S. attorney general to stop the enforcement of state laws and policies “favoring aliens over any groups of American citizens that are unlawful, preempted by Federal law, or otherwise unenforceable, including State laws that provide in-State higher education tuition to aliens but not to out-of-State American citizens.” Texas was the first state the DOJ pursued over such policies. The Justice Department challenged in June 2025 the Lone Star State’s 2001 law — the first of its kind in the country — signed by former Gov. Rick Perry, a Republican. Rather than defend the law, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Trump-aligned Republican, sided with the DOJ to try to permanently block the state law and signed an agreement the same day the DOJ filed suit. A federal judge then blocked the Texas law.  A federal appeals court in July rejected an attempt from two advocacy groups, a Texas community college and a student to intervene in the case and defend the Texas law. The appeals effort came after the federal judge had earlier rejected the groups’ attempt to intervene. “It’s not the end of the road yet, but it’s been an uphill battle,” said Efrén Olivares, vice president of litigation and legal strategy at the National Immigration Law Center, one of several public interest groups that sought to intervene on behalf of one of the advocacy groups, the Texas community college and the student. “It’s a shame because for the last year, thousands of kids who, all they’re doing is trying to get a college education to better themselves and their families, are now prevented from doing so by exorbitant tuition.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT inspector general rules prison death a suicide
description: The OIG determined that Segundo Gamboy Guaranda died by suicide. Tt also found CT Dept. of Correction was 'negligent' in monitoring his cell.
text:
Editor’s Note: This article discusses suicide. Please take care while reading. If you or someone you know needs help, call the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or text 741741 for the Crisis Text Line.
The 33-year-old New Havener who died in a Whalley Avenue prison earlier this year left a suicide note claiming that his cellmate had extorted him out of more than $5,000 — in exchange for not telling other prisoners the charges he was facing.
That note was included in a report released Wednesday by the Office of the Inspector General that revealed the office’s finding that Segundo Gamboy Guaranda’s death was not caused by criminal activity. The OIG did find, however, that the Department of Correction was “negligent” in monitoring his cell. (Click here to read that report in full.)
The OIG investigates all deaths in DOC custody.
Guaranda was found dead and alone in his cell at the New Haven Correctional Center on Whalley Avenue on April 16. The OIG and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, OCME, determined that Guaranda, who appeared to have hanged himself, died by suicide.
“The evidence shows that the DOC was negligent in monitoring Guaranda’s cell,” Inspector General Eliot Prescott wrote. “There is, however, no evidence that another person was involved in Guaranda’s death. I conclude, as did the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, that Guaranda’s death was a suicide. I further conclude that his death was not the result of any criminal action.”
The Department of Correction thanked the inspector general for his diligent work.
“The DOC takes the wellbeing of all the individuals under its supervision — as well as the wellbeing of its staff — very seriously. The death of an incarcerated individual is traumatic for all involved,” DOC Public Information Officer Andrius Banevicius said in a statement to the Independent. “The DOC is continuing to review the findings with an eye toward strengthening our policies and practices, where and if appropriate, to ensure the safety of the individuals under our supervision.”
Guaranda had been arrested in August 2025 and was facing felony charges of first-degree sexual assault and risk of injury to a child. Guaranda had expressed concern that he would be unsafe due to his charges back in October to a counselor, who determined that Guaranda did not have suicidal ideation.
In a note that counselors found in Guaranda’s cell after his death, which was written in Spanish and appeared to be addressed to his brother, he said that the man who had been his cellmate for a month — before being moved to another prison the day before Guaranda’s death — had threatened to expose his charges to the others in the prison if Guaranda didn’t pay him $5,330.
In an interview with Guaranda’s brother, according to the report by Prescott, Guaranda had asked him to send money to various people who would use the money to obtain a bail bonds agency to help Guaranda get out of prison. Guaranda’s brother was in contact with multiple members of the cellmate’s family. After they received the money from him, they blocked him.
On the day of Guaranda’s death, his brother learned of the alleged extortion.
“I hope that one day you will forgive me,” Guaranda wrote in his suicide note, according to a translated version in the OIG’s report. “You have all the receipts for the transfers. If I say something about him, he has threatened to tell the others about my case. I ask you to make a complaint for all of the money.”
“Nano,” he wrote, “take care of yourself and take care of mother too.”
On the day of his death, Guaranda put up a sign in his cell window at 7:10 a.m. that read “Using Bathroom Give Me A Minute.” At 7:27 a.m., the sign was still up, and a correction officer shined his flashlight in the window but made no move to communicate with Guaranda or remove the sign.
At 8 a.m., the shift changed and another correction officer toured the unit. He saw the paper in the window and, when he got no response from Guaranda through the door, opened the door and saw Guaranda, who had hanged himself. He wasn’t breathing and had no pulse. The correction officer called for backup.
Guaranda was pronounced dead at Yale New Haven Hospital at 8:37 a.m.
“This is another tragic case illuminating the desperation of a person in custody who decides to take his own life. It is no secret that inmates with sexual assault charges or convictions face abuse from other inmates, particularly when the offenses relate to a minor,” Prescott wrote at the conclusion of Wednesday’s report.
“There is no dispute in this case that Guaranda committed suicide,” he continued. “His death, however, raises significant questions of law and fact regarding whether criminal responsibility for his suicide death could be imposed on any person under these circumstances.”
The report points to two people who could have acted criminally. First the correction officer, who falsely logged that he had properly conducted tours of the cell block the morning Guaranda died. Ultimately, the inspector general determined that the correction officer’s actions, which “may have been negligent and contrary to DOC policy,” could not be characterized as criminal conduct.
The second is the former cellmate, who may have committed larceny by extortion. Still, that conduct had been completed by the date of Guaranda’s suicide, and he had already been transferred to the custody of federal authorities.
“Finally, it is entirely unclear whether Guaranda’s decision to take his own life was the result, in whole or in part, of other mental health factors or depression from being faced with the real possibility of a lengthy prison sentence for sexually assaulting a minor,” he wrote. Therefore, his office would take no further action in the case.
“He was a decent individual,” Guaranda’s lawyer, William Gerace, said in April about his client, who was originally from Ecuador. Gerace said that Guaranda’s family had been “concerned about him for a while” and had been supportive of him during his time in prison. He said they were particularly concerned about his “mental state” during the weeks leading up to his death. Gerace also told the Independent at the time that Guaranda was facing “facing a jail sentence and deportation.”
Guaranda’s brother, Wilson, told the Independent for that same April article that Guaranda came to the United States a little more than two years ago in pursuit of work. Wilson said he had been shocked to learn about his brother’s death and said he would never suspect that his brother would take his own life.
Prison-reform advocates from across Connecticut — including in New Haven — have stepped up their critiques of the state prison system’s failures. 
Former state Commissioner of Correction Angel Quiros retired in May of this year after six years in the role. Sharonda Carlos has served as interim commissioner since. She has said that would train staff in new practices and promote transparency. The state also recently appointed an independent ombuds for the DOC.
Thirteen people have died in DOC custody so far in 2026.
This story was first published Aug. 12, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A Cambridge turf battle offers broader lessons
description: The Ahern Field saga is a reminder that when all stakeholders—parents, neighbors, young people, and taxpayers— show up together, they can move government.
text:
WHEN CAMBRIDGE OFFICIALS announced recently that the city was reversing its decision to install artificial turf at a local playing field,  the case could have been read as a small local victory for advocates of natural grass for a field surface. It was, however, far more than that. It exposed a larger problem in local governments in Massachusetts: Residents are often forced to become researchers, organizers, and oversight bodies just to get public systems to take their evidence seriously before decisions are made. 
Ahern Field is a small community field adjacent to a public school in East Cambridge. As part of a proposed $7.5 million improvement project, the city of Cambridge planned to install an artificial turf surface estimated to cost $3.5 million. For many residents, the concern was not merely the surface itself, but that artificial turf appeared to have been chosen first, with the public process coming afterward. 
The city did hold three public engagement events in total — though many residents later said they were unaware of them — and this is where the process issue becomes clear. At the first two sessions, residents who participated were invited to share ideas, and a majority expressed preference for natural grass. Yet by the third public event, a design open house in March 2026, artificial turf appeared in the plan as a settled direction.  
A local news outlet later quoted the deputy city manager saying staff entered the community process trying to be clear that shifting to turf was “a decision that was already made.” That is the difference between genuine engagement and check-the-box engagement: Residents are asked for input only after the most important choice has already been narrowed. 
Upon learning about the decision, residents organized, citing concerns about safety, heat, stormwater, microplastics, lifecycle costs, disposal, and community access. Over 2,000 residents signed a petition asking the city to retain natural grass and invest in a professionally designed, well-maintained grass field. The issue was brought to the attention of the City Council, which asked the city manager to explain the turf decision and pause construction.  
Community members persistently pressed the city with questions, and city councilors pushed for answers. The city eventually reversed its decision to install artificial turf. 
Ahern Field should not become just a story about grass. It is a reminder that when all stakeholders—parents, neighbors, young people, field users, and taxpayers— show up together, they can move government. But local democracy increasingly depends on residents doing investigative, organizing, and oversight work that public institutions should have done earlier. 
This pattern is not unique to Cambridge. Active community meetings and legal battles over similar issues are unfolding across the region right now, though outcomes do not always lead to the same favorable result.  
In Brockton, a $14 million to $18 million school budget deficit blindsided the school community and exposed serious failures in financial oversight and accountability. In Boston, the White Stadium debate has raised questions about public land, private partnership, cost escalation, and whether residents received sufficient information early enough.  
These cases point to the same civic problem: public trust breaks down when residents are asked to accept decisions before they can fully understand how they were made. Different issues may involve different facts, but the pattern is familiar: residents are asked to trust the process only after the process has already shaped the outcome. 
Government decision-making should be people-focused from the beginning. Major public decisions should invite input from affected communities, release source documents, show timelines, disclose who was consulted, compare realistic alternatives, and require independent review when health, environment, equity, or long-term cost is involved. 
No process can please everyone. Residents, however, should be engaged from the beginning, informed throughout, and given a meaningful opportunity to provide feedback before decisions are finalized. When officials make a misjudgment, they should take responsibility. Trust is not built merely by writing policies or issuing statements. It is earned through practice. 
The Ahern Field experience shows that local democracy can still work. Yet, it also shows how much labor residents must now do simply to be heard: requesting and reading reports, checking claims, organizing neighbors, pressing elected officials, and using evidence to challenge predetermined choices. 
Residents should not have to fight this hard to be heard. They are not obstacles to good government; they are the reason government has legitimacy in the first place. 
Jia-Jing Lee is a medical scientist, education advocate, and systems strategist based in Cambridge. A former postdoctoral fellow at Harvard Medical School, she works on local education, public process, and community governance issues.

name: Nevada Current
title: Colorado River negotiations continue as states await fed decision
description: Nevada’s top Colorado River negotiator said lower-basin states are still pressing for adjustments and attempting to forge consensus-based alternatives before federally mandated water cuts are finalized. Last month, the Bureau of Reclamation released its long-awaited 10-year plan to manage worsening water shortages along the Colorado River, including deep cut[...]
text:
John Entsminger, Southern Nevada Water Authority General Manager and Nevada’s lead negotiator on the Colorado River. (Photo Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Nevada’s top Colorado River negotiator said lower-basin states are still pressing for adjustments and attempting to forge consensus-based alternatives before federally mandated water cuts are finalized.
Last month, the Bureau of Reclamation released its long-awaited 10-year plan to manage worsening water shortages along the Colorado River, including deep cuts to Nevada’s allocation of the drought-stricken river. 
Arizona and Nevada criticized the framework for placing a disproportionate burden on the lower basin while sparing upper-basin states — Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and New Mexico — from mandatory water cuts.
John Entsminger, Southern Nevada Water Authority General Manager and Nevada’s lead negotiator on the Colorado River, provided limited details on the status of negotiations Wednesday during Nevada Democratic U.S. Rep. Susie Lee’s fourth annual Southern Nevada Water Summit.
“I’ve been on four or five phone calls this morning already. Negotiations are ongoing,”  Entsminger said. “I think there’s a short-term solution.”
At the center of the rift is whether upstream states will agree to evenly share mandatory water cuts and accept long-term conservation plans in order to spare downstream states from taking steeper cuts.
Entsminger said there is still hope for change in the federal operational guidelines proposed last month, and said negotiations have continued to move from the initial proposal toward a more acceptable outcome for lower basin states.
“We’ll keep talking to people, and that’s the overall goal. We saw a version A, and now we’re trying to land on version C or D that everyone can live with,” Entsminger said. 
The federal government’s framework for how to manage the river’s largest reservoirs has narrowed negotiations by presenting a preferred alternative, said Entsminger, but he believes another round or two of negotiation is still needed.
Entsminger said he sees a path to a possible short-term 1 to 3 year operating plan, but not yet a durable multidecade solution. If negotiations collapse, the federal government will issue its own operating decision.
This week, Lake Mead – the largest reservoir in the U.S. – dropped to a record-low water level, imperiling a crucial source of water and power for millions of Americans. 
Entsminger noted that the river’s century-old legal framework fails to address modern climate conditions, which have reduced the Colorado River’s flow by 20% over the last two decades. 
The 1922 Colorado River Compact, which allocated 7.5 million acre-feet for each basin, was based on a faulty model that assumed the river system could supply 15 million acre-feet annually.
Today, officials acknowledge only 12.4 million acre-feet flows from the river each year, meaning western states will have to agree on massive cuts to their water supply for the sake of the river. Since the turn of the century, Lake Mead has lost more than 65% of its storage.
“The challenge that confronts us right now is climate change and drought has been so severe that our ability to negotiate those kinds of compromises hasn’t been keeping up to this point,” Entsminger said. 
The Interior Department has yet to put out its finalized operating agreement, however state leaders have pushed back on the agency’s preferred alternative. 
Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo last month said the federal plan “seeks to impose unrealistic reductions on Nevada and our water users,” and “could have devastating economic and environmental impacts on Nevada.”
The governor called for “shared sacrifice from all water users across the Colorado River Basin.”
Nevada’s preference remains negotiation over litigation, said Entsminger, but each state will evaluate the eventual federal record of decision independently. Entsminger said Nevada would also protect its interests if litigation arose.
“On behalf of Nevada, our first, second, and third choice is negotiation and cooperation,” Entsminger said. “But at the end of the day, if somebody wants to challenge something, we also have to protect our rights.”
The Bureau of Reclamation’s 10-year plan laying out a new operating blueprint for the Colorado River beginning in 2027, comes amid record low snowpack across the West. Those conditions have motivated states to reach a compromise, said Entsminger. 
“Bad water years always incentivize negotiation,” Entsminger said. “ I would harken back to 2019. Right as we were about to sign the drought contingency plan, we got one of the four wettest years in the 21st century. And that wet year almost derailed the deal.”
Mike Connor, a water official for the Biden, Obama, and Clinton Administrations, also warned states against litigation when it comes to Colorado River matters.  
“Quite frankly, if you’ve got any certainty that you’re going to win, I ask you to look at the history of litigation in the Supreme Court in water cases and reconsider your position,” Connor said.  
Lee highlighted federal funding which has kept Lake Mead from collapsing, including $141 million in federal funding for 20 water projects across Nevada under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law enacted during the Biden administration.
The Bureau of Reclamation, which manages the Hoover Dam, also recently authorized investing $52 million in three wide-head turbines capable of operating at low water levels, which would help protect hydropower capacity at the  dam.
“Despite everything going on right now, I do believe there’s still hope, and as Nevadans, we’ve consistently demonstrated that economic growth and responsible water management go hand in hand,” Lee said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Who is Marty O’Donnell?
description: Marty O’Donnell has taken the road less traveled to running for Congress. A Republican, O’Donnell has never held elected office. His website, which lists his many accomplishments as a composer of jingles and video game scores, details no civic involvement.  O’Donnell “is a composer with time on his hands. He’s looking to bring sanity back […]
text:
Marty O'Donnell at a Donald Trump event in Las Vegas on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Marty O’Donnell has taken the road less traveled to running for Congress. A Republican, O’Donnell has never held elected office. His website, which lists his many accomplishments as a composer of jingles and video game scores, details no civic involvement. 
O’Donnell “is a composer with time on his hands. He’s looking to bring sanity back to Congress, stopping the government from being an impediment to our families and more of a champion for them,” says his website. 
O’Donnell’s first foray into politics came in 2024 when he ran for Congressional District 3 just three years after moving to Southern Nevada to be closer to his grandchildren, he said on his podcast. He still owns a home in California near Montecito.
O’Donnell came in fourth in the 2024 Republican primary with 21% of the vote, following a campaign focused on border security and traditional family values. Rep. Susie Lee, a Democrat, went on to defeat Republican Drew Johnson by less than three percentage points. President Donald Trump won the district. 
Congress, O’Donnell said on his podcast, is not on his bucket list. 
“It’s not on anybody’s bucket list except bad people who just want power,” he said, recalling being approached by a political operative. “When they asked me to run, I’m like, ‘Why would I do that?’ And he goes, ‘You know, Marty, you have to understand how hard it is to find good people to run for Congress.’ And I thought, ‘Oh, there it is in a nutshell.’”
O’Donnell will go head to head against Lee, who is serving a fourth term, and who O’Donnell deemed “horrible” on his podcast. He has loaned his campaign $3 million, according to federal election records.
As of August 1, the Nevada Secretary of State reports CD3 has 176,605 registered Democrats, 155,094 Republicans, and 265,991 nonpartisan voters. 
O’Donnell declined to be interviewed for this story and did not respond to questions in writing about the most pressing issues facing Nevada and the U.S. 
At a campaign office opening last weekend, O’Donnell, in audio provided to the Current, said that if elected, he would “absolutely, in a heartbeat” vote to authorize President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, and said the president “needs to be able to do quick military action” because Congress is slow.
On his podcast, O’Donnell says he wants to be part of Trump’s team “so he has a four-year presidency rather than a two-year presidency.”
“The magic part of Donald Trump – former Democrat, not really a lifetime conservative — but someone who’s seen that the goose has been neglected, and he’s being nice to the goose again,” O’Donnell stated. “So he’s this great populist who is recognizing, you know, where wealth comes from, and he’s being nice to the people. That’s why he’s 80/20, 90/10 on all these issues because most of the people are like ‘yeah this is let’s get back to the common sense stuff.’”
Manly men
O’Donnell’s podcast, the Marty O’Donnell Show, features interviews with guests ranging from former Superman actor and Republican activist Dean Cain to O.J. Simpson’s house guest, Kato Kaelin. None of his 29 guests are women. 
In an August 2025 interview, O’Donnell introduced Dr. Charles Cornish-Dale, who he noted has been “accused of many weird — fascist, nationalist, white nationalist, misogynist, you name it — he’s been accused of everything. And of course I’m being accused of those things too, so I had to talk to him to find out what’s true and what’s not true.”  
He called the interview “one of those sort of marriages made in heaven.”
On another episode last year, O’Donnell noted he has Swedish ancestry and attributes the good looks of some nationalities to Viking marauders, who he says were selective in their sexual assaults. 
There’s “probably some truth,” he says, to the theory ”that the reason all the Swedes and the Norwegians are such good-looking people is that the Vikings came over, raided England, and only took the good-looking women back.”
“Yeah, they’re gonna take back the hottest broads they find. Yeah, that’s absolutely a thing,” responded his guest, Aaron Visconti. 
O’Donnell went on to say the Vikings scored “double booty.” 
“You realize this is why so many people hate men like us because we… people don’t understand that we’re telling the truth, but there’s some humor involved,” he observed.
O’Donnell is an adherent to the traditional family – a husband, wife, and children, as the American ideal. Other iterations of family, he suggests, are a threat to Western culture.  
“Marriage defined as a union of one man and one woman isn’t just a Christian definition,” he said on social media in 2024. 
This week, O’Donnell posted the rescission of his invitation to attend a Halo reunion in California next month because LGBTQ staff did not “feel comfortable” about his attendance, citing his statements on the campaign trail. 
“If you thought we defeated Cancel Culture in 2024, guess again!” O’Donnell wrote. 
“What they’re accusing me of, of course, came from my political opponent and her, you know, lackeys in the industry, political industry,” O’Donnell said on a podcast Wednesday morning. “So there are magazines and websites that will, you know, try to support the Democrats in this case and say things about me that I didn’t say, and write headlines that are completely misleading and false.”
In a recent interview, O’Donnell cited Marxism as an “existential threat.” He noted “a weird alliance of all these groups that are, you know, like to pretend like they’re oppressed. So the LGBTQ+ people, the Islamists, the Marxists, you know, they’re all together now, acting like they’re all together on the same side.”
On his podcast last year, O’Donnell warned “We can’t be apologetic about being men and doing manly things, and having you know womanly, and you know, having families. Like, it’s like, being apologetic about that is going to cause the downfall of society.” 
He went on to say “that doesn’t mean you have to be, you know, you don’t have to be misogynistic and patriarchal and all the rest of it.”
In the same episode, the candidate asserted that families led by single parents can be “healed” but are not to be celebrated.
A traditional family, he asserted, “is the smallest, most fundamental building block of society, and for years it was like if you didn’t have that, you had what was known as a broken family.”
A  broken family, he added, “is not the end of the world. You can heal that. You can help that. We can have systems to help families that are not intact, but that’s not the ideal. You don’t celebrate broken families.  You help broken families because they’re broken, and I’m just surprised that we have to be explicit about that.” 
He asserted “it’s shocking” that not everyone agrees. 
About one-quarter of Nevada households with a child under the age of 18 are led by single parents.
“I don’t want a dentist who’s a weirdo in my community. I want a dentist who probably has a wife and a couple kids too, right? It’s like, or a husband and a couple kids,” he asserted. “Although I’ve never actually gone to a female dentist, That’s just me. I don’t know. I’m old-fashioned. I just haven’t seen one.” 
O’Donnell argues diversity, equity, and inclusion policies have ruined some video games and prompted a backlash. The re-release of Halo “is in large part due to the woke-ification of the gaming industry,” he wrote on an anti-DEI website that has since been taken down. “After years of gamers fighting the infiltration of DEI in the industry, we are finally winning.”
He also complained that some games offer the option to choose transgender characters. 
“It’s hard for gamers to immerse themselves in a game when they are required to choose a ‘body type’ instead of gender and provide pronouns for their character at the start,” he complained on the same website.
Boys’ club
In October 2017, when the #MeToo movement went viral and survivors of sexual harassment and assault emerged as a force in the political and corporate worlds, O’Donnell asked “Did Twitter do something to women that I missed? #soconfused”
O’Donnell’s former co-workers at Bungie have called him “the most right-leaning employee at the company.” 
“Well, Bungie made better games when it was a ‘boys club’,” O’Donnell said on the Marty Army Discord platform in 2024 of the news that a former colleague had been fired for sexual harassment. “I still remember trying to erase the artists’ white boards before women came to visit. I’ll never understand how Lorraine tolerated it.”  
‘Lorraine’ is O’Donnell’s former Bungie colleague, artist Lorraine McLees.
In social media posts from 2024 that have since been removed, but were preserved in screenshots on another account, McLees recalled an office Halloween party in 1999.
O’Donnell, disguised in a Telly Savalas mask , trench coat, and leather gloves, approached McLees who was cutting a piece of cake. McLees says when the unidentified figure got too close, she wielded the knife in his direction and told him to back off. 
O’Donnell countered on social media that he “NEVER touched anyone. The Bungie Halloween party story is hilarious,” he said. “Yes, the women got really creeped out but I made sure to never touch anyone, just loom.” 
According to McLees, the next day at work the women recalled their encounters with the masked O’Donnell, who, she noted, put roses on their desks and apologized.
“But that moment when I put up the knife was still a bad time. It wasn’t ok. I forgave Marty afterwards,” McLees wrote in 2024. “The ‘boys club’ mentality was laughable in how awful it was, because by this time I thought we were past that. But where are we now?”
Bungie employees, she added, ”laughed about it what, 11 years ago? Same way we laugh about inappropriate pranks we did as kids—but it is no longer funny when we demonstrably do not grow tf up and learn from it.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Labor, progressive groups launch $1M push to flip Missouri legislative seats
description: The organization that led the 2024 campaign to raise Missouri’s minimum wage and require paid sick leave is launching a $1 million grassroots campaign to defeat Republican lawmakers who helped repeal the paid leave requirement.  Missouri Jobs with Justice Action has joined Progress Missouri, the Missouri Voter Project — State PAC, Missouri Workers Power, Abo[...]
text:
Daniel Tucker, a leader with the Missouri Workers Center, teaches chants customized to an initiative petition to raise the minimum wage and mandate paid sick leave outside of the Secretary of State's office building in Jefferson City in May 2024 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The organization that led the 2024 campaign to raise Missouri’s minimum wage and require paid sick leave is launching a $1 million grassroots campaign to defeat Republican lawmakers who helped repeal the paid leave requirement. 
Missouri Jobs with Justice Action has joined Progress Missouri, the Missouri Voter Project — State PAC, Missouri Workers Power, Abortion Action Missouri and PROMO, an LGBTQ+ rights organization, to form Will of the People.
Missouri Jobs with Justice Action provided half of the money. The money will pay for canvassing and community events, said Executive Director Caitlyn Adams.
Missouri Jobs with Justice Action first used the initiative process in 2006 to establish a state minimum wage above the federal minimum,, and followed it with successful campaigns for increases in 2018 and 2024. 
The first initiative included annual adjustments for inflation. The 2024 measure also required employers to provide a minimum amount of paid sick leave that workers could use for personal illness or to care for a family member. 
The Republican-controlled legislature repealed those provisions in 2025. No Democrat supported the bill and only two Republicans opposed it. 
Other legislative actions, from redistricting to the two failed amendments on the primary ballot, are hurting supporters of the organizations in the coalition, she said.
“I feel very accountable to the folks that were impacted by those policies, and expect leaders to fight for those policies,” Adams said. “And we’ve got to start holding those politicians who ignore the will of the voters accountable.”
The money will be just a fraction of the cash that will be spent to influence the 16 state Senate and 129 Missouri House races that have candidates from both major parties on the Nov. 3 ballot. 
The most recent reports to the Missouri Ethics Commission show the following about campaign finance in Missouri:

The 53 Missouri Senate candidates and PACs aligned with them held $8.4 million in late July and have raised $11.2 million since the start of 2025.
House members seeking reelection and candidates who survived the primary had $7.7 million in campaign and PAC accounts after raising $10.2 million.
The 71 PACs that represent business, labor and political interests tracked by The Independent had just under $10 million in late July and have raised $22 million since the start of 2025. They combined to spend $5.8 million on operations and efforts to influence the Aug. 4 primary and contributed $9.1 million to candidates and other PACs.

The next reports, which will include spending totals through the primary, are due Sept. 3.
Legislative seats and ballot questions will be the battlegrounds this fall.
The only statewide office on the ballot is state auditor, and neither Republican incumbent Scott Fitzpatrick nor Democratic nominee Quentin Wilson have raised as much as some candidates for state Senate seats.
Fitzpatrick has raised $393,752 since the start of 2025, and a PAC working on his behalf, Missourians for a Responsible Budget, has raised almost $500,000. Together the two committees had just under $820,000 in late July. Wilson has raised $84,000. 
Will of the People will not try to compete for voter attention through broadcast advertising, Adams said.
“There’s a very smart way to run these campaigns and make sure that we’re heard,” she said. “That is going to be grassroots volunteer efforts, knocking doors, hosting events, doing town halls, and actions like that.”
Missouri Republicans hold a 24-10 edge in the state Senate and won 111 of the 163 Missouri House seats in the 2024 election. Based on fundraising, two Senate seats appear particularly competitive — the 8th District in Jackson County and the 30th District in Springfield.
House Speaker Jon Patterson, the Republican nominee in the 8th District, has raised the most among all candidates for legislative seats. His campaign committee raised $534,725 in the same period, while Missouri Alliance PAC, working on Patterson’s behalf, took in $1.4 million. The two committees held a combined $2.9 million in late July.
State Rep. Keri Ingle, the Democrat running against Patterson, has raised $317,837 for her campaign committee and $112,950 for KERI PAC. The two committees had a combined $440,000 in late July.
Twenty-one Missouri House districts were decided by 10 percentage points or less in 2024. Democrats won 11 and Republicans won 10. 
Three of those seats won by Democrats are uncontested this year. Democrats need to win three of the others — or score an upset elsewhere — to break the GOP’s two-thirds supermajority.
Among the 10 competitive seats Republicans won in 2024, GOP incumbents have substantial fundraising advantages in five. The candidates were roughly even in four others at the most recent reporting deadline. In the open 12th House District, Democratic candidate Tracy Steele held a 3-to-1 cash advantage over Republican nominee Jerry Hickey.
In the contested competitive seats won by Democrats in 2024, Democratic candidates have a fundraising advantage in six and are roughly even with their Republican opponent in the other two.
Republicans have a big cash advantage in their fund designed to help candidates in tight races. The House Republican Campaign Committee has raised $3.5 million for this election cycle and had $2.4 million on hand in late July. The House Democratic Action Fund, in contrast, has raised $791,472 and had $364,648 on hand in late July.
In the 2024 election, the House Republican Campaign Committee spent $2.9 million, almost four times what Democrats were able to spend.
“There are some key races across the state where grassroots organizing can have the greatest impact,” Adams said. “We’ll work aggressively to defeat candidates who continue to undermine democracy, take money out of our pockets, and put their corporate and political interests ahead of us.”
Part of the goal of the Will of the People PAC is to expand the list of districts that are competitive because that will make the winner more responsive, Adams said.
“We definitely,” she said, “want to hold people who are in leadership and in charge of making some of those decisions accountable.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ACLU-KY: Data shows 300% increase in ICE detainer requests after Louisville policy change
description:
Last year, Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg reinstated a detention policy for immigrants following complaints from the Trump administration. 

Since then, the move has led to a dramatic increase in requests to hold immigrants detained so the federal government can assume custody of the people, according to a new report from the American Civil Liberties Union[...]
text:
Federal immigration officers were at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on March 23, 2026, to help with airport security during the shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security. ICE agents are increasingly making arrests at airports.(Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)Last year, Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg reinstated a detention policy for immigrants following complaints from the Trump administration. 
Since then, the move has led to a dramatic increase in requests to hold immigrants detained so the federal government can assume custody of the people, according to a new report from the American Civil Liberties Union of Kentucky released Thursday. Data shows a nearly 300% increase in the average number of monthly detainer requests since the policy change. 
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) says those “detainer requests” ask jails to notify the federal government as early as possible before they release an immigrant, and hold them 48 hours beyond the time they would normally release those people.
Using data from the Deportation Data Project, ACLU-KY said that between Aug. 1, 2025, to March 1, 2026, a seven-month period, ICE filed 344 detainer requests, or an average of 49.1 requests per month. From Jan. 1, 2024 to Aug. 1, 2025, a 19-month span, ICE made 326 requests, which averaged 17.2 per month. 
Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg, who is currently seeking reelection, announced last summer the city would reinstate a 48-hour hold for “inmates who are arrested for crimes, are booked in our jail and are subject to deportation notices” to allow federal officers time to take custody of those inmates. The move came after the Trump administration called Louisville a “sanctuary city” for not having the hold policy and threatened its federal funding. ACLU-KY had asked the city to reconsider the policy at the time. 
“Louisville residents were told this would be a limited policy affecting a relatively small number of people. The federal government’s own data show something very different,” said Amber Duke, executive director of the ACLU-KY in a Thursday statement. “This policy has made Louisville’s jail a far more direct pathway into federal immigration detention and removal. That is especially troubling when we are talking about an already overcrowded jail where 23 people have died since May 2021.”
In light of the recent findings, ACLU-KY is asking Greenberg to reverse the 48-hour policy and provide a public account of: 

The number of ICE detainers Louisville has received and honored.
 The number of people held beyond their scheduled release
 The number transferred into ICE custody
 The additional jail time created by the policy
 The financial cost of the policy to Louisville taxpayers.

ACLU-KY also found ICE had requested detainer holds for 311 people between August 2025 to March 2026, and 286 of those people were booked into ICE detention. Plus, 157 of those people were removed from the U.S. by ICE. 
Per the ACLU, the data said that since the city policy change, the average number of monthly ICE detention stints increased by about 350% and the average number of monthly non-custodial ICE arrests increased by more than 150%. 
Across Kentucky, 10 jails hold immigration detainees. According to data from Relevant Research, about 1,200 people are in a county jail on behalf of ICE. About 71% of them, or 863 people, are in the non-criminal population. 
ICE arrests in Louisville have made headlines in recent weeks. Sarafinah Bukirwa, who was detained at the Louisville airport before a flight, was released by a federal judge after her family and Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey said she was not receiving adequate medical care for sickle cell anemia. Online records did not list a clear charge for Bukirwa at the time. 
This is a developing story.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ towns, school districts owe millions to public worker health plans
description: As state-run health benefits plans rise in cost, some towns and school districts owe the plans tens of millions of dollars.
text:
As state-run health benefits plans rise in cost, some towns and school districts owe the plans tens of millions of dollars. Newark owed the State Health Benefits Program $11.4 million more than three years after it dropped coverage from the state-run plan. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)Municipalities and school districts owed New Jersey’s public worker health programs nearly $50.5 million in arrearages earlier this year, months before experts recommended steep rate increases for health plans that insure hundreds of thousands of school and government workers.
The debts owed by nearly 50 local units are part of the mix behind another year of steep premium increases for state-run health plans that have become increasingly unstable in recent years amid what actuaries have called a “death spiral.” Mounting costs drive some towns and school districts to leave the state-run plans for private plans, driving costs yet higher and leaving the state-run plans in distress.
Assemblyman Mike Inganamort (Photo by Hal BrownNew Jersey Monitor)
“The delinquent payments just put salt in the wound, and I recognize they are not alone driving the death spiral. Don’t get me wrong — I’m not suggesting they are. But if there’s death by a thousand papercuts, these are quite a few papercuts,” said Assemblyman Mike Inganamort (R-Morris).
Thirty-five local governments owed the State Health Benefits Program $28.1 million in April, while 13 school districts owed $22.3 million to their state-run plan, according to a tally of April arrearages drafted by the Treasury and released by Inganamort.
Though the arrearages are not the main drivers behind trends that could push premiums for current school workers up by as much as 34%, or 17.3% for local government workers, they contribute to rate growth by reducing the amount the state collects in premiums.
“It all adds up,” said Dudley Burge, the AFL-CIO representative for local government workers on the State Health Benefits Commission, which sets rates and approves contracts for the government worker health plans. “A one or one-and-a-half percent decrease in premium helps, right?”
It’s unclear how or whether individual local units’ debts have changed since April in most cases, but the overall level of outstanding balances has ticked up a bit since then. More recently, the plans were owed about $58 million, $43 million to the plan for local government workers and $13 million to the plan for school workers, according to the Treasury. Unlike the data provided to Inganamort, it’s unclear how the $58 million cited by the Treasury breaks out across individual towns and school districts.
Debts are marked delinquent if a town or school district is at least 31 days late on its payments.
The debts varied wildly by size and age. Paterson, which held the largest outstanding debt, owed the State Health Benefits Program $11.8 million in April, while Hope, a Warren County Township with fewer than 2,000 residents, owed just $4.04.
Some of the debts are held by local units that left state-run plans years ago or that have dissolved entirely. While state officials said they continued to work with locals to secure payment, it is unclear when those funds would arrive or, in some cases, if they ever would.
Darryl Isherwood, a spokesperson for the Treasury, said most disenrolled districts eventually pay off their balances. The department had not moved to forgive any debts owed to public worker health plans, Isherwood said.
“Treasury continues to work with local employers to try to collect all outstanding amounts owed,” he said.
The department had boosted outreach to governments in arrears, both to collect what’s owed and to help towns and school districts avoid expulsion, Isherwood said.
In April, disenrolled districts’ debts were significant, accounting for about $26.9 million across school and local government plans.
In general, those debts were concentrated in a handful of units: Newark (which owed $11.4 million), the Hudson County Schools of Technology ($11.6 million), and the Orange Board of Education ($2.4 million).
Both Newark and the Orange school board left state plans in 2023. They last made payments on their debt that February and March, respectively. A spokesperson for Newark did not provide comment.
The Hudson County Schools of Technology last made a payment on its debt last October. They separated from the public plan this February.
Burdge said Paterson’s debt did not appear on a separate report drafted for health benefit commissioners in March, suggesting its arrearages are new. Diana Nunez, a spokesperson for the city, said its debt was related to the timing of state transitional aid and would soon be resolved for the rest of the year.
“Because many of the city’s largest costs come before a significant portion of its revenue is received, the city must prioritize certain payments until those funds become available. If transitional aid were distributed evenly over the course of the year, the city would be current on all of its financial obligations at all times,” Nunez said.
Inganamort said the state should get more aggressive in collecting health benefit debts, including by cutting or withholding state aid to districts that owe money to the state plans.
“What I think we should consider is any public entity that has a delinquent payment to the state, that should be reflected in any aid that they do get from the state of New Jersey, whether it’s to the municipality or the school district,” he said. “I don’t believe we should continue to give aid to entities that owe the state money.”
In some cases, debts may be unrecoverable because the unit that owes them has closed.
That appears to be the case for the Wildwoods Joint Construction Office, which owes government workers’ plan $7,714.45 and, according to Civil Service records, ceased to exist in 2007.
The School Employees’ Health Benefit Commission is due to vote on rate increases for next year on Aug. 19. The State Health Benefits Commission has tentatively set its rate renewal vote for Aug. 26.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Treating opioid misuse with mindfulness therapy could save thousands of dollars, new study says
description: A mindfulness treatment created at the University of Utah in recent years has proved to be effective at decreasing opioid misuse. Now, a new economic study found it could also save hundreds of thousands of dollars per patient. That’s if healthcare, criminal justice and lost productivity costs are taken into account.  An opioid addiction epidemic […]
text:
The J. Willard Marriott Library on the University of Utah campus in Salt Lake City is pictured on Saturday, Aug. 23, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A mindfulness treatment created at the University of Utah in recent years has proved to be effective at decreasing opioid misuse. Now, a new economic study found it could also save hundreds of thousands of dollars per patient.
That’s if healthcare, criminal justice and lost productivity costs are taken into account. 
An opioid addiction epidemic can cost the United States as much as $4 trillion per year, according to a study by the firm Avalere Health. However, a form of therapy called Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement, or MORE, can save $12 for every dollar spent in those costs, according to a University of Utah health economist’s evaluation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The treatment, according to the analysis, is two to six times more cost-effective than other addiction treatments and can save more than $324,000 throughout a patient’s life.
University of Utah economics professor Fernando Wilson, who conducted the economic analysis, said in a news release the results suggest that a wide implementation of the MORE therapy could be a potent and cost-effective solution for the opioid crisis.
“At a relatively low cost, MORE has strong potential to reduce opioid misuse and generate substantial economic benefits for patients, health systems and society,” Wilson said. “The cost of implementing MORE is small, and its potential payoff in averting misuse and risk of opioid use disorder is very large.”



Let us know what you think...


 


The therapy was developed by former University of Utah professor Eric Garland, who also co-wrote the economic evaluation. It aims to teach mindfulness skills to regulate cravings and pain, as well as other tools to manage stress and negative emotions and to “savor pleasant, healthful and life-affirming experiences,” according to a past release about the therapy.
“Rather than getting caught up in the pain or craving, we teach people how to step back and observe that experience from the perspective of an objective witness,” Garland said then. “When they can do that, people begin to recognize that who they truly are is bigger than any one thought or sensation. They are not defined by their experiences of pain or craving; their true nature is something more.”
Opioid overdose deaths have decreased this year in the state, according to data from the Utah Department of Health and Human Services, but remain an issue. This year there have been 172 deaths linked to opioid overdoses in Utah, 10% fewer than in 2025. And, there have been almost 700,000 opioid prescriptions dispensed, also a 10% decrease from last year.
A clinical trial on the therapy following 250 adults with chronic pain on long-term opioid therapy who misused opioids found that the treatment “reduced opioid misuse by 45%, led to improvements in pain symptoms and opioid dosing and strengthened the brain’s responses to positive experiences to reduce cravings,” the university said this month.  
“Opioid misuse is a major driver of overdose deaths, hospitalizations, homelessness and economic loss, so substantially reducing opioid misuse could have huge positive consequences for society,” Garland said. “Our study suggests that MORE could be part of a scalable solution that improves outcomes for patients while also reducing burdens on the health care system and society at large.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington poised to elect its first openly trans legislator
description: Jaelynn Scott is set to become Washington’s first openly transgender legislator after sailing through last week’s primary.  She also could be one of only two members of the Democratic Socialists of America in the Legislature.  “I think it’s important that people see themselves in me, and the fact that they can run and they can […]
text:
Jaelynn Scott is likely to represent the 37th District in the Washington state Legislature. (Photo courtesy of the Jaelynn Scott campaign)Jaelynn Scott is set to become Washington’s first openly transgender legislator after sailing through last week’s primary. 
She also could be one of only two members of the Democratic Socialists of America in the Legislature. 
“I think it’s important that people see themselves in me, and the fact that they can run and they can win,” Scott said.
Scott, who leads the Black trans advocacy organization the Lavender Rights Project, will represent the 37th Legislative District in south Seattle. She’s received over 88% of the primary vote, facing only a college student running as an independent. 
She feels being the first is a “heavy burden.”
“You sometimes feel like you have a weight on your shoulder because you’re carrying the sort of hopes, dreams, wishes, concerns,” Scott said. 
“I don’t want to do it alone for long, and so I need people to join me,” she added.
Scott will also be the first Black openly trans state lawmaker elected in the country. In Massachusetts, Althea Garrison served one term in the 1990s, but was outed while in office and didn’t publicly confirm she was transgender until years later.
Scott is an ordained Buddhist minister, but isn’t practicing currently. She moved to the Central District in the 37th in late 2024, and has worked in the district for nearly a decade. She grew up in Mississippi. 
The seat opened up with Rep. Chipalo Street seeking the state Senate position Rebecca Saldaña is vacating to run for King County Council. 
Scott will be on the ballot in November alongside a conservative-backed initiative to bar transgender girls from competing in girls’ school sports. She recently spoke at the rally launching the “No Hate in WA State” campaign to defeat the Let’s Go Washington initiative.
The Trump administration has also tried through various means to restrict the ways transgender Americans can participate in society.
Scott says the Legislature has taken an “incrementalist approach and one that is too moderate.”
“This urgency of this moment actually kind of demanded that I try at least to go in to be a voice for the community,” she told the Standard this week.
Rep. Shaun Scott, the Legislature’s other democratic socialist, hopes Jaelynn Scott’s presence on the House floor can “change the ways issues related to the LGBTQ+ and the trans community are discussed.” 
Some recent debates over parental rights have spiraled into diatribes about transgender people from conservative lawmakers. Let’s Go Washington also has a parental rights measure on the November ballot.
Shaun Scott also believes Jaelynn Scott will be an ally in his push to tax major corporations. 
“When there are two different Rep. Scotts making that point, it helps,” he said, noting the two are not related.
The first-term Democrat from the 43rd District proposed a payroll tax on large employers, but it didn’t go anywhere this year as progressives instead forged a successful effort to pass an income tax on high earners.
Jaelynn Scott’s top focus is raising more revenue for state services via taxes. 
“It’s a matter of life and death at this point and the moment for a very careful strategy is well beyond that,” she said.
She’d like that money to go toward investing in housing construction, education and healthcare. The Legislature’s cuts this year to state childcare funding troubled her. Scott’s Lavender Rights Project helped lead the charge to recently open a new supportive housing complex. She wants the state to build more public-owned housing.
She has also expressed support for legislation considered this year to bar law enforcement in the state from employing former federal immigration agents hired under President Donald Trump. 
The 37th district’s other state House member faces a tough reelection campaign. Rep. Sharon Tomiko Santos, D-Seattle, trails in a two-candidate primary to Kelabe Tewolde, who is running to her left. Santos is the longest-serving active member of the Legislature. Jaelynn Scott supports Tewolde, despite having a “lot of love and respect” for Santos. 
The district covers diverse south Seattle communities like Beacon Hill, Rainier Valley, Columbia City and the Central District.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Sen. Amy Klobuchar needs to tell us who she might name as her successor if she becomes governor
description: If Sen, Amy Klobuchar becomes Minnesota’s next governor, then she’ll be in the unique position of potentially appointing her own successor to the U.S. Senate. Klobuchar’s seat has been held by the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party since the turn of the century. Klobuchar has won each of her four Senate campaigns by double-digit margins. It’s likely that […]
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to audience members after the candidate forum for Minnesota governor at Farmfest in Morgan, Minnesota Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)If Sen, Amy Klobuchar becomes Minnesota’s next governor, then she’ll be in the unique position of potentially appointing her own successor to the U.S. Senate. Klobuchar’s seat has been held by the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party since the turn of the century. Klobuchar has won each of her four Senate campaigns by double-digit margins. It’s likely that whoever Klobuchar appoints to this seat will shape federal representation in Minnesota for years to come. 
There’s a possibility that Gov. Tim Walz could appoint a successor if Klobuchar resigns in the interim period between the November election and being sworn in as governor in January, but Walz can and likely would defer to Klobuchar, allowing her to make the appointment upon her inauguration. Speculation of a handshake deal — wherein Klobuchar would appoint Walz to her seat — was quickly put to rest when Walz told reporters he’d “rather eat glass” than be appointed to the U.S. Senate. Neither Walz nor Klobuchar has made any public comment on whom they’d appoint in the likely scenario that she wins her campaign for governor. 
Former Gov. Mark Dayton appointed Minnesota’s junior senator in 2018, and Sen. Tina Smith won two subsequent elections before announcing she’ll be retire at the end of this year. Now that Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has won the DFL nomination to replace Smith, does Klobuchar plan to appoint the runner-up, U.S. Rep. Angie Craig?  Does she have someone else in mind? Is there a shortlist of potential candidates? 
What kind of governor would Amy Klobuchar be?

There are very few instances in the modern era of a sitting U.S. senator running for governor and being in a position to appoint their own successor. Sen. Frank Murkowski of Alaska won the governor’s race in 2002 and appointed his daughter Sen. Lisa Murkowski (prompting Alaska to change laws around appointments). Sen. Jon Corzine was elected governor of New Jersey in 2005 and appointed Sen. Bob Menendez to replace him. Menendez is currently in prison for federal corruption charges.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This isn’t to imply Klobuchar would appoint someone problematic to replace her in the Senate, but it does raise concerns about the importance of transparency with the appointment process. If Klobuchar is elected, the Senate appointment will likely be her first significant act as governor. Her choice to fill her Senate seat could be there for decades to come and have a much greater impact on the lives of Minnesotans than, say, Klobuchar’s lieutenant governor. 
Klobuchar owes it to voters to tell us ahead of time whom she plans to appoint to replace her.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge sides with Holly Springs in correcting electric grid issues, for now
description: Downtown Holly Springs, Miss., photographed on Wednesday, Dec. 4, 2024. The town has faced ongoing power reliability issues due to maintenance challenges with the Holly Springs Utility Department.
text:
HOLLY SPRINGS — A chancery court judge has put his faith, at least for now, in the city of Holly Springs’ ongoing efforts to revitalize its long struggling power system.
In a courtroom on the city square on Monday, Chancery Judge Lawrence Little told state and Holly Springs officials he would allow a consultant hired by the city, Michael Watson, to take charge of the department for the time being. Watson has spent the past nine months working with the city through a list of needed improvements.
Little’s hearing came at the end of a receivership hearing where the state Public Service Commission offered a different nominee to lead the utility, which provides electricity to about 12,000 customers in north Mississippi. 
Even though the city runs the Holly Springs Utility Department, the utility has expanded to the point where most customers live outside the city. For years now, the utility’s ratepayers have reported constant problems with the department, namely frequent power outages. Dealing with unmaintained infrastructure, failing substations and overgrown vegetation, the power grid has seen extended outages not only in recent winter storms, but also sporadically during sunny weather.
In 2024, state lawmakers gave the PSC authority to intervene over the department’s issues. Using that power, the commission last year unanimously found that the city failed to provide “reasonably adequate service” to its customers. The ruling paved the way for the PSC to petition a court to place the utility in a receivership.
The commission chose Frank Simon, a Michigan-based attorney who has worked as a receiver for a variety of businesses, including hospitals, cannabis companies and gas stations. State attorney Stephen Schelver described Simon as a “professional receiver” who could build a team of experts to lead the utility.
Vegetation grows on power lines near Ashland, Miss., on Wednesday, Dec. 4, 2024. Persistent maintenance issues have contributed to years of unreliable power for residents served by the Holly Springs Utility Department, a problem worsened by an ice storm in 2023. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Holly Springs attorney John Keith Perry contested that Simon had no utility experience while Watson, the city’s consultant, spent decades in the industry and had already become familiar with the local power grid.
In the end, Little opted to put Watson in charge of the department for now, reasoning that the move would provide some stability in a messy situation. The judge also said he wanted to be kept up to date about the utility’s performance and whether it’s meeting expectations set by the PSC and Tennessee Valley Authority, which has sold wholesale power to Holly Springs since 1935.
Initially, there was some confusion around the details of the decision from Little, who repeatedly coughed while delivering the message in the small courtroom. 
While Perry and Holly Springs Mayor Charles Terry celebrated the outcome as a “victory” for the city, Northern District Public Service Commissioner Chris Brown said he wasn’t sure that Little had officially named Watson as the receiver. 
“There is a lot of reporting right now regarding todays hearing,” Brown wrote on Facebook following the meeting. “Nobody has seen the Judge’s orders with his instructions on what happens moving forward.”
While Little still has yet to release an order, his staff attorney, Tara Scruggs, confirmed to Mississippi Today on Wednesday that Watson would be the receiver. Scruggs said she couldn’t give a timeline for when the order would be filed.
Most details of the receivership, such as how long it will last and what reporting the court will require, are unclear for now. Perry said Watson would have to update the court on his progress every 30 days. 
Terry, who took office as mayor last year, said the power provider has already seen improvements since Watson came on as a consultant, adding that he was a “great help” in enduring Winter Storm Fern. The storm knocked out power to 95% of the system’s meters and forced the city to borrow $10 million to pay contractors, Perry wrote in a February update to the PSC.
Holly Springs Alderman at Large Dexter Shipp, Mayor Charles Terry and City Attorney John Keith Perry outside a courtroom in Holly Springs, Aug. 10, 2026.  Credit: Alex Rozier
“I think we’ve been doing a good job on the outages and recovery time as well,” Terry said. “We’re still having outages, but not as bad as they used to be.”
With Watson’s help, the city has spent $500,000 on rights-of-way maintenance, replaced old meters, rebuilt relationships with neighboring power companies, and has started to catch up on its payments to TVA, Perry said Monday. The city is also developing a new mapping system, set to be ready in 2027.
Perry added that the city has found a long-term general manager to run the system, but declined to name that person for now.
After the hearing, Brown said the commission suggested Simon, who “does this all the time,” to give the city a new type of leadership. 
“It’s a system that desperately needs help. It’s in a crisis, so why not go a different direction?” he said.
TVA also offered its own candidate: Dana Jeans, former chief executive officer for Memphis Light, Gas and Water.
In another ongoing legal matter, Holly Springs is facing a federal lawsuit TVA brought against the city last year. In addition to owing TVA $18 million, Holly Springs violated the parties’ contract by committing a series of financial missteps, such as misallocating revenue and not raising rates appropriately, the lawsuit alleges. The two sides are set to meet Monday to discuss a settlement.

name: VTDigger
title: Killington passes budget after second vote but tumult still reigns
description:
Killington’s town manager is on administrative leave pending a disciplinary hearing, and large scale infrastructure projects are on hold because of a staffing shortage.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Killington passes budget after second vote but tumult still reigns.
text:
Killington’s welcome sign pictured in 2022. File photo by Natalie Williams/VTDigger

Local issues drove high voter turnout in Killington for the August primary Tuesday as residents weighed in on a special revote on the town budget. 
Over 40% of the town’s voters cast ballots on the $7.6 million budget, with 59% of those who voted supporting the measure. Voters previously shot down a budget that was $600,000 more on Town Meeting Day in March.
The budget vote comes against a backdrop of tumult in Killington’s town government: large water and road infrastructure projects have ground to a halt due to a staffing shortage and town operations are being managed by an interim employee after the selectboard placed the current manager on administrative leave earlier this summer. Meanwhile, the town’s finances are undergoing a forensic audit after voters called for the accounting in March.  
Town politics can be byzantine but the turmoil in Killington has been going on for some time and the list of grievances is long. The selectboard chair has faced ethics complaints from town residents and the board faces a pending unfair labor practice charge from the municipal employees’ union, for allegedly retaliating against unionization efforts by discussing slashing town positions.
On Tuesday, voters elected a fresh face to the selectboard, Celia Clancy, by a landslide. Clancy ran against Roger Riveria, who was appointed to the board after a selectboard member resigned in May. 
Gary Scannevin, a Killington voter who works in psychiatric rehabilitation, said at the polls that he hopes the town moves beyond animosity and “comes to some peace.” 
At a selectboard meeting on Monday, board member Bill Vines said the town has “made some mistakes” and the problems the town is facing date back several years when “irregularities” appeared in the town’s financial reports, causing members of the community to request a forensic audit. 
Disruption in Killington’s town leadership including the lack of a financial director has caused at least a six-month delay for water and road infrastructure projects, which have already seen holdups due to the Act 250 state land use permitting process, said Stephanie Clarke, planning consultant for the town. The projects are necessary for Killington Resort’s plans for a 450-acre retail and residential center. 
Town leaders face scrutiny
The role of town manager has been filled by an interim manager since the selectboard placed the current manager, Patrick Cushing, on administrative leave on July 9, only months after he filled the post.  
He faces potential disciplinary actions, including possible termination, due to alleged misconduct, according to a July letter from the selectboard to Cushing. Among other allegations, the board wrote that Cushing was “insubordinate” because he refused to follow a selectboard directive to identify a town position to cut from the budget.
In a two-part response letter provided to VTDigger, Cushing defended his actions. He wrote that the finance director left after the selectboard directed him to cut a position, and the remaining two positions — office manager and bookkeeper — were both part of a newly formed municipal union. 
“I continued to tell the Board that I did not believe either position could be eliminated without harming the Town operations and financial operations,” Cushing wrote.
In Cushing’s absence, Robert Kovalesky is serving as interim town manager, making him the seventh person in that role in the past five years. 
The selectboard chair and zoning administrator Jim Haff also has been under a cloud of two ethics complaints lodged by Killington residents in the spring. At Monday’s board meeting, the  board voted to accept part of the findings of a probe of the complaints by an outside investigator that found no wrongdoing and exonerated Haff.
The selectboard discussed adopting a formal ethics policy going forward. In the process of addressing the allegations, the town discovered its previous policy had not been properly vetted by the public.
‘Not in a bad place’
Despite the turmoil, the finances and staffing issues are being worked out, Kovalesky, the interim town manager, said. 
The town paid off maturing debt and is securing a loan to cover expenses while working to hire a contracted finance director, Kovalesky said.
“As the interim town manager, I am moving with appropriate urgency and transparency to stabilize to help our financial position and establish sustainable administrative practices,” Kovalesky said.
The town of Killington is focused on establishing better processes and procedures, said Jon Wysocki, vice chair of the selectboard. 
“We are moving in the right direction and contrary to what some people have said, we are not in a bad place,” Wysocki said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Democrats launch State Fair billboard ad criticizing Hinson’s wealth
description: The Iowa Democratic Party launched an ad campaign Thursday targeting U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson’s finances, aiming to reach voters at and around the Iowa State Fair. The campaign is part of IDP’s “Iowa Can’t Afford Ashley” tour, which has included events and ads criticizing Hinson for becoming more wealthy since she began serving in the […]
text:
Fans with the text "Iowa can't afford Ashley" will be distributed by the Iowa Democratic Party at the Iowa State Fair in 2026 as part of a campaign which includes a billboard ad near the fairgrounds. (Photo courtesy the Iowa Democratic Party)The Iowa Democratic Party launched an ad campaign Thursday targeting U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson’s finances, aiming to reach voters at and around the Iowa State Fair.
The campaign is part of IDP’s “Iowa Can’t Afford Ashley” tour, which has included events and ads criticizing Hinson for becoming more wealthy since she began serving in the U.S. House. Democrats, including Hinson’s opponent in the U.S. Senate race, state Rep. Josh Turek, have said Hinson has misrepresented herself in statements and interviews saying she is a “working mom” who understands the pressure Iowa families are facing because of rising costs.
Hinson has said she relates to struggles with affordability, but her opponents argue she has become significantly wealthier since first taking office in 2021, partially related to her husband not divesting from stock in his former company.
The new ad campaign focuses on sharing this information with visitors to the Iowa State Fair, an IDP spokesperson said. Blocks away from the Iowa State Fairgrounds, a billboard advertisement stating “Ashley Hinson got up to 10x richer in Congress” and saying the Republican made “up to $7.5 million while in Congress” will appear and be seen by “thousands of Iowans leaving the fair” for the 10-day state fair, according to a news release. The numbers used in the ad refer to analysis of federal financial disclosures of Hinson’s finances between 2021 and 2026 published by the progressive news organization Heartland Signal.
A billboard near the Iowa State Fairgrounds in Des Moines on East University Avenue will feature an ad, paid for by the Iowa Democratic Party, criticizing U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson’s personal finances as she runs for the U.S. Senate seat in 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Iowa Democratic Party)
The ad, paid for by the Iowa Democratic Party and authorized by Turek’s campaign, will be on East University Avenue between East 27th and East 28th streets, according to the party.
IDP spokesperson Drew Myers said the ad campaign is a way to ensure Iowans heading to the State Fair know how the Republican candidate’s personal finances differ from an average Iowa family, and how her policies would raise costs.
Democrats have criticized Hinson’s vote to pass the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act, for not supporting extending premium subsidies under the Affordable Care Act as well as her decisions not to oppose President Donald Trump’s tariff policies or the war in Iran as positions that have driven up costs for Iowans, especially for healthcare and gas.
Hinson has not directly responded to statements about her personal finances, but has defended her position on measures like the 2025 tax and spending law, saying that the measure helped working families by repealing taxes on tips and overtime. Billy Fuerst, a campaign spokesperson for Hinson’s campaign, said in a July statement Turek “will only make life more expensive for Iowa families by voting with Chuck Schumer and the Radical Left in D.C.”
The IDP will also be distributing fans and placards from the party booth at Iowa State Fair saying “Iowa Can’t Afford Ashley” as part of the campaign.
