name: WyoFile
title: Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise.
description:
New analysis of more than 300 bear encounters suggests canine companions often increase odds of conflict and rarely serve as the early warning systems many recreationists assume.
The post Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Earlier this summer, I was jogging on a local trail with my 7-year-old black lab mutt, Camas, when she suddenly froze. The fur along her spine bristled. Then she let out a single, sharp bark — a timbre I’d never before heard. 
I caught the unmistakable musk of an animal and my hand shot to the bear spray on my chest. Halfway up a tree less than 20 yards away, a beautiful, small cinnamon black bear stared back at us.

The author’s companion, Camas, in bear country. (Nick Mott)

The bear scampered off as Camas growled, standing her ground in front of me on the trail. “Good girl,” I told her, my heart rate slowing to a normal pace. My dog, I assumed, warned me early of a potential threat. I was proud. 
In bear country, common wisdom holds that dogs serve as early bear alarms, or even deterrents. That belief, however, has long rested mostly on anecdote. Until recently, almost no one had tested whether it was actually true.
A new study in the Journal of Wildlife Management analyzed bear-dog conflicts involving black, polar and brown bears from Alaska to Florida. The results challenge the idea that dogs make people safer in bear country and they have me rethinking my relationship with Camas in the woods.

(Journal of Wildlife Management)

“If you think a house pet is likely going to be your bear, not only detector but deterrent, you might want to think twice about that,” lead author of the paper Tom Smith told me over Zoom, one of his dogs begging for attention in the background while mine snoozed next to me. 
Smith, a research wildlife biologist at Brigham Young University in Utah, analyzed 326 bear-dog encounters spanning more than a century, drawing from newspaper articles, federal and state government reports, books, records compiled by other bear specialists, and internet searches. 
Smith began working with bears more than 30 years ago in Alaska’s Katmai National Park. He’s published influential research on bear spray and guns as bear deterrents, and has become one of the world’s leading experts on human-bear interaction. “As soon as you become the bear guy, then everybody comes running to you for advice on how to be safe,” he said. “So I thought, ‘I’m going to have to get to the heart of this.’”
Smith has long been interested in the way dogs impact humans’ odds of an encounter in bear country. But the issue became urgent and tangible to him following a 2023 attack that left two people and their dog dead in a tent in Canada’s Banff National Park. The issue hasn’t gone away. This summer alone, a jogger and his dog were mauled near Island Park, Idaho, while recordings of separate encounters involving dogs in Banff and Alberta went viral online. 
The findings
The data show people are largely unprepared for bear encounters and naive to their possible consequences. Dogs ran away, fought with bears, provoked confrontations, drew owners in to fight off bears barehanded, and even boomeranged bears back to people. 
The first surprise in the data was how few people carried any deterrent at all. That might be because people thought, erroneously, Smith says, that dogs would be sufficient to keep bears away. Recreators wielded bear spray in only about a tenth of cases and a firearm in roughly a third. All told, five people and 56 dogs died in the encounters Smith analyzed.
Contrary to some common wisdom, dogs also weren’t effective warning systems for bears. In fact, they alerted their owners early of a bear in only 1 in 11 of the encounters the study analyzed. Dogs provoked the bear, instigating the encounter, in more than half the cases. After the bear conflict began, things didn’t look much better: Dogs tangled with bears about 40% of the time, ran away in 20% of encounters, and didn’t engage at all in about 17% of cases. So much for dogs being excellent protectors.

(Journal of Wildlife Management)

Other findings were less surprising. Leashes were a major decider in the severity of the interaction. Unleashed dogs were involved in six times as many incidents as leashed pets. Smith said dogs without a leash can dart ahead of owners or crash through brush and spook a bear. Canines can also act as bear boomerangs. In 27 of the encounters, dogs brought a bear back to their owners. In 70% of these instances, the dog owner was injured. Worse yet, many owners in the data came to rescue their pet when it got in a scuffle with a bear, often with no deterrent. The result: 85% of the time, those owners were injured. 
Additionally, the data reinforced something bear experts have known for years: the larger the group of people, the less likely the encounter. However, the presence of a dog dramatically shifts that risk. Dogs roughly doubled the odds of a conflict compared to the same-sized groups with no canine companions. 
Taken as a whole, the data paint a portrait in which bears and domestic dogs don’t get along. Smith suspects it’s part of the long evolutionary relationship between bears and wolves. For thousands of years, wolves competed with bears for food, killed cubs and even kicked bruins off carcasses. Some of this behavior is on public display in places like Yellowstone National Park, where populations of both species flourish. Modern dogs may still trigger those ancient instincts. 
Smith recognizes limitations and nuance in his data, too. For one, it’s important to note that the dogs in the analysis were domestic companions, not highly-trained guardian dogs meant to fend off predators — which data show can reduce bear presence at ranches and farms. Also, data on human-bear conflict inherently shows a bias, depicting only the encounters that went majorly wrong rather than the majority of experiences when people venture into the places bruins live and the species coexist without incident. “For the most part, people and their dogs pass through bear country without incident,” Smith wrote in the paper.
Should your pup join the hike?
“The takeaway isn’t to keep dogs out of bear country,” Smith said. “The takeaway is there are things you can do that greatly improve your odds.”
Best practices, backed by Smith’s data, say to travel in groups, eliminate smells if you’re camping and make noise. Bear bells, he says, don’t work. Above almost all else? “You have no business being in bear country without a deterrent,” Smith said. 
Dogs just don’t cut it on that front. According to Smith, bear spray has the highest likelihood of fending off an aggressive bear for the vast majority of recreationists in bear country. But firearms can work too for experienced users. Carry your spray (or gun) where you can reach it in a split second. No matter what deterrent you choose, practice with it. Bear encounters can happen in seconds. 
Sota the pudelpointer follows a ridge in the northern Wyoming Range in 2023. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
If you do take your dog, consider a leash. “It’s not just dogs and bears,” Smith said. “It’s also dogs and everything else.” Smith’s own dog had been sprayed by a skunk twice in the last month. Mine finds few greater joys in life than chasing ground squirrels, marmots and grouse. So, we’re both faced with navigating how to behave in wild places with these family members that, if they see a deer or elk or bear, may not be able to hold themselves back.
Since talking with Smith, I’ve thought about the role Camas plays in bear country in a more nuanced way. She’s warned me about bears — even since that encounter on my jog. But she’s also ignored bears less than 30 yards away, chased wildlife she shouldn’t and, even in her younger days, treed a black bear.
The lesson isn’t that dogs don’t belong in bear country writ large. It’s that they’re dogs. If recreating in bear country is an odds game, they’re not doing you any favors. As much as we love and trust them, they’re unpredictable. And they can make things worse as often as they make things better. 
“It’s a personal thing, it really is,” Smith said. “We work in statistics with a pool of instances. But you are not a pool of instances. You’re you.”
The post Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise. appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: State management of grizzlies would be a disaster
description:
Grizzlies make the landscapes we share feel larger, wilder and more alive. They deserve more than bare-minimum population objectives, write guest columnists Chris Kassar and Ryan Kempfer.
The post State management of grizzlies would be a disaster appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
We moved to Jackson because few places still feel as whole as this region does, with Grand Teton and Yellowstone national parks, abundant public lands and waters and a quality of life shaped by wildness.

Opinion

Most of all, we moved here for the incredible wildlife. That includes elk, moose, mule deer, wolves and pronghorn. And also, the iconic grizzly bear, a true symbol of Northern Rockies wildness and the vast, connected landscapes that sustain it.
Our business also benefits from having these magnificent animals in the landscape. Every year, people come from around the world to watch and photograph wildlife. They are in awe of the abundance and diversity here — the sight of a moose coming out of the willows on a misty morning or an elk herd during the rut in fall.
But nothing moves people more than seeing a grizzly bear.
As wildlife guides, we see this again and again. Each time we meet a new group, we ask what they hope to see most. Without fail, the answer is “a grizzly.” Visitors know there are only a handful of places in the Lower 48 where seeing one is even possible. They understand, instinctively, that grizzlies mean something larger: intact habitat, protected public lands, and a landscape still wild enough to hold them.
Yet at the same time, grizzlies are fragile. By that, we mean they are a conservation-reliant species with slow reproduction, large habitat needs and little margin for unnecessary mortality.
They need habitat to roam and survive; wild places where they can gather and scavenge natural foods and rear young free from disturbance. They’re among the slowest-reproducing mammals in North America, and that fragility is why grizzlies were nearly wiped out during the western expansion of our country.
We treated them like vermin to clear the land for livestock, and it showed. By the early 1970s, only an estimated 136 grizzlies remained in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. The population was dangerously close to disappearing. In total, fewer than 600 grizzlies remained in the Lower 48 states, with the largest population living in Glacier National Park and the surrounding wildlands.
Today, there are roughly 1,900 grizzlies in the Lower 48, clearly a conservation improvement. But that didn’t just happen. It took tremendous work over decades by federal and state wildlife officials, conservationists, landowners and communities.
Now the Trump administration is ready to pull the rug out from the progress we’ve made recovering grizzlies and hand management to the states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming. Their argument is simple: Grizzlies have met the population targets in existing recovery plans, so the job is done and the states should take over management. They’re proposing to do this under a provision of the Endangered Species Act that allows some take of animals under specific conditions, known as “4(d)” rules.
But meeting minimum numbers in isolated recovery zones is not the same as lasting recovery. Those targets were created when grizzlies were on the brink, and we have learned far more since then about what they need to survive over the long term. In 2025, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service laid out a broader vision for recovery — one that recognized the importance of connected habitat and connected grizzly populations across the region. Wyoming, Montana and Idaho rejected that vision and challenged the decision.
That response says a lot. Rather than managing for true recovery, the states appear intent on managing for the fewest grizzlies they can get away with, in populations kept isolated from one another. Montana has pushed to make it easier to kill grizzlies linked to livestock conflicts on public lands. Wyoming even floated the idea of giving elk hunters “kill coupons” for grizzlies. That is not modern wildlife management. It is a throwback to the same 1800s mindset that nearly wiped grizzlies off the map in the first place.
At the same time, the Trump administration is working to industrialize our public lands through a range of policies that protect wildlands. These include undoing the Roadless Area Conservation Rule on national forests, a major push for industrial logging, and moves to dramatically increase motorized use across public lands. All of these are major threats to grizzlies because they rely on secure habitat, as do many wildlife species.
Long-term recovery depends on more than counting bears. It depends on limiting unnecessary killing, protecting movement between populations and allowing grizzlies enough connected habitat to remain genetically healthy and secure for generations to come.
We don’t value grizzlies only because our business depends on people coming here to see them. We value them because they change how this place feels. Their presence makes the landscape feel larger, wilder and more alive. It reminds us that we are lucky to share these public lands with animals that still embody true wildness.
Grizzly bears still need federal safeguards and robust habitat protections because the states have made their management intentions clear. These bears are not just management units or population targets. They are national treasures, and their presence is part of what makes this region whole, wild, and unlike anywhere else in the Lower 48.
Public comments on the proposed changes to protective grizzly bear regulations are due by Aug. 17.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Legislators, anti-abortion group promote data that says ID hasn’t lost OB-GYNs. Doctors push back.
description: Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal-fetal medicine physician, practices in Minnesota after she left Idaho in the spring of 2023, shortly after Idaho’s criminal abortion ban went into effect.  Although it has been nearly three years since she left, Cooper retained her Idaho medical license, she said.   “I have a sliver of hope that maybe things […]
text:
As campaigns for and against a proposed voter initiative that would repeal Idaho's abortion ban ramp up, an anti-abortion advocacy group has begun to question whether Idaho OB-GYNs have left the state since it went into effect. The state says it's hard to track, and doctors say the effect has been real. (Thanasis Zovoilis/Getty Images)Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal-fetal medicine physician, practices in Minnesota after she left Idaho in the spring of 2023, shortly after Idaho’s criminal abortion ban went into effect. 
Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal fetal medicine specialist .(Photo courtesy of Kylie Cooper)
Although it has been nearly three years since she left, Cooper retained her Idaho medical license, she said.  
“I have a sliver of hope that maybe things will get better in the future,” Cooper said. 
Cooper’s license, as well as every other active medical OB-GYN license in the state, would have shown up in data recently shared by the Idaho Family Policy Center — a Christian advocacy group that lobbied for Idaho’s criminal abortion ban and helped author a 2022 law allowing family members of a fetus aborted after six weeks to the sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. 
As campaigns for and against Proposition 1 — a citizen-led ballot initiative that would repeal the state’s strict abortion ban and provide protections for contraception and in vitro fertilization, ramp up for the Nov. 3 general election — the abortion law’s effect on the number of practicing OB-GYNs in Idaho has become a talking point. But determining the true number of doctors providing obstetrician-gynecologist care in the state isn’t easy. 
The state has said the number of active licenses do not reliably reflect how many OB-GYNs are currently practicing in Idaho. 
The Idaho Family Policy Center has underscored the licensing data to question, and file a lawsuit over, a 2025 Boise State University study that found Idaho had lost 35% of its OB-GYNs since 2022, when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and Idaho’s criminal abortion law went into effect.
The Idaho Family Policy Center posted this graph on Facebook Aug. 3. (Screenshot)
The policy center on Aug. 3 posted a graph on Facebook showing the number of active licenses increasing from 2022 to 2025, writing “Pro-abortion advocates are lying to you.” 
“The number of actively licensed OB/GYNs in Idaho has actually increased since our pro-life laws went into effect, according to data from the Idaho Board of Medicine,” the post said. 
The center’s posts about the licensure numbers have been shared by Idaho state legislators, such as Twin Falls Republican Rep. Clint Hostetler and Middleton Republican Rep. Tammy Nichols. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho medical board says it has no ‘reliable way’ to count active physicians 

The Idaho Board of Medicine, which is under the state Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses, shows the number of active OB-GYN licenses in Idaho going from around 280 in 2022 to just under 340 in 2024, according to the policy center’s graph. 
Bob McLaughlin, spokesperson at the Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses, known as DOPL, told the Idaho Capital Sun that there are limitations to the state’s data to try and determine how many doctors are practicing in the state. 
“1. It’s a two year license,” McLaughlin said in an email. “The number of licenses could fluctuate since the licensee is required to renew on their birthdate every two years and not annually. 2. Physician specialty information is self-reported and is not required as part of licensure. DOPL does not have a reliable way to determine how many licensed physicians are actively practicing in Idaho. 3. Our records reflect licensure status, and an active license does not necessarily mean an individual is currently practicing.”
Doctors left Idaho after abortion ban, study confirms

The 2025 study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, found that Idaho experienced a net loss of 94 out of 264 OB-GYN physicians between August 2022 and December 2024. 
Those numbers were compiled from “from publicly available credentialing files and sources, licensing boards, physician websites, Idaho’s American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists registry, Idaho Medical Association database, local knowledge of the practices, and direct physician confirmation,” the study’s abstract said. 
The researchers tracked relocations, those who stopped practicing obstetrics, died or retired, and counted newly credentialed doctors, the study said. It did not include temporary physicians  or family medicine doctors who also practice obstetrics. 
Idaho Medical Association CEO Susie Keller (Photo courtesy of Susie Keller)
“The unique thing about that JAMA Open study was that it was an actual count of actual individuals in Idaho,” said Susie Keller, CEO of the Idaho Medical Association. “It wasn’t an extrapolation. It wasn’t based on estimates. So it was very unique and went through many, many layers of scrutiny before being published.” 
Keller said physicians left in that time period for a variety of reasons, some of which included Idaho’s abortion laws but others were personal, such as to be closer to family. 
“There are a lot of factors that play into our physician shortage,” Keller said. “And for this particular subset, I think the study did a good job of explaining those different reasons.” 
A spokesperson from St. Luke’s, which has hospital clinic locations across southwest Idaho and Twin Falls, told the Idaho Capital Sun there were limitations to using licensing data to try and quantify how many doctors there are practicing. 
“While we cannot speak for statewide physician licensing trends, our experience is that licensing figures alone do not necessarily reflect the number of physicians actively providing obstetrical care to Idaho patients or available for long-term practice in Idaho,” spokesperson Joy Prudek said in an email.
She said that licenses may include those who “practice intermittently,” or temporary physicians who fill in gaps, or those who retain licenses from multiple states, 
 What are Idaho doctors saying? 

Cooper, the material-fetal medicine specialist, said she left Idaho because of the threat of prison time under Idaho’s criminal abortion ban and her fear she wouldn’t be able to provide the care she normally would. 
As a doctor focused on high-risk pregnancies, she said there were too many potential complications that could warrant an abortion that wouldn’t fall into the law’s exception to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest within the first trimester, if there’s a police report filed. 
“It was a very difficult decision that we made,” Cooper said. “Thinking through a lot of scenarios, thinking through if I went to prison, what would happen to my husband and children? I mean, it’s just very insane conversations that I never anticipated ever having to have.”
Idaho has had a shortage of doctors for years, said Keller of the Idaho Medical Association. The association has been part of an effort to try and increase physician training opportunities for more than 10 years. 
Keller said OB-GYNs have been the focus of tracking because the abortion ban very directly impacted that speciality. 
“This particular law that all of a sudden, made evidence-based practice that many of those OB-GYNs had been providing for their patients for many, many years … one day in 2022, it became illegal,” Keller said. “And it very much changed their ability to practice in Idaho.” 
Idaho needs 1,400 more medical professionals just to catch up to national average

Dr. Brenna McCrummen is practicing as an OB-GYN in Coeur d‘Alene, and told the Sun on Monday she feels the pressure from the loss of other specialists in North Idaho. In 2023, Sandpoint’s Bonner General Health closed its labor and delivery unit, citing the political climate and staffing issues.
Many women in the area now must travel for hours to seek care in Coeur d’Alene, McCrummen said. She said this can be especially problematic if a pregnant mom experiences unexpected complications. 
“Those problems can get much, much worse the farther out you are,” she said. “Those outcomes for baby and for mom are much worse, and I have definitely seen people arrive to our hospital much sicker than they should be, and that’s all due to the time that they have to travel.” 
Prudek, of St. Luke’s, said the health system has made progress in attracting obstetricians and gynecologists, but challenges remain. 
“From St. Luke’s perspective, recruiting and retaining OB-GYN physicians remains a priority,” Prudek said. “We have had some success recruiting OB-GYN physicians, particularly by attracting physicians with ties to Idaho and graduates of regional medical education programs. At the same time, our need for OB-GYN physicians continues to exceed the available workforce, and we have experienced limited success recruiting OB hospitalists.”
 Why is the family policy center suing BSU over the study? 

The policy center filed its lawsuit against Boise State University in Ada County District Court on July 24, Idaho EdNews reported. 
The advocacy group had sought records related to the 2025 study and its data. Its request returned only a two-page document with the raw data, showing a decline in OB-GYNs. 
The complaint alleges the university is withholding records, and that it should not have charged the policy center $257.02 for legal review of the two-page document it received. 
Stephany Galbreaith, director of media relations at Boise State, told Idaho EdNews, “We do not comment on pending litigation.”

title: Late July heat wave was Colorado’s hottest 4-day period on record
description: A record-breaking stretch of high temperatures late last month was Colorado’s worst heat wave in the 75 years that such records have been collected, state climatologists said Tuesday. text:
Low water levels on Lake Granby, a reservoir on the Colorado River and part of the Colorado-Big Thompson water storage project, are pictured last month. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)A record-breaking stretch of high temperatures late last month was Colorado’s worst heat wave in the 75 years that such records have been collected, state climatologists said Tuesday.
The four-day period from July 25 to 28 included the first- and third-hottest days in Colorado’s recorded history, as measured by the statewide average temperature. The statewide average of 78.75 degrees Fahrenheit on July 27 exceeded the previous daily record, set in 2005, by more than 1.5 degrees.
That one-day average included a high of 113 degrees Fahrenheit in the Eastern Plains town of Burlington, just two degrees shy of the state’s all-time record high, according to the monthly summary released by Colorado State University’s Colorado Climate Center.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Overall, it was Colorado’s second-hottest July in 132 years of record-keeping, exceeded only by July 2003 — though significant portions of the state, including the Denver metro area and northwest Colorado, recorded their hottest July ever. Nationally, it was the contiguous United States’ single hottest July on record, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said this week.
More frequent, more intense heat waves are the most direct and unambiguous result of human-caused climate change to be felt in Colorado, the Climate Center concluded in a comprehensive 2024 report, which said with “very high” confidence that the trend is attributable to a changing climate. Impacts like worsening droughts and wildfires were also judged to be attributable to global warming with “high” confidence, relative to more uncertain impacts like higher-frequency severe weather and hail.
Rising levels of greenhouse gases in the Earth’s atmosphere, mostly the result of burning oil, gas and coal, caused average global temperatures to rise by more than 2.3 degrees Fahrenheit over pre-industrial levels as of 2024, according to NOAA data. Parts of Colorado, including much of the Western Slope, are among the areas in the U.S. where average temperature increases have been most severe — a trend that has accelerated during the 2020s.
Colorado was one of nine states in the West to have experienced its warmest winter on record in 2025-26, and the record-breaking heat has persisted throughout the “water year,” a period beginning in October, as statewide snowpack sank to the lowest level in decades.
“Water year 2026 continues to be the warmest on record by a large margin,” Tuesday’s report said. “Statewide average temperature has been 6.2 degrees Fahrenheit higher than the 20th-century average, 4.6 degrees above the 1991–2020 average, and 1.7 degrees warmer than any previous October through July period.”
A map shows the average temperatures recorded in the lower 48 states during July 2026. (NOAA)
Researchers have also concluded with increasing confidence that a warming climate is driving the Colorado River Basin’s post-2000 megadrought, through both reduced precipitation and higher rates of evaporation of moisture from water surfaces and soils. These drought conditions, the worst dry spell the region has experienced in at least 1,200 years, are being influenced by human activity “more intensely — and more directly — than previously understood,” researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder warned last year.
As of Aug. 4, 78% of Colorado was classified as experiencing at least “severe” drought conditions, with nearly half the state, including much of the Colorado River Basin on the Western Slope, experiencing “extreme” drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Precipitation last month was roughly average for July, the Climate Center said.
“The North American Monsoon finally set in during July, but as is often the case, rainfall was spotty,” said the report, with northwest Colorado and the Denver metro area missing out on most of the rainfall.
The National Weather Service’s Climate Prediction Center continues to predict a wetter-than-normal monsoon season for western Colorado, offering hope that relief from extreme drought conditions could be in sight. The arrival of a strong El Niño pattern this summer could also mean higher-than-average precipitation in the fall and winter — though the state Climate Center cautions that “with El Niño in Colorado, it’s important to keep in mind that nothing is guaranteed.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Grant-funded program to bring cooking labs, fresh local foods to Northwest Tennessee schools
description: School lunch menus in Northwest Tennessee will be a bit fresher over the next two years thanks to a local food organization, area farmers, chefs from a New York-based nonprofit and federal grant funding. Cafeteria cooks from five districts trained alongside chefs in late July, learning techniques for handling the fresh, local produce that they […]
text:
School cafeteria cooks prepare sandwiches using fresh ingredients during a training day for the Children’s Health through Education and Food program in Northwest Tennessee. (Photo Courtesy of Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network)School lunch menus in Northwest Tennessee will be a bit fresher over the next two years thanks to a local food organization, area farmers, chefs from a New York-based nonprofit and federal grant funding.
Cafeteria cooks from five districts trained alongside chefs in late July, learning techniques for handling the fresh, local produce that they will help introduce to students this fall as part of the Children’s Health through Education and Food, CHEF, program.
Integrating fresh produce into school lunches is a complex task. Schools have limited budgets and strict nutrition regulations they must meet. Cafeterias often turn to more affordable pre-processed products instead of pricier, fresh produce from local farms. 
The Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network, a nonprofit organization dedicated to strengthening local food systems, has worked for years to change that equation, now alongside New York-based nonprofit Wellness in the Schools, WITS, the Tennessee Farm2Future Coalition and Healthy Flavors Tennessee. 
The organizations piloted the CHEF program in select Tennessee and Arkansas schools over the last two years, and the Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network was the only Tennessee organization to receive a $500,000 Patrick Leahy Farm to School Grant this year, allowing the program to continue and expand.
It will span 12 schools in Crockett and Lake County school districts and the Milan, Trenton and South Carroll special schools districts, reaching nearly 6,700 students.
Cafeteria cooks from Northwest Tennessee school districts slice tomatoes and vegetables during a training day for the Children’s Health through Education and Food program, which will bring fresh, local foods to schools for the next two years through a federal grant. (Photo Courtesy of Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network)
The program helps train cafeteria cooks with WITS chef ambassadors and teaches students how to make simple foods in classroom cooking labs — foods that they will later see and sample on the cafeteria line. Recipes and activities are tailored to each school’s needs, according to Samantha Smith Goyret, co-director of the Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network.
The program’s success depends on administrators, federal funds, food organizations, and farmers working together, Co-Director Caroline Ideus said.
The goal: Students will learn the seasonality of foods and what grows locally, and how they can be prepared.
“For our labs particularly, we really try to source as much as we can locally, so that way we could share with the kids, ‘This was grown by Darrell Bell and Bell Family Farms is out in Gleason, and you can go visit there,’” Smith Goyret said. “Just building that excitement, giving the kids that opportunity to cook, to be responsible for a recipe, and seeing them digest that, in a figurative and literal sense.”
The art and science of school lunch
Ideus typically opens any conversations about freshening up school lunches with a question: “When’s the last time you had school lunch?”
“School lunch components and requirements have changed so much,” she said. Nutrition staff and directors have many factors to balance: taste, cost, federal requirements and more.
“Your school lunch is going to taste a little different, because there’s basically no salt, no sugar, and limited fat,” Ideus said. “That’s going to taste different than what people eat at home. This is why we’re trying to teach kids to cook, so that they can cook healthier foods at home and develop those taste preferences to eat it at school, too.”
Schools serve a lot of carrots, Smith Goyret said, because they are a vegetable that “meets the orange component.” (The U.S. Department of Agriculture requires certain quantities of vegetables to be served each week, including specific amounts of red or orange vegetables).
Seasoning carrots and changing their flavor profile is a challenge without adding salt, she said.
During the program’s pilot, a chef ambassador with Weakley County Schools added a chimichurri sauce — an Argentinian sauce made with herbs, garlic, olive oil and vinegar — to carrots to spice things up.
The program will try to focus on Tennessee’s “Harvest of the Month” crops, seasonally available produce highlighted by the state. During their July training, cafeteria cooks learned to make homemade applesauce, for example (October’s crop is apples).
WITS Director of National Programs Marion Williams said teaching students “juicy chef words” to describe how foods taste and look helps keep them open to trying new foods.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
During training, a few students attending summer camp approached and asked what the group was cooking. 
“We’re making a golden applesauce,” Williams answered. 
“It’s going to look very different from the one they get in the package, because we’re using the skins of the apples, so it does have more of a richer color,” she said. “You have to start describing it, because if you just say it’s applesauce, the kids will look and say, ‘Well, that doesn’t look like applesauce.’”
Telling students that homemade applesauce is a little sweeter or a little chunkier helps, she said.
And for cafeteria cooks, WITS writes recipes tailored to the equipment each school has in its kitchen. That applesauce recipe will be written for cooking with a stove top, oven or steamer, for example. Recipes are also written to fit fresh food availability; If a school can’t source pricier fresh tomatoes for a from-scratch marinara sauce, WITS provides a “speed scratch” recipe that uses canned tomatoes, still giving cafeteria staff more control over flavor and freshness than a can of pre-made marinara sauce would, Williams said.








Wellness in the Schools Director of National Programs Marion Williams, right, works with cafeteria cooks in Northwest Tennessee during a hands-on training in July 2026. The training focused on preparing school lunch recipes using fresh, local foods. (Photo Courtesy of Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network)









Wellness in the Schools NYC Program Manager Jason Forella demonstrates knife skills during a training day for school cafeteria cooks in Northwest Tennessee as part of the Children’s Health through Education and Food program. The program is funded through a federal grant and led by Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network. (Photo Courtesy of Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network)






Cooking foods with students in the classroom before introducing them to the school lunch menu also helps.
“Once these kids have cooked this item, have tried that item, when we do the school-wide taste test, they’re the cheerleaders that are saying, ‘Hey, you’ve got to try this! We made this in class the other day,’” Smith Goyret said.
Students can sample the new food, rate it, and describe what they like and don’t like about it.
“The children are learning how to bravely try something, be okay if it doesn’t taste the way they feel it should taste, but also be open to the idea that maybe if you communicate how you feel about it, someone can alter the recipes,” Williams said.
Ultimately, the goal is to make the new, fresh-prepared food part of the school’s lunch menu rotation.
Locally grown
The federal grant for the CHEF program also allows schools to buy more food fresh from local farmers.
“The biggest barrier for the schools for getting more local products is cost,” Ideus said. Schools are still feeling the absence of funding that came from Local Foods for Schools, a USDA program cancelled by the Trump administration in early 2025.
The funding loss also dealt a blow to farmers, who must prepare well in advance to provide the large quantities of produce needed to feed students on a large scale, Ideus said.
“When that Local Food for Schools money disappeared … that’s when all the farmers were planting their crops, so we lost (their) trust,” she said.
The Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network is working with five farmers as part of the CHEF program, both in purchasing fresh food from their farms and in helping equip their operations for larger-scale production.
Wellness in the Schools NYC Program Manager Jason Forella holds a tray of sliced tomatoes while one of the training participants stirs. The training prepares school chefs for the Children’s Health through Education and Food program, which will bring fresher, local ingredients into select Northwest Tennessee schools under a 2-year federal grant. (Photo Courtesy of Wellness in the Schools)
A beef producer partnering with the program will receive a larger-capacity, more efficient freezer to allow her to handle the quantity of meat the schools need. Darrell Bell, owner of Bell Family Farm, will receive a new pea sheller that he’ll use to provide the schools with purple peas and lima beans. 
While Bell sells crops wholesale to distributors, he said he has also supplied a variety of produce to schools through grants in the past. He switched from growing row crops on his family farm to growing produce about nine years ago. He grew up with his grandfather growing watermelons in the garden, and now he grows them on a broader scale for his community.
“Feeding thousands of kids, giving them nutrition through your food that you grow, that’s pretty rewarding in itself, right there,” Bell said.
He said he appreciates the Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network for seeking grants that allow him to serve schools. Fruits and vegetables lose nutrients starting right after they’re harvested, he said, so working directly with schools allows students access to fresher, more nutrient-dense produce.
Bell acknowledges that grants are taxpayer money.
“It’s being used for good things, good purposes,” he said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama special primary round-up: Low turnout, few surprises in congressional races
description: Tuesday’s special Alabama congressional primaries had two things in common: few voters and few surprises.  Those who cast ballots in four of the state’s seven congressional districts — setting up races under a congressional map the U.S. Supreme Court once ruled racially discriminatory — largely favored incumbents, familiar faces or establishment-backed candi[...]
text:
Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, giving a victory speech after winning a special primary election for Alabama's 2nd Congressional District on Aug. 11, 2026, in Enterprise, Alabama. Turnout for the Tuesday's primaries in four congressional districts around the state came in at just over 5%. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Tuesday’s special Alabama congressional primaries had two things in common: few voters and few surprises. 
Those who cast ballots in four of the state’s seven congressional districts — setting up races under a congressional map the U.S. Supreme Court once ruled racially discriminatory — largely favored incumbents, familiar faces or establishment-backed candidates. 
Repeated concerns about low turnout in the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th congressional districts, where the primaries took place, also appeared to be realized Tuesday night. As of 10:34 p.m., the Alabama Secretary of State’s office reported turnout of 5.24%, continuing a downward trend through the year. The May 19 primaries drew about 23% turnout, while fewer than 11% of registered voters cast ballots in the June 16 runoff. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The special primaries were called after U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, which substantially raised the bar for challenges to congressional maps under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. The decision eventually cleared the way for the court to overturn Allen v. Milligan, a 2023 case that led to Alabama’s congressional maps being redrawn and allow the the Legislature to approve the use of a prior map. As a result of the Legislature’s actions, the May 19 votes in the affected districts were invalidated.
The act setting up Tuesday’s primaries did not allow for runoffs, meaning the winners of the elections only needed to secure a plurality of votes, not a majority.
In their statements after the results were announced Tuesday, Republican winners tended to focus more on national issues than state ones and accused Democrats of embracing socialism. Democrats, who had fewer contested races Tuesday, tended to focus on affordability.

1st Congressional District

Former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl of Mobile won the Republican nomination over two other candidates with about 75% of votes, according to unofficial returns. The district covers Mobile, Baldwin and Escambia counties, and most of Covington County. He will face Democratic nominee Clyde Jones, Jr. in November. 
Carl campaigned on his previous congressional experience and his desire to go back to Capitol Hill. He hopes to return to the House Committee on Appropriations and the House Committee on Natural Resources.
He represented the district from 2021 to 2025. Carl narrowly lost a Republican primary for the seat in 2024 to U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, after the district was redrawn to take in more of the Wiregrass. The seat was left vacant by Moore, who is the party’s nominee for U.S. Senate. 
Read the full story.

2nd Congressional District

Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, won the Republican nomination in the redrawn district Tuesday night, setting up a contest with U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in a race that could determine control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
Marques during the campaign touted his endorsement from President Donald Trump and his conservative record in the Alabama Legislature. 
“Basically they are communists who are trying to control their party and they’re letting them, and that’s scary,” Marques said to about 100 supporters in Enterprise Tuesday evening. “Do you really want Alabama to look like New York and California?” 
Figures said in a statement that he had worked for the people of Alabama “because that is who we should be working for.”
“My opponent would be just another rubber stamp on the same policies that are making life more expensive for the people right here in Alabama,” Figures said. 
Read the full story.
6th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, easily won nomination for a seventh term in Congress Tuesday and will face former Pelham City Council member Maurice Mercer, who won the Democratic nomination for the seat, considered strongly Republican.
Palmer, first elected in 2014, ran on a platform calling for repeal of the Affordable Care Act, abortion restrictions and gun access. Mercer, like other Democrats running this year, focused on affordability issues and said he would work to raise the minimum wage. 
Read the full story.

7th Congressional District

Former educator Ammie Akin won the Republican nomination for the 7th Congressional District Tuesday evening. Akin said in a statement that she would work to strengthen agriculture and business opportunity and would share “a new vision for our district.”
Akin will face U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, who has represented the district since 2011. While the new map altered the boundaries of the 7th Congressional District compared to the map used in 2024, it is still considered strongly Democratic.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado laws around sports betting, social media search warrants take effect
description: Dozens of new laws passed during the Colorado legislative session this year go into effect Wednesday. They range from proper produce labeling to artificial intelligence in health care settings. These are bills that passed without a “safety clause,” so they become law 90 days after the legislative session ends, after a constitutionally-required period of time[...]
text:
An image from the DraftKings website. (Illustration by Colorado Newsline)Dozens of new laws passed during the Colorado legislative session this year go into effect Wednesday. They range from proper produce labeling to artificial intelligence in health care settings. These are bills that passed without a “safety clause,” so they become law 90 days after the legislative session ends, after a constitutionally-required period of time referendum petitions can be filed against bills.
Sports betting limits
Starting Wednesday, people who gamble in Colorado will no longer be able to use credit cards to make deposits on sports betting apps like FanDuel and DraftKings. They will also be limited to six deposits per day. The law also prohibits sports betting companies from advertising to people in Colorado under 21 years old.
Senate Bill 26-131 was a bipartisan effort to put in place some protections around the growing sports betting industry and its addictive products. Last year, gamblers in the state bet $6.4 billion on sports, according to the Colorado Department of Revenue’s Division of Gaming.
“Since Colorado’s legalization of online sports betting in 2019, technology has rapidly transformed the industry, catching more and more people in the cycle of devastating gambling addiction,” bill sponsor Sen. Matt Ball, a Denver Democrat, said in a statement. “As online sports betting continues its rise in popularity, we must ensure there are reasonable protections in place to help prevent addiction, protect underage Coloradans, and uphold the integrity of the game and its athletes.”
The new law also requires companies to report annual transactional data starting in February 2028.
Missing college students
Police officers renewing their state certification will now need to complete missing person alerts training, including education about Amber Alerts, Silver Alerts, Blue Alerts, and the State Emergency Alert System. Those are all different public emergency notifications for missing vulnerable people, such as children and older adults with cognitive disabilities.
Senate Bill 26-120, which was a bipartisan effort in the Legislature, also requires that when a student goes missing on a college campus, the school needs to either conduct their own wellness check or immediately contact law enforcement. If the student remains missing after six hours, the school needs to alert the police.
The law was partially inspired by the disappearance and death of the University of Colorado Boulder freshman Megan Trussell last year.
“I brought forward this bill in partnership with the brave families who have lived through the unthinkable — their child going missing, on or off a Colorado college campus,” bill sponsor Sen. Janice Marchman, a Loveland Democrat, said in a statement. “This new, bipartisan law ensures that our peace officers are trained to properly use the full range of missing persons alert systems. It also creates a clear, consistent process for colleges and universities to respond quickly, protect students, and ensure families get the answers they need.”
AI in therapy settings
Artificial intelligence in mental health care settings will be limited under House Bill 26-1195 to only administrative tasks. Providers will need to disclose the use of AI for tasks like transcribing sessions.
Therapists and other professionals will be banned from using AI to provide therapy, and all treatment must be provided by a licensed human.
The Democrat-backed law also prohibits companies such as OpenAI and Character.AI from advertising AI chatbots as the equivalent of a therapist or counselor, as more and more people turn to AI chatbots for that type of support. An October 2025 report from OpenAI showed that over 1 million people per week share suicidal thoughts with ChatGPT. It also comes as AI companies face wrongful death lawsuits after their chatbots allegedly contributed to a person’s suicide and discouraged them from seeking professional support.



Quotation







This new law ensures that vendors who falsely label their produce as Colorado-grown can be held accountable for deceiving consumers and harming Colorado producers.


– Colorado state Rep. Matthew Martinez


Colorado-grown produce
Palisade peaches earned new protections with House Bill 26-1031, a bipartisan bill that cracks down on false produce labels. The new law prohibits sellers from labeling a product as grown in Colorado unless it actually is.
“This new law ensures that vendors who falsely label their produce as Colorado-grown can be held accountable for deceiving consumers and harming Colorado producers,” bill sponsor Rep. Matthew Martinez, a Monte Vista Democrat, said in a statement. “Pueblo green chile and San Luis Valley potatoes are iconic Colorado agricultural products, and no one should be able to slap a ‘Colorado-grown’ label on out-of-state goods. Our law protects local farmers and gives consumers peace of mind.”
Violations of the law fall under the state’s deceptive trade practice statute, which can result in hefty civil penalties.
Social media search warrants 
Large social media companies will now need to respond within 72 hours to search warrants from law enforcement. Bipartisan legislation, Senate Bill 26-11, applies to companies that have at least 1 million monthly users who can create profiles and share content.
“This bill ensures that when tragedy strikes, families and law enforcement are not left waiting indefinitely for answers held by covered platforms,” House Minority Leader Jarvis Caldwell, a Colorado Springs Republican, said in a statement when the bill was signed into law.
Those social media companies will also need a staffed hotline that law enforcement can reach. Lawmakers said the bill is important to follow up on reports of fentanyl sales, gun trafficking and sexual exploitation on social media platforms.
School traffic safety
House Bill 26-1318 sets roadway signage requirements around schools and defines school zones as streets within 1,000 feet of school boundaries. Signs in that area will need to indicate that driving penalties are doubled.
If a local government wants to reduce the size of a school zone, it will need to hold a public hearing about it. Those governments can also use technology such as an automated vehicle identification system to find traffic violations in a school zone.
The law was inspired by Liam Stewart, a Littleton middle schooler who was hit by a car while biking to school in 2023.
“Too many parents have suffered the tragic loss or injury of their child because of speeding and distracted drivers, and our law seeks to make roads around Colorado schools safer for all,” bill sponsor Rep. Meg Froelich, an Englewood Democrat, said in a statement.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Half of WV homeless students suspended during school year, state data shows
description: Half of West Virginia's homeless students were suspended as a result of behavior last school year, according to new data from the state education department.
text:
Information from the West Virginia Department of Education shows that half of the state's homeless students were suspended as a result of behavior during the 2025-2026 school year. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Half of West Virginia’s homeless students were suspended as a result of behavior last school year, according to new data from the state education department. 
There were 4,962 students identified homeless under federal reporting requirements, which includes students living in shelter, cars, tents, hotels or doubled up with friends. 
State data showed that there were more than 16,000 disciplinary incidents and actions like suspensions involving the state’s homeless students during the 2025-26 school year.
The West Virginia Department of Education said 2,473 homeless students were suspended after around 4,000 referrals for suspension in that population. 
Sen. Amy Grady, R-Mason
“It’s eye-opening and surprising,” said Sen. Amy Grady, R-Mason, who chairs the Legislative Oversight Commission on Education Accountability. “But when you think dig into it, it’s not really surprising because those kids are the ones who are living through situations that they’re not getting what they need at home.”
The commission reviewed a new school discipline report Tuesday at the state Capitol.
“Over half of the children who are homeless have been suspended. Wow,” said Sen. Joey Garcia, D-Marion, as he looked over the data. 
Sen. Joey Garcia, D-Marion
Garcia said these are children “that need extra help.”
“We need to have active measures to try to fix it,” he said. 
Drew McClanahan, the Department of Education’s legislative and policy officer, said the data brings up questions about what support was lacking for these students. He noted the high number of foster children referred for disciplinary action.
“It begs the question of … are students who are in some of the most dire consequences really struggling without the support at home?” he said. “Maybe the grandparents aren’t equipped to handle the situation or the needs of the grandchildren that they have.”
There’s no dedicated line-item funding for homeless students in West Virginia’s budget.
Counties split the state’s allocation of federal McKinney-Vento funds, which target homeless students, to help them access needed services and items. 

For multiple years, Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, D-Cabell, has sponsored a bill to place full-time, dedicated homeless education coordinator in the state’s more urban counties to recognize and help homeless students. Woelfel is retiring at the end of this year. 
“Sen. Woelfel has done tremendous work … and brought it into the spotlight so that the light shined on it,” Garcia said. “I plan to continue that work and try to hopefully get something to accomplish something that can take the numbers that we saw today and make specific improvements.”
Grady said that rather than adding another administrative role, she plans to push legislation that will delegate homeless student support to someone already in the school system.
“I like the idea of school counselors being a part of that role because they do that already in their schools,” Grady said. “They’re already in contact with those homeless families and the homeless children … They know what they need.”
More than 26,000 West Virginia students were suspended for disciplinary incidents last school year, and males were suspended at a much higher rate. Students with Individualized Education Plans facing disciplinary action have met the threshold of it not meeting their diagnosis, McClanahan explained. 
Expulsions are a very serious and rarely used consequence for the most significant disciplinary incidents, according to the Department of Education. During the 2025-26 school year, 474 students were expelled, and 67 of those were homeless students. 
Drew McClanahan, the Department of Education’s legislative and policy officer, speaks to the Legislative Oversight Committee on Education Accountability in Charleston, West Virginia, on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Lawmakers review data following new school discipline requirements  
Lawmakers also reviewed for the first time student discipline data related to their 2025 landmark school discipline bill. It was implemented in school districts for the first time this past school year.
Senate Bill 199, years in the making, was meant to address the growing classroom discipline crisis in West Virginia. Teachers asked lawmakers for help addressing an uptick in violent and disruptive student behavior like punching, kicking and classroom destruction while police often left them with limited options to remove children. 
WVDE data showed 477 students — 366 males and 81 females — were referred under those bill’s requirements as educators use a state-specific code to track this discipline referral. 
Lawmakers tried to craft a bill that protected teachers and staff while supporting students in a state with limited mental health resources. Child trauma connected to the state’s high child poverty rate and substance use crisis has regularly impacted classrooms across the state. 
“A large part of what our office of leadership and support did this past year was for the principals and superintendents on the appropriate implementation of Senate Bill 199,” McClanahan said, noting that there may be some work to do in clarifying how schools handle a kindergartener who commits battery on a teacher versus a teenager. 
Not every county has an alternative learning center for students removed from their schools due to disciplinary reasons.
“We grant funded support for 10 elementary alternative education pilots throughout the state,” McClahanah said. 
Grady, a public school teacher and sponsor of Senate Bill 199, said school districts’ mixed interpretations of the bill could have impacted the data.
“There was a little disconnect there, so I wonder if this data will change significantly,” Grady said. “I think we might see something different. Whether that’s more or less, I don’t know.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: ‘This year is different’: The water reality Idaho can no longer ignore
description: I’ve spent the majority of my career managing water on the Snake River in Idaho, and I can tell you plainly: This year is different.  According to the most recent calculations by the Idaho Department of Water Resources, the amount of water needed across southern Idaho to feed crops this past spring ran at nearly […]
text:
A person looks over the South Fork of the Snake River Canyon in Idaho. (File photo courtesy of the Bureau of Land Management)I’ve spent the majority of my career managing water on the Snake River in Idaho, and I can tell you plainly: This year is different. 
According to the most recent calculations by the Idaho Department of Water Resources, the amount of water needed across southern Idaho to feed crops this past spring ran at nearly 140% of the historical average. This is the highest number we’ve ever had on record. 
On top of the increase in agricultural demand, the reservoirs we count on to carry us through the summer sit far below where they need to be, and our backup storage water is now also running low.
The issue is clear: Idaho does not have enough water.
This isn’t a hypothetical problem we can push off to next year or the next decade. The lack of water is affecting Idaho farmers’ fields right now, forcing them to choose which crops to water to make it to harvest, and which fields need to be cleared now or even abandoned. 
We must address the underlying issues regarding Idaho’s water levels and how it is managed now, or this difficult, low-water year will become the norm we have to live with going forward.
Idaho Surface Water Coalition says severely needed water supply ‘simply is not there’

I serve as general manager of the Minidoka Irrigation District and have worked alongside my fellow irrigators and farmers of the Surface Water Coalition for years. Our members deliver water to roughly 550,000 acres of Idaho farmland, and this season, nearly all of them have been forced into significant reductions. My own users are dealing with a 15% reduction; others are grappling with as high as 33% less water every day.
This reality is not because of a single dry winter. It’s the combination of a historically low snowpack, a statewide drought emergency, and something fewer people may even know about but that matters enormously: declining natural flows along the Snake River. 
Those flows are the water the river gains naturally as it flows downstream, fed in large part by the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer. This spring, precipitation across our watershed fell to a fraction of normal, even as temperatures ran consistently above average. Storage is now being drawn at an alarming rate. Many surface water entities will exhaust their entire storage supply before the end of the season, forcing curtailment of their users who have senior water rights.
Here’s what I want Idahoans to understand, because it doesn’t get said enough: surface water users are absorbing a disproportionate share of this shortage. State regulators now calculate the Surface Water Coalition members’ predicted in-season shortfall at roughly 741,000 acre-feet. That is the same amount of water as roughly 366,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools. 
Unfortunately, the mitigation water junior groundwater users can provide toward that shortfall this year comes to only around 80,000 acre-feet. That gap between what’s constitutionally owed and what mitigation water is actually delivered means surface water users are being hit twice. 
Surface water users are absorbing deeper cuts because mitigation alone can’t come close to closing the difference. I want to be clear that the Surface Water Coalition is not blaming groundwater users for this. We just want to be honest about how today’s balance isn’t sustainable for anyone, surface or groundwater, for the long run.
The emergency measures keeping us afloat this year, like curtailing junior groundwater rights, might offset a portion of the gap, but let’s not mistake short-term triage for a long-term strategy. 
Curtailment doesn’t restore the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer, which remains at historic lows. It doesn’t rebuild storage or increase the spring flow into the Snake River. And with forecasters now pointing to a strengthening El Niño pattern this winter, which could mean even drier and warmer conditions, we may not be able to count on next winter’s snowpack to bail us out either. 
We have to plan as if this water shortfall will continue and not just hope it disappears.
This current situation is here in part because of a long-term decline in the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer, a decline that a handful of good water years temporarily masked but never reversed. Recovery, if we’re serious about it, will take years too. It will take years to collect the data, years more to develop and implement a plan, and even more years before we see real results.
That means the work has to start now. We cannot put this off any longer.
My fellow Surface Water Coalition members and I truly appreciate that the Idaho Legislature approved $30 million in annual funding for statewide water infrastructure projects in 2025. It’s a meaningful step in the right direction, and it needs to continue. But funding alone isn’t a plan, and infrastructure alone won’t recover an aquifer that’s been declining for decades.
We don’t have to guess what happens when a region puts off hard decisions year after year. The Colorado River is a sobering example of what happens when declining storage becomes accepted as the new normal. 
Idaho still has an opportunity to make a choice that other states didn’t make in time. We must capitalize on it.
This year’s record water demand, drought conditions and depleted water availability are red flag warnings. Idaho can keep reacting to each irrigation season as it arrives, or we can start building the kind of enforceable, long-term groundwater management plan that actually restores the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer, not just stabilizes it at today’s deficient levels.
The time to prepare for 2027, and the many decades after it, is now.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Refugees among thousands of North Dakotans losing SNAP benefits amid federal changes
description: For years, most of Shahin Azizi’s clients at Global Refuge in Fargo participated in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to help them cover the cost of food while they got settled and looked for work. Some stayed on the program even after they found jobs to help them provide for their larger families. But a […]
text:
Food waits on shelves on Aug. 5, 2026, at the Dream Center in Bismarck before being distributed community members in need. Changes to federal food assistance are increasing demand at local food pantries. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)For years, most of Shahin Azizi’s clients at Global Refuge in Fargo participated in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to help them cover the cost of food while they got settled and looked for work. Some stayed on the program even after they found jobs to help them provide for their larger families.
But a 2025 federal budget bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made sweeping changes to SNAP, including restricting noncitizens’ access to the program.
That included refugees, who make up the bulk of Global Refuge’s clients. The nonprofit organization works with the U.S. government to help resettle refugees and other newcomers to the U.S.
Great Plains Food Bank sees record numbers seeking food assistance

Azizi said the loss of SNAP has left a mark on his clients.
“Sometimes, when I go (to their homes), I see and I feel it, that it’s really hard for a mom or a dad — they have children and they do not have nutritious food in their home,” he said. “That creates an anxiety in their minds.”
As a case manager, Azizi works with individuals and families navigating physical or mental health problems, immigration issues and other challenges. He said many of his clients have lost SNAP, including at least five families “which are really needy.”
The North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, which administers the state’s SNAP program, estimated that around 1,000 noncitizens would lose food benefits in North Dakota under the new law, according to Rebecca Askins, interim director for the department’s Economic Assistance Section.
They’re not the only ones. Another estimated 5,600 North Dakotans are expected to lose SNAP due to stricter work requirements for “able-bodied adults without dependents” that were included in the 2025 law. 
For several decades, SNAP has had a time limit work requirement for some groups, meaning applicants who meet certain criteria were required to work for at least 80 hours a month in order to qualify for SNAP benefits, according to a report from the Brookings Institution. 
That requirement previously applied to people between ages 18 and 54 who were physically and mentally able to work and didn’t have dependents under the age of 18. Now, the age limit has been raised to 64 and the maximum dependent age has been reduced to 14. 
That expands the number of adults who must now log at least 80 hours a month working, attending job training, going to school, caregiving or volunteering in order to keep their benefits. 
Those who don’t fulfill the requirements will lose their benefits after three months. Unless they reapply after fulfilling the requirements or citing another exemption, they will not be able to get SNAP benefits for three years, at which time they’ll be able to access them for another three months before the cycle repeats.
North Dakota could pay millions for high SNAP error rate

Askins said the department expects a 10% enrollment drop as a result of the federal changes. The full impact of the changes isn’t yet known because households are only impacted when their benefits come up for recertification, which happens throughout the year.
During a budget committee meeting June 24, Askins told state lawmakers that between April 2025 and April 2026, the number of North Dakotans on SNAP dropped 4.3% from just below 56,900 to less than 54,400. 
Askins told the Monitor that enrollment will likely tick up again in the coming months as people begin working part time or apply under a new exemption.
In the meantime, she said the changes have caused some confusion among applicants, but the number of applications being submitted has remained steady. 
For those who see their benefits cut or reduced under federal changes, Askins said economic assistance staff generally try to refer households to food banks and other local resources.
The Great Plains Food Bank serves North Dakota and Clay County in Minnesota. The food bank and its partners across the state have seen growing demand for food over the last several years, according to Darby Njos, a food bank spokesperson.
In its last fiscal year, the food bank served more than 186,000 people, a 16% increase and a new record for the organization, according to previous Monitor reporting.
 


	Njos said it’s difficult to pinpoint which factors are most responsible for the increase, but many who rely on the food bank say they’re struggling with rising grocery prices and sometimes have to choose between paying for bills and paying for food.
The food bank also offers staff outreach services to help residents apply for SNAP. Njos said demand for the service hasn’t gone up since the federal changes went into effect, but “it definitely has shifted.”
She said that before, applicants asked questions about how to apply or how the application process worked, but now, they mostly ask whether they qualify or if it’s even worth applying given the new restrictions.
‘Doing our best to sustain our families’ 
For his clients at Global Refuge, Azizi said food pantries are “kind of the only source” of food now that SNAP restrictions are tighter for noncitizens.
But they can also be hard to access for those without transportation, so Azizi said he, other Global Refuge staff and volunteers either drive families to a nearby pantry or pick up food and drop it off at their home.
Pantries also only cover the basics. Azizi said many families miss the fresh or culturally significant ingredients they used to be able to buy at the grocery store when they had SNAP. 
Other than food pantries, Global Refuge’s clients are able to grow food in a community garden run by the organization, according to Dan Hannaher, Global Refuge’s North Dakota field director. They also sometimes get support from local ethnic community-based organizations.
Beyond that, he said, they often rely on donations from the broader community.
“Congregations come forward to help and assist with anything they can do to sustain a family’s food and nutrition needs,” he said. “So while it’s certainly a struggle, it’s something the community seems to be coming forward with, and we’re doing our best to sustain our families.”
Azizi said the change came as a shock for many of his clients who had been brought to the U.S. by the government through its refugee resettlement program. 
“(When) they come here, we provide for them an extended cultural orientation,” he said. “We say, ‘In this country, people are helpful. People are kind. The community is good. Peace is here. There is no way that you should not have food here.’”
That message contrasts with refugees’ recent experience, he said.
“They say, ‘This is the first time in history that we hear (of) a country which spends billions and billions of dollars on stuff but cuts food for their own people that they brought here,’” he said.
