name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds says he’ll remove local officials who indulge in ‘sanctuary’ policies
description: One of the hallmarks of the Ron DeSantis administration compared to its GOP predecessors has been removal of locally elected officials from office — or threats to do so — for actions they claim are unlawful. Now Byron Donalds, positioned to succeed Ron DeSantis in the governor’s mansion next year, is promising more of the […]
text:
Protesters gathered in front of the Florida Capitol building on May 30, 2025, a day after ICE raided a Tallahassee construction site, detaining more than 100 workers. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)One of the hallmarks of the Ron DeSantis administration compared to its GOP predecessors has been removal of locally elected officials from office — or threats to do so — for actions they claim are unlawful.
Now Byron Donalds, positioned to succeed Ron DeSantis in the governor’s mansion next year, is promising more of the same.
The impulse extends to DeSantis’ allies. Over the past year and a half, Florida Attorney General (and former DeSantis chief of staff) James Uthmeier, placed in the job by the governor, has threatened to remove elected municipal officials because they balked at fully supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) efforts in removing undocumented immigrants.
Under a state law passed in 2025, “the sheriff or the chief correctional officer” operating a county detention facility must enter into 287(g) cooperation agreements with ICE. It does not require municipal officials to do so, and several Florida cities have opted not to.
Yet Uthmeier threatened city officials in Fort Myers, Key West, Tampa, and Orlando with removal over the past 18 months because they acted or spoke about loosening their 287(g) agreements.
Donalds told the Phoenix over the weekend that Florida is not now and will never be a sanctuary state.
“If we have local officials decide that they want to ignore federal immigration law and the laws of the state of Florida and create sanctuaries, they’ll be removed from office, as well,” he said following a campaign rally in Tampa.
In Miami, Mayor Eileen Higgins campaigned last year on a promise to revisit the city’s 287(g) agreement. In a statement issued last week, she said she intends to fulfill that promise.
“Since my campaign and since taking office, I have made clear to the community that we must all treat all residents humanely and with dignity, which is why I said the City should revisit the 287(g) agreement,” Higgins said as reported by NBC 6 South Florida. “Since then, the Commission held a discussion at the end of June, and I look forward to a legislative item reaching my desk so I can sign it quickly.”
Meanwhile, Charlie Crist, running for St. Petersburg mayor next week against incumbent Ken Welch and four other candidates, told WMNF radio Friday that ICE was “an interesting animal” and that he would consider rescinding the city’s agreement with the agency.
“I’m not a fan of ICE. I’m a fan of enforcing the law but not murdering fellow Americans. That’s unconscionable,” he said, referring to the deaths of two U.S. citizens by ICE agents in Minneapolis in January.
Crist was asked in the interview if he would sign a 287(g) agreement.
“With ICE? Why would you?” he replied. He did not return a message Monday seeking clarification about his position.
St. Petersburg’s police department did sign a 287(g) agreement last year. Welch noted last month that the city had not been trained in the 287(g) program and had no officers “who are active in it now.”
‘Soros prosecutors’
Florida did pass legislation in 2019 that bans state and local governments from enforcing sanctuary policies, defined as any “law, policy, practice, procedure, or custom adopted or allowed by a state entity or local governmental entity which prohibits or impedes a law enforcement agency from complying with federal immigration laws or which prohibits or impedes a law enforcement agency from communicating or cooperating with a federal immigration agency.”
The confusion over whether municipalities need formal agreements with ICE led the city of South Miami to go to court a year ago. During testimony, attorneys representing the state told the judge municipalities are not required by law to enter into 287(g) agreements, WLRN reported.
Donalds also told the Phoenix that he wouldn’t hesitate to suspend state attorneys who he says are not enforcing the law.
DeSantis suspended two elected Florida state attorneys for what he called “incompetence” and “neglect of duty” and replaced them with former prosecutors he had initially appointed to be judges.
“Let me be very clear. You have a responsibility to follow the Constitution and follow the law in our state. If you have a state attorney that is not prosecuting the law and enforcing the law, they’re going to be removed from office, because it destabilizes law and order in safe communities in our state,” Donalds said.
“We’re not going to tolerate that the way that they’ve done in these blue states,” he added. “That’s one of the reasons why people are coming into our state. Because they want to be safe. So, we’re not going to ask some state attorney who’s going to go rogue and follow [George] Soros and the DSA thinking that they’re not going to uphold Florida law.”
Republicans have attacked “Soros prosecutors” over the years, referring to the millions of dollars that Hungarian-American philanthropist George Soros has contributed to the campaigns of reform-oriented prosecutors around the nation. Soros has been a general bogeyman for conservatives because of his financial support of progressive causes.
DeSantis suspended Hillsborough County Democratic State Attorney Andrew Warren in 2022 and Orange/Osceola County Democratic State Attorney Monique Worrel in 2023. Both went to court to win their jobs back. Worrell ultimately returned to office in 2024, winning re-election by more than 15 points.
Worrell’s predecessor, Aramis Ayala, was removed from murder cases on two separate occasions by Florida governors (first by Rick Scott in 2017 and by DeSantis in 2020) because of her public objection to the death penalty, but was never removed from her position.
DeSantis suspended Warren because he pledged not to prosecute people seeking abortions or gender-affirming care for minors. After Warren filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging his suspension, a judge ruled in January 2023 that the governor had violated the First Amendment in removing him because of political differences and anticipated “political benefit” to the governor.
That judge added, however, that he lacked power to reinstate Warren. A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit ruled in January 2024 that the judge should reconsider that decision, but the DeSantis administration appealed. Two months after Warren lost his bid for re-election in November 2024, the same 11th Circuit panel ruled that Warren’s challenge was moot, since his four-year term in office had expired.

title: ‘MAGA activist’ who wants to eliminate elections commission wins GOP nod for secretary of state
description: A self-described “authentic MAGA activist” who vows to bring election administration under control of the secretary of state won the Republican nomination for the office Tuesday. The Associated Press called the secretary of state primary election for Jay Schroeder at 8:42 p.m. With 90% of the ballots counted by 10:30 p.m., Schroeder had 47% of […]
text:
Wisconsin State Capitol (Wisconsin Examiner photo)A self-described “authentic MAGA activist” who vows to bring election administration under control of the secretary of state won the Republican nomination for the office Tuesday.
Jay Schroeder, Republican nominee for Wisconsin secretary of state. (Campaign photo)
The Associated Press called the secretary of state primary election for Jay Schroeder at 8:42 p.m. With 90% of the ballots counted by 10:30 p.m., Schroeder had 47% of the votes — far outpacing the candidate endorsed by the Republican Party.
Schroeder declared himself to be an “authentic MAGA activist” and a “MAGA aligned candidate on election integrity.” He focused his campaign message heavily on election administration, including eliminating the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission.
The Democratic candidate for the post is JoCasta Zamarripa, a second-term Milwaukee alder and former five-term member of the state Assembly. Zamarripa was unopposed in the Democratic primary for secretary of state.
The secretary of state’s duties have been narrowed over the last several decades, but the office remains an elected position under the Wisconsin Constitution and cannot be eliminated without a constitutional amendment.
The remaining duties of the office include haveing responsibility for the official state seal and validating the certificate of Wisconsin’s electoral votes in presidential elections. But the office is otherwise unrelated to election administration.
The secretary of state also sits on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands, which distributes revenues from timber sales on former federal land that now belongs to the state, donating proceeds to public school libraries and making loans to public projects.
Schroeder’s campaign has focused on moving Wisconsin elections from the bipartisan elections commission, established in 2016 by the Republican majority in the Legislature, to place them under the control of the secretary of state’s office. That would require the passage of new legislation.
Schroeder has run for the office previously. He was the Republican nominee in 2018, losing to incumbent Democrat Doug La Follette, and ran for the party’s nomination in 2022, coming in second to Amy Loudenbeck in the primary, who lost to La Follette that November.
At a 2022 Republican rally, Schroeder told a crowd that he would not have signed “a sheet of paper for the election,” apparently a reference to the certification of electoral votes in the 2020 Wisconsin presidential election, Bill Lueders reported in a commentary for the Wisconsin Examiner.
On his website Schroeder calls the elections commission “corrupt” and “a disaster.”
Nathan Pollnow, a beef farmer endorsed by the state Republican Party, came in a distant second in the primary, with just under 26% of the vote.
Pollnow ran on a platform of promoting government transparency, vowing to create a publicly accessible guide to laws, administrative rules and other actions of government.
Two other Republicans finished in the low double-digits: Cindy Werner, with 14% of the vote and Brayden Myer with just under 13%.
The 2026 election will be the first in more than 40 years without an incumbent running for reelection. The incumbent, Democrat Sarah Godlewski, opted to run instead for lieutenant governor. Godlewski also had no primary opposition Tuesday.
Godlewski was appointed in 2023 after La Follette, a long-time incumbent, resigned only a few months after winning reelection in November 2022.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: License plate readers are a tool – not a threat
description: Hartford residents deserve a straight explanation of how license plate readers work and how they should be governed.
text:
As Council President and co-chair of the Quality of Life and Public Safety committee, I hear from Hartford residents every week about the same thing: they want their neighborhoods safe, and they want to know the tools we use to keep them safe aren’t being misused. 
Automated license plate readers, or LPR technology, are part of that conversation, and Hartford residents deserve a straight explanation of how this tool works and how it should be governed.
License plate reading cameras, whether mounted at fixed intersections or on patrol vehicles, photograph the license plate of every passing car and convert the image to text. That plate is checked against a database tied to stolen vehicles, active warrants, and AMBER or Silver Alerts. A match sends a real-time alert to an officer. No match means no one reviews the record.
This tool has already proven itself across our state. In Waterford, LPR cameras helped identify the suspect vehicle in an armed robbery at a credit union where two men held employees at knifepoint. In Windsor, an LPR alert on a stolen vehicle led officers to apprehend three suspects without incident, and a separate alert helped detectives connect a van to nearly $880,000 in stolen copper piping and electrical wiring. 
In Southington, stolen vehicle reports dropped from 100 in 2023 to just 23 through 2025, a trend the department credits in part to its camera network. During an active AMBER Alert, an LPR hit on the Berlin Turnpike helped narrow the search for a missing child who was found safe hours later. LPR technology has created real results for communities, these results are not inconsequential.
Hartford residents are also right to ensure LPR is used with proper oversight. Statewide reporting raised concerns about how LPR data was accessed in connection with immigration enforcement. That kind of overreach is what erodes public trust in this technology. It is also why the state legislature barred police departments from sharing LPR data with agencies conducting immigration enforcement. 
It is important to note sharing the data with other agencies is not always in relation to immigration. It is often used for missing person’s cases that have crossed state lines, often LPR being pivotal to identifying the location of the missing person.
LPR technology should be used by communities but with strong policies for data retention limits with automatic deletion of any record not tied to an open investigation. The Connecticut General Assembly worked hard to develop legislation for safeguards of the use, they developed a policy that balances the use of LPR to keep our communities safe, along with procedures to ensure its data is used responsibly.
Hartford can recover stolen cars, find missing children, and solve violent crimes with this technology. A strong local policy will make sure it is never turned against the residents it is meant to protect.
TJ Clarke is President of the Hartford City Council.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Lisa Demuth beats Trump-endorsed Mike Lindell in GOP primary for Minnesota governor
description: House Speaker Lisa Demuth won the Republican Party’s nomination for governor on Tuesday, beating President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidate, Mike Lindell, as well as Kendall Qualls — the choice of GOP state convention delegates.  Demuth is the first Republican woman to be nominated for governor and the rare Republican to beat a Trump-endorsed candidate this[...]
text:
Lisa Demuth speaks at the Minnesota Republican Convention in Duluth, Saturday May 30, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)House Speaker Lisa Demuth won the Republican Party’s nomination for governor on Tuesday, beating President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidate, Mike Lindell, as well as Kendall Qualls — the choice of GOP state convention delegates. 
Demuth is the first Republican woman to be nominated for governor and the rare Republican to beat a Trump-endorsed candidate this year. But she’ll face an even bigger challenge in November against U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who won the Democratic-Farmer-Labor nomination against nominal competition Tuesday. Klobuchar is also the first woman nominee for governor on the DFL side.
Demuth in a statement said Minnesotans want a fresh start and a clean break from Democrats running the state.
“We can’t afford more of the same. And that’s exactly what Amy Klobuchar would be as governor. Amy Klobuchar is a career politician and 20-year Washington D.C. insider,” Demuth said. She’s been running for office for more than 30 years. She simply cannot deliver the kind of change Minnesotans want.”
Klobuchar said Tuesday that Minnesotans need a governor who won’t bow to Trump. 
“I am running for governor to lower costs and make life affordable, expand our economy with a growth agenda and root out the fraud,” Klobuchar said in a statement. “We need a governor who is going to put Minnesotans first — not be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump or anyone else.”
Demuth, who has served as Minnesota House speaker since early 2025, pitched herself as the experienced candidate with the best shot at beating Minnesota’s most accomplished vote-getter, Klobuchar.
Demuth has the backing of a conservative billionaire, which helped finance several television and social media advertisements and statewide mailers.
Demuth back in May lost the Minnesota Republican Party’s endorsement after 10 rounds of voting. Despite her previous pledge to drop out of the race if she didn’t receive the party’s endorsement, Demuth continued her campaign, citing voting irregularities at the convention. Her gamble paid off — GOP primary voters evidently didn’t care — while calling into question the future of the GOP convention endorsement. 
Demuth was first elected to the Minnesota House in 2018 after serving on her local school board in Cold Spring — about 20 miles southwest of St. Cloud — for over a decade. 
Demuth, who served as the GOP House minority leader during the Democrats’ 2023-2024 trifecta, raised money and recruited candidates to topple the trifecta in 2024. Republicans flipped three key swing districts in 2024, bringing the House to a 67-67 tie between Republicans and Democrats and earning the respect of party insiders and donors.
After a power struggle between the two parties, she cut a deal with Democrats to become Minnesota’s first Black House speaker and first Republican woman speaker.  During a pair of legislative sessions, she used her caucus’ power of exactly half of the House to force the DFL to roll back state-subsidized health insurance for undocumented immigrant adults.
Though the tie hasn’t allowed Republicans to pass significant legislation, Republicans blocked Democratic priorities like tax increases and new spending— while propelling Demuth to emerge as the face of Republican opposition.
Demuth is arguing that a Klobuchar governorship would essentially be a Gov. Tim Walz third term, and that Klobuchar would not adequately address Minnesota’s fraud crisis in the state’s social safety net programs. 
Until Klobuchar got in the race, Minnesota Republicans began the year hoping to break their 20-year losing streak, as the fraud permeating programs under Democrats’ watch has become a top issue for many Minnesotans.
If nothing else, Demuth’s candidacy may save Republicans from a midterm wipeout, which many feared if Lindell had been the nominee. All 201 legislative seats are on the ballot, and Democrats believe Trump’s deep unpopularity; midterm headwinds against the party in the White House; and Klobuchar’s broad popularity could grant them a DFL trifecta. 
Demuth’s win also demonstrates the crumbling credibility of the Minnesota Republican Party’s endorsement. Minnesota Republicans in recent years have always backed the party-endorsed candidates — a trend bucked this year with GOP-endorsed candidate Qualls coming in a distant third to Demuth and Lindell. 
This is the first time since 1994 that a Republican candidate who lost the party’s endorsement has prevailed in their primary election. Former Gov. Arne Carlson that year lost the GOP endorsement, but went on to win the primary and reelection to another term as governor.
If elected governor, Demuth says she will cut income taxes and end taxes on Social Security for senior citizens. She also has proposed a fraud prevention plan, which includes appointing her lieutenant governor as a fraud czar who will single out fraud in state agencies. 
Restore Sanity, the new political action committee supporting Demuth’s campaign for governor, has spent nearly $2.8 million in favor of her campaign so far. It reported $156,00 in cash as of July 20. Despite the outside spending, Demuth will still be vastly outspent by Klobuchar.
As of July 20, Klobuchar’s campaign reported about $4.5 million in cash, and her campaign has raised $9.3 million since launching in January. The senior senator’s staggering cash advantage is likely to be compounded by outside spending by DFL-aligned allies like the Alliance for a Better Minnesota.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Peggy Flanagan wins Democratic Senate primary in Minnesota in victory for progressive flank
description: Progressive Democrats notched another major victory over the moderate wing of the party in Minnesota Tuesday night, when Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan defeated U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in what’s believed to be the most expensive primary in state history. Flanagan’s commanding win, coming on the heels of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan took the stage at the First Avenue rally on July 20, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)Progressive Democrats notched another major victory over the moderate wing of the party in Minnesota Tuesday night, when Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan defeated U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in what’s believed to be the most expensive primary in state history.
Flanagan’s commanding win, coming on the heels of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, provides fuel to the progressive argument that the party’s base demands an uncompromising response to the second Trump administration and a bold policy agenda to address the rising cost of living.
The two-term lieutenant governor will face former sportscaster Michele Tafoya in November, setting up a critical test of the progressive platform’s appeal to general election voters in a purplish state.
Tafoya handily defeated a crowded field of Republicans, including Adam Schwarze, a former Navy SEAL and the GOP-endorsed candidate, and Royce White, a former NBA player and 2024 Republican nominee for Senate.
Tafoya is widely seen by Republicans as their best shot in years to end a 20-year losing streak for statewide office. She was able to win over Republican primary voters despite her more moderate views on abortion rights, which has been the undoing of previous statewide Republican candidates especially in the wake of the Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision.
In a statement celebrating her primary win, Tafoya previewed her campaign pitch to voters over the next three months: Democrats have failed at governing by allowing student test scores to fall, crime to rise and fraudsters to raid the state’s social service programs.
“This isn’t about red versus blue. It’s common sense versus crazy. We will not reelect politicians who let criminals steal billions and treat accountability as optional. We deserve better, and it’s time we demand better,” Tafoya said.
Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation, would make history as the first Native American woman to serve in the U.S. Senate if elected. Her name in Ojibwe, as she always introduces herself, is Gizhiiwewidamikwe — “speaks in a loud and clear voice woman.”
She energized the party’s base and won its convention endorsement with a soaring progressive platform: Medicare for all, universal childcare, a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants.
Her platform makes her a fitting successor to progressive scions who held the seat before her — Tina Smith, Al Franken and Paul Wellstone — and she won the endorsements of heavyweights Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren.
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan speaks after winning the endorsement for a U.S. Senate seat at the 2026 DFL State Convention Saturday, May 30, 2026 in Rochester, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Flanagan’s biography allows her to speak personally and knowledgeably about the causes she champions. She was raised mostly by a single mother and benefited from the stability of Section 8 housing and food stamps.
After college she worked on Wellstone’s campaign and then worked for Wellstone Action, the nonprofit dedicated to carrying on his legacy by training organizers and candidates. She served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children’s Defense Fund-Minnesota before winning election to the state House and being tapped as Walz’s running mate.
For Walz, then seen as a moderate Democrat from a swing congressional district in southern Minnesota, she helped drum up enthusiasm from the urban progressive wing. With Sen. Amy Klobuchar at the top of the ticket in her bid for governor, the same dynamic could help them both.
Flanagan’s success was fueled in large part by Democratic voters’ outrage over Trump’s violent immigration crackdown. Flanagan blasted Craig for her vote to support the Laken Riley Act and pledged to “tear ICE apart” — though she’s been careful not to repeat the slogan “Abolish ICE.”
Outside his polling place in Apple Valley, 64-year-old Carson Medcalf, a hardwood flooring installer, said he voted in a primary election for the first time to vote for Flanagan because of Operation Metro Surge; his wife is an immigrant from Vietnam, and they were terrified all winter.
“I like Angie (Craig), but I didn’t like her support of ICE, and Flanagan’s a little bit more progressive,” Medcalf said.
Flanagan’s campaign, which she dubbed “the many over the money,” prevailed despite being significantly outspent.
Flanagan claimed to not accept any “corporate PAC money” — though her campaign was boosted by super PACs — and painted Craig as a corporate Democrat beholden to taboo special interests like cryptocurrency and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
Craig’s campaign raised $12.7 million as of late July, and the main super PAC backing her campaign, North Star Dawn, spent more than $25 million in the race. Millions more were spent by other super PACs and dark-money nonprofits.
Flanagan’s campaign raised about $6.5 million, and the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association PAC spent another $6 million to boost her campaign. Another super PAC, Clear Voice, spent more than $650,000.
The primary campaign spending is sure to be just prologue to an expensive three-month general election campaign, as a Republican victory in Minnesota could crush Democratic hopes of retaking the Senate and providing a meaningful check on the Trump administration.
Tafoya accumulated a significant war chest for what was not a particularly competitive primary. Her campaign raised $5.3 million while the National Republican Senatorial Committee already has $56 million cash on hand to help Republicans keep control of the Senate.
Craig tried to persuade voters that she is Democrats’ best shot at beating Tafoya in the Senate, having flipped a competitive congressional district and won re-election three times. But Democratic voters in Craig’s district were about evenly split between her and Flanagan.
In a state where Republicans hold half the seats for U.S. House and often control one chamber of the Legislature, Flanagan’s success in November is not assured.
Flanagan comes with significant baggage, having been second-in-command during an unprecedented raiding of the state’s social service programs by fraudsters.
Gov. Tim Walz, who faces criticism from across the political spectrum for not acting sooner to stop the fraud, dropped his bid for a third term. It was an acknowledgment that the issue had become so radioactive that his chances to win were seriously compromised. Walz did not endorse Flanagan, despite having worked with her for the past eight years, while his wife Gwen endorsed Craig.
Flanagan has answered questions about fraud with the same refrain that puts all the blame on the governor’s shoulders.
“The governor has said that the buck stops with him and he took the lead here,” Flanagan said in an interview with the Reformer.
Madison McVan contributed reporting.

Tiffany easily won his primary campaign, while David Varnam won the nomination to be his runningmate. Tiffany at a press conference in October 2025.  (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)U.S. Rep Tom Tiffany easily defeated challenger Andy Manske in the GOP primary for governor. The AP called the race at 8:21p.m. With 45% of the ballots counted, Tiffany was leading 92.4% to Manske’s 3.8%.
Tiffany’s victory was a foregone conclusion. He was endorsed by the Republican Party after President Donald Trump endorsed Tiffany and two other GOP hopefuls who had launched campaigns dropped out.
Manske, a 27-year-old medical service technician from suburban Milwaukee, has said he entered the race to ensure GOP voters had a choice. On his website he said he was campaigning “to challenge a political system that’s stopped working for everyday Wisconsinites and to fight for a state that works for all of us.”
Tiffany’s running mate will be David Varnam, who defeated Will Martin, a former staffer in the administrations of Tommy Thompson and Scott Walker during their terms as governor, in a surprise upset. Martin had been endorsed by the state party.
David Varnam was mayor of Lancaster, Wisconsin, from 2016 to 2022 and previously a Common Council member. He has worked as a congressional aide and as a policy analyst for the Christian organization Focus on the Family. He ran in the 2022 Republican primary for lieutenant governor, finishing seventh.
Varnam defeated Martin 54.1% to 45.5%, with 69% of the vote counted. AP called the race at 9:36 p.m.
With both Martin and Tiffany having the Republican Party’s endorsement, the two campaigned together. Tiffany was a guest on the weekly radio show Martin hosts on Milwaukee radio station WNOV, and the two appeared jointly during the summer in community parades.
Ahead of Election Day, Democratic candidates had been discussing uniting following the primary to defeat Tiffany.
Democrats, including Lt. Gov. candidate Sara Godlewski, U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin and U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan, plan to meet for a unity breakfast Wednesday morning in the Madison area, seeking to move past the divisiveness of the  primary with less than three months until the general election.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘A long shot’: Amanda Janoo wins Vermont’s Democratic primary for governor
description:
The economist, who was virtually unknown before announcing her campaign, beat out Aly Richards, the former CEO of a prominent child care lobbying and advocacy group.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘A long shot’: Amanda Janoo wins Vermont’s Democratic primary for governor.
text:
Amanda Janoo celbrates her victory in her race to be the democratic nominee for governor in Burlington on Primary Day, Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Updated 11:57 p.m.
BURLINGTON — Amanda Janoo narrowly won Vermont’s Democratic primary for governor Tuesday, according to the Associated Press, after a campaign that called for sweeping progressive policy changes and limiting how much the state relies on federal funding.
Janoo, an economist, has never run for office before and was virtually unknown before announcing her campaign. She beat out Aly Richards, the former head of a prominent childcare lobbying and advocacy group who also had the backing of a well-endowed political action committee, with 49% of the vote as of 11 p.m., the AP reported. Richards had 46% at that point.
In a victory speech at her campaign’s election night watch party in Burlington, Janoo said that when she decided to run for governor, she knew “it was going to be a long shot.”
“We didn’t have the establishment for support, or big political kingmakers on our side,” she told a crowd of at least 250 people. “But we had something so much more powerful. We had you.”
Janoo’s comments echoed how she framed herself on the campaign trail this year: the race’s anti-establishment choice. She was openly critical of the power and influence of large technology companies, calling for a new tax on advertising revenue they earn and new state regulations on large data centers used for artificial intelligence.
She also made the case that the federal government could not be trusted to fully fund key human services programs and proposed finding new revenue at home instead. That includes using a surcharge on personal income over $500,000 to pay for free primary care for every person in the state, her campaign has said.
In a statement issued around 11:30 p.m., Richards conceded the race, calling it “the honor of a lifetime to run for governor of this amazing state.” She said she would do everything she could to help Janoo beat Republican Gov. Phil Scott this fall. Scott did not have an opponent in Tuesday’s GOP primary for governor.
“Now that the primary is behind us, it’s time for Vermonters to come together and rally behind Amanda,” Richards said.
Janoo’s win means Democrats will again have a gubernatorial nominee who has never held state-level office before. Janoo, who grew up in Strafford but now lives in Burlington, has made the case that her experience working with think tanks and international development organizations, both in the U.S. and abroad, gives her the know-how to tackle the state’s biggest economic and social challenges.
Her challenge now will be to sell her ideas to voters across the political spectrum, many of whom — including Democrats — have for years supported Scott in general elections. Scott remains the most popular governor in the country, according to the firm Morning Consult, though another poll from the University of New Hampshire showed his job approval rating slouching in recent months.
This year’s Democratic primary was the most competitive in years. Janoo and Richards both raised more money for their primary campaigns than any Democratic candidate for governor since 2020.
Notably, Janoo’s support proved strong enough to overcome an eleventh-hour purchase of more than $200,000 worth of digital advertising by a PAC created to support Richards, but that was not affiliated with Richards’ campaign. Pro-Richards ads have blanketed websites and social media feeds in Vermont over the past week. 
Several of Janoo’s supporters said at the watch party that they decided to vote for her because of her policy positions. Jackie Stanton of Johnson, for one, cited Janoo’s views on healthcare, taxes and housing as what drew her to the campaign. 
“She is by far the most progressive candidate for governor we’ve ever had,” Stanton said. “This is a people-powered movement, and so many everyday people have worked very hard to bring us to this moment.”
As live music played throughout the evening, people clapped and sang along to lyrics such as, “All these fascists got to lose” and “Out with the old and in with Janoo, that’s what Vermont has got to do.” 
At the start of the event, attendees were instructed to go up to at least one stranger, introduce themselves and share their astrological sign and the first concert they attended.
Janoo told her supporters during her victory speech that, even with her uncertainty about the result, she’d only prepared one version of the address. 
“In all honesty, I really only wrote one speech this evening because when I sat down and thought about what I wanted to say if we won or if we lost, I realized it was pretty much the same thing: Thank you,” she said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘A long shot’: Amanda Janoo wins Vermont’s Democratic primary for governor.

title: Berman wins Democratic nod to challenge Steil in Wisconsin’s 1st District
description: Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse, won handily Tuesday in a three-way primary of active Democrats seeking to take on Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District. “I never imagined running for Congress, but I saw a culture of corruption in Washington that protects corporate special interests and insiders instead of solvin[...]
text:
Mitchell Berman, right, talks with a voter during a visit Aug, 5 to a United Auto Workers union hall in Janesville. Berman won the Democratic primary Tuesday for Wisconsin's 1st Congressional District. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse, won handily Tuesday in a three-way primary of active Democrats seeking to take on Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District.
“I never imagined running for Congress, but I saw a culture of corruption in Washington that protects corporate special interests and insiders instead of solving problems, and knew I had to do something about it,” Berman said in a statement after the race was called. “Tonight proves that when working people stand up, we can make a difference.” 
A little more than an hour after the polls closed,  Berman ran away with the contest. The Associated Press called the race at 9:02 p.m. With 63% of the ballots counted, Berman was leading with 42% of the vote.
Milwaukee Alder Peter Burgelis garnered just under 22% of the vote despite dropping out more than two weeks ago. Burgelis, who lives outside the 1st District, threw his support to Berman after his first campaign finance report came in with receipts that were less than 10% of Berman’s.
Lorenzo Santos, a former Racine County emergency services director, was in third place, with just over 20% of the vote.  Miguel Aranda, a Whitewater school board member and an administrator at the University of Wisconsin-Whitewater, had just under 15%.
Berman emerged as the best-funded Democrat in the primary, with more than  25 times as much money raised by July 22, as Santos and Aranda put together, according to Federal Election Commission data. Berman was endorsed by the United Auto Workers union and by several the Democratic state lawmakers whose Assembly districts are in the 1st CD.
The outcome sets up Berman to take on Steil in the Nov. 3 general election. While the seat has been safely in Republican hands for 30 years, the 1st CD is among a list of districts that the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has targeted this fall.
In a statement, DCCC chair Suzan DelBene said Steil “is a creature of Washington with a rolodex of special interests and insider allies” and who “backed every Trump price hike now hurting Wisconsin families in order to give a handout to his wealthy donors.”

text:
President Donald Trump endorsed Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of Department of Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy, in the Republican primary for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District Tuesday evening. (Alfonso headshot courtesy of campaign) The battle to compete for U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany’s open seat in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District ended Tuesday night in victory by Michael Alfonso, son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who previously held the 7th CD seat. Alfonso was endorsed by President Donald Trump. 
The AP called the race at 9:16 p.m. with 59% of the vote counted.
Alfonso will compete in the Republican-leaning district to replace Tiffany, a strong Trump ally, who announced his retirement from Congress when he launched his campaign for governor.
Alfonso entered the race in Oct. 2025, saying that “Northern Wisconsin needs to continue to have a representative who will truly put our families, communities, and America first.” He gained Trump’s endorsement in January. 
The other candidates in the race were Niina Baum a lifelong Northwoods resident and dog musher who founded Northwoods Young Professionals to attract and retain workers in northern Wisconsin; Jessi Ebben, a public relations professional who describes herself as a “Trump Republican,” and who previously ran to represent Wisconsin’s 3rd CD, Kevin Hermening, a financial advisor and former United States and Marine Don Raihala, an accountant.
Republicans from local county parties and his primary opponents criticized Alfonso’s lack of experience and his father-in-law’s help as he tried to win the race. He has also enjoyed support from other Republican members of the Wisconsin congressional delegation, Turning Point USA and has campaigned with Moms For Liberty, including criticizing a small rural school district in the district over its bathroom policies for transgender students.
In the last days of the primary campaign, a negative ad calling Alfonso a “nepo baby” was launched by American Future Fund Political Action, which reported spending $135,100 on broadcast advertising targeting Alfonso, according to State Affairs.
“I’m the only candidate on this stage that our great president, the greatest president of my lifetime, President Donald J. Trump, trusts to get his agenda into law,” Alfonso said during the only primary debate. “We hear a lot about politicians saying they’re pro-Trump only in the year of an election. What the Trump endorsement means is that I will support the president, I will fight for his agenda.”
Alfonso said he sat down with Trump for an interview and promised the president that no one would out work him in Congress.
Alfonso, 26, also directly addressed concerns about his lack of experience during the debate, including saying that he is currently employed as an accountant. Prior to running for Congress, Alfonso worked in construction while a student at UW-Madison. After graduating, he moved to Florida and worked on a podcast hosted by Dan Bongino for a year. He has since moved back to Hayward, Wisconsin.
Alfonso argued that young people can bring energy to politics and that experience is not the only measure of effectiveness.

description: Matt Little won the Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary in Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, winning a three-way race to face Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt in the November general election. Little beat state Sen. Matt Klein, a Mayo Clinic doctor who sought centrist and swing voters; and state Rep. Kaela Berg, who championed labor as a union flight […]
text:
Former state Sen. Matt Little, who is running for Congress in the 2nd Congressional District. Campaign photo. Matt Little won the Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary in Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, winning a three-way race to face Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt in the November general election.
Little beat state Sen. Matt Klein, a Mayo Clinic doctor who sought centrist and swing voters; and state Rep. Kaela Berg, who championed labor as a union flight attendant. 
Little is the former two-term mayor of Lakeville who represented the area in the state Senate from 2016 to 2020, when he lost to a Republican. He won the DFL endorsement in the primary and presented himself as a more progressive successor to Rep. Angie Craig, who left the state’s most competitive congressional district for a Senate bid.
“This win proves that even $3.5 million dollars of outside money couldn’t buy this election,” Little said in a statement. “It proves people believe real change is possible; that if we are bold and brave, we will stop Trump’s corruption, we will hold ICE accountable, and we will make life affordable, so the American dream is real for everyone!”
The 2nd Congressional District is purple but leaning towards Democrats, according to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report — and a must-hold if they’re to have a shot at taking over the U.S. House. Craig has represented the south suburban district since 2019.
Little positioned himself as the race’s progressive candidate, following a tide of progressive candidates who have won Democratic primaries around the country. Most recently, in Michigan, Democratic Socialist Abdul El-Sayed beat out U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a Senate primary. 
Little’s commanding win — added to fellow progressive Berg’s vote total  — signals that even in Craig’s purple district, voters are seeking a stronger stance against President Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts. 
During Operation Metro Surge, Little posted videos of himself following immigration agents as part of the effort to observe and document their activities. (He took the New York Times on a ridealong.) 
Little promised to advocate for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding to be immediately reduced to pre-Trump levels and for the agency to be replaced “with a federal immigration agency that Americans can trust and that obeys the law and Constitution.”
Klein’s website didn’t mention immigration. 
In November, Little will face state Sen. Eric Pratt, a four-term state senator and the highest-ranking Republican on the Senate Finance Committee. He ran uncontested on the Republican side of the primary ballot, promising to “crack down on fraud, abuse and the people who exploit the system” and to support law enforcement, including ICE.

title: Rebecca Cooke wins 3rd CD primary to set up rematch against Derrick Van Orden
description: Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic primary in Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District Tuesday, riding a massive monetary advantage and support from the national Democratic party to set up a rematch after her narrow 2024 loss to Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden. Western Wisconsin’s purple 3rd District is one of the Democratic Party’s main targets in the […]
text:
Democratic candidate for the 3rd Congressional District Rebecca Cooke meets with voters. (Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic primary in Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District Tuesday, riding a massive monetary advantage and support from the national Democratic party to set up a rematch after her narrow 2024 loss to Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden.
Western Wisconsin’s purple 3rd District is one of the Democratic Party’s main targets in the country in their effort to flip majority control of the House of Representatives.
Cooke’s name recognition, advantages in fundraising and institutional support helped her win 57.1% of the vote to 47.9% for Emily Berge, the former president of the Eau Claire City Council — who had attempted to leverage an old-school ground campaign and her popularity in the district’s largest city to achieve the upset. 
AP called the race at 9:21 p.m. with 64% of the vote counted.
The race was far closer than initial expectations. This spring, the Cooke campaign touted internal polling that showed her more than 40 points ahead of Berge — who when she entered the race, against the wishes of members of the party, had little name recognition outside Eau Claire.
Cooke, a former fundraiser for Democratic party campaigns and organizations, a former small business owner and a part-time waitress, jumped into the race almost immediately after the 2024 election — earning endorsements from U.S. Sens. Tammy Baldwin and Bernie Sanders, as well as support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Cooke also ran for the seat in 2022, losing the Democratic primary to state Sen. Brad Pfaff (D-Onalaska). 
In nearly two years of campaigning, Cooke has raised massive amounts of money — $8.6 million since the beginning of 2025. That total far surpasses Berge, who raised $728,000, and squeaks past Van Orden, who has raised $7.5 million. 
But the closer than expected primary challenge pushed Cooke to spend a significant chunk of that cash advantage. Cooke has $1.8 million in cash on hand while Van Orden has $4.6 million, according to the most recent campaign finance reports, filed in late July. 
Democrats in the district are now turning their focus to the divisive Van Orden, who has been a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump. 
Since the 2024 race, Van Orden and the Republican party have been relentlessly attacking Cooke, frequently calling her a “commie.” As national attention focuses on the district while Republicans fight to hold onto their thin majority, Van Orden spent Tuesday evening posting AI videos of Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker yelling at a CNN anchor.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Doug McCrory loses Democratic primary for CT 2nd Senate District
description: Sen. Doug McCrory, a veteran Democratic lawmaker of more than two decades, lost a bid to hold onto his state Senate seat on Tuesday night.
text:
Sen. Doug McCrory, a veteran Democratic lawmaker of more than two decades, lost a bid to hold onto his state Senate seat representing Hartford, Bloomfield and Windsor in one of the state’s most closely watched legislative primaries on Tuesday night. 
McCrory, who is the subject of an ongoing federal criminal investigation, came in third in a three-way race behind state Rep. Maryam Khan and Ayana Taylor, the chairwoman of the Windsor Board of Education, according to early results compiled by the candidates. The Associated Press had not called the race by 10:05 p.m.
Khan, who won the Democratic endorsement in the race at a hotly contested convention in May, declared victory in the race early Tuesday night.
“Tonight, the voters of Hartford, Windsor, and Bloomfield sent a message that’s been building for years: our government belongs to the people who show up for it, not the people who buy their way into it,” Khan, who was also backed by the Working Families Party, said in a statement. “My opponent spent six years chairing the Education Committee … watching our public schools close one by one. I ran because I believe this district deserves more — a government that taxes the wealthy their fair share, holds Eversource accountable, and puts real money into the neighborhood schools that raised us.”

Rep. Maryam Khan, D-Windsor, speaks at a press conference at the Parker Memorial Community Center on May 15, 2026. Credit: Theo Peck-Suzuki / CT Mirror

“I’m proud to run as a Working Families Party candidate, because that’s exactly what WFP was built for: proving that working people don’t have to wait for permission to lead,” Kahn added. “This is one seat, but it’s part of a bigger fight … We’re not managing decline anymore. We’re building something new, together, and tonight is just the beginning.”
[Click here for complete CT primary results]
McCrory’s election defeat comes roughly a year after news broke that the Democratic senator was being investigated by the FBI for his role in dispersing millions of dollars in state grant money to a number of Hartford nonprofits. 
The shadow of that investigation trailed McCrory this year as Khan and Taylor both decided to challenge him for the 2nd Senate District, which he has held since 2017.
McCrory aggressively campaigned across the three-town district in recent weeks and received endorsements from prominent Democrats, including outgoing Senate President Martin Looney and Sen. Bob Duff, the current Senate majority leader. But it was not enough to salvage his political career.
After watching the election results roll in on Tuesday night, McCrory took the stage at a restaurant in Bloomfield to conceded and to thank his supporters for continuing to stand behind him after more than 20 years in the Connecticut General Assembly.

Incumbent state Sen. Doug McCrory delivers a concession speech at Sarah’s On Park restaurant in Bloomfield on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Andrew Brown / CT Mirror

“I’m not as disappointed as I thought I was,” McCrory added. “But hey, we did the best we can.” 
“Don’t be upset. Do not be upset,” McCrory added. “Another time will come and we will figure this out to make sure our community gets the representation that we deserve. Two more years is not a long way from here. Who knows what will happen then.” 
Taylor, who also challenged McCrory in 2024, also issued a conciliatory statement on Tuesday congratulating Khan on her election victory.  
“Clearly today didn’t go the way we hoped it would go,” Taylor said. “We ran a clean, honest, open campaign… I will forever be proud of what we accomplished in this race.” 
The contest in the 2nd Senate District was one of the more competitive legislative races during Tuesday’s elections. But it was just one of nearly a dozen legislative primaries that took place.
In total, there were eight Democratic races for legislative seats in both the House and Senate. And there were three Republican primaries. 
The most attention-grabbing race on the Republican side took place in the stae’s northeast corner, where the Republican Party sought to defeat Jadon MacCormack, the who was the endorsed candidate in the 50th House District that covers seven towns in the so-called Quiet Corner.
Republican leaders in the state rallied last-minute support behind Anthony Emilio in the race due to MacCormack’s remarks denouncing Pride Month and his calls for gay people to be put to death.
Unofficial election results from Tuesday night showed that Emilio was capturing roughly 78% of the vote, easily outpacing MacCormack, in a low-turnout election. 
Meanwhile in New Haven, Rep. Patricia Dillon, the longest-serving member of the House seeking reelection, lost her primary in the 92nd House District to Eli Sabin, according to the preliminary results.

text:
Former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl, R-Mobile, won the Republican nomination in Alabama's 1st Congressional District in a special primary election on Aug. 11, 2026, defeating two others in a winner-take-all primary. He will face Democratic nominee Clyde Jones, Jr. in November. (courtesy of candidate)Former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl, R-Mobile, won the Republican nomination for Alabama’s 1st Congressional District Tuesday night, defeating two others in a winner-take-all special primary election.
As of 8:48 p.m., Carl, boosted by an endorsement from President Donald Trump, had 21,221 votes, about 74.6% of the total, with 40% of ballots counted in unofficial returns. Austin Sidwell, who works at a private security firm, had 5,067 votes, about 17.8% of the total. John Mills, a Navy veteran, had 1,631 votes, about 5.7% of the total. 
Carl will face Democratic nominee Clyde Jones, Jr. in the general election, who was the only Democratic candidate to qualify in the race. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I look forward to taking the fight to the socialist Democrats this November and serving alongside a fantastic delegation that puts America First,” Carl said in a statement posted to Facebook.
Carl campaigned on his previous experience in Congress. He was elected to represent the district in 2020 and won re-election in 2022. But after the district was redrawn in 2024 to take in more of the Wiregrass, Carl narrowly lost the Republican nomination to U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise.
The seat was left vacant by Moore, who is the party’s nominee for U.S. Senate. The election in the 1st Congressional District will take place under a 2023 map passed by the Legislature that was previously ruled racially discriminatory in a case known as Allen v. Milligan. 
A 2026 U.S. Supreme Court ruling known as Louisiana v. Callais cleared the way for the Alabama Legislature to pass a law allowing the special primary and Gov. Kay Ivey to reinstate the 2023 map. Under that map, the 1st Congressional District boundaries more closely resemble the district as constructed in 2020.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Luke Bronin defeats Rep. John Larson in CT 1st District primary
description: Luke Bronin decisively defeated U.S. Rep. John Larson in the Democratic primary for the 1st District, effectively guaranteeing him the seat.
text:
Luke Bronin, the former mayor of Hartford who campaigned on the need for new voices in Congress, soundly defeated long-time incumbent U.S. Rep. John Larson in the Democratic primary on Tuesday, all but guaranteeing Bronin the seat.
The Associated Press called the race around 10 p.m. on Tuesday with Bronin besting the congressman, 53.5% to 34.7%, with an estimated 51% of votes counted.
The other candidates, Jillian Gilchrest and Ruth Fortune, combined for about 11.8% of the votes at 10 p.m., according to AP.
The healthy margin of victory suggested that Bronin’s primary message — that Democratic voters want a change in leadership — resonated in the district.
Larson, the 78-year-old congressman who was in the fight of his political life, is the latest Democratic incumbent to lose a primary as younger candidates around the country launch intra-party bids in an effort to reorient the party and reshape Congress. After serving 28 years in Congress, he fell short of the Democratic nomination for a 15th term.
Bronin, his most well-financed challenger who upset him at the nominating convention for the party’s endorsement, premised his campaign around the need for generational change and newer candidates who can take on President Donald Trump, especially if Democrats can retake the majority in the U.S. House in November. 
Bronin, 47, served as the mayor of Hartford for two terms, leaving office in 2024.
Tuesday’s primary tested whether voters want experience and seniority in Congress or a fresh face to bring a new energy as incumbent lawmakers faced challenges in primaries across the country. Before Tuesday, half a dozen Democratic incumbents in Congress lost primaries that turned on ideological and generational issues.
Larson entered his election night watch party at Connecticut River Academy in his native East Hartford shortly before the race was called for Bronin. He was quickly swarmed by dozens of his supporters who gave him thunderous applause and cheered “JBL.”
As attendees circled around him, Larson decided to speak in the middle of the room instead of going to the podium. He gave a heartfelt speech thanking the other four Democrats in Connecticut’s congressional delegation who supported him, including U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, who attended the party.
“In some respects, I feel apologetic that I let them down,” Larson said about his colleagues, as the crowd shouted, “No you didn’t.”
“At the beginning of this debate, people said, well, now is when you find out who your friends really are,” he continued. “Nothing truer could have been said. When I look around this room this evening, now’s when you know who your friends really are.”

U.S. Rep. John B. Larson hugs his wife Leslie Best as he addresses supporters during a primary election watch party at Connecticut River Academy at Goodwin University in East Hartford on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

He said after his speech that he spoke with Bronin and congratulated him.
“The people of this district have spoken, and it’s time for us to come together and make sure that we all join forces,” Larson said to an emotional crowd. “Because the issue here as I said throughout this campaign is Donald Trump and what he’s doing to this country.”
The four-way primary for the 1st Congressional District, which is centered around Hartford, was unprecedented. Larson won an open House seat in 1998 and hadn’t faced a primary challenge since.
Because Connecticut rarely sees primaries, it garnered attention that started to break through nationally as super PACs got involved in the final weeks. Outside groups poured in more than $2.5 million into the race on behalf of Bronin and Larson, with the former mayor getting a much bigger boost in spending. The congressman was ultimately outspent.
The outcome of the race won’t have any bearing on which party controls Congress next year since it’s a safe Democratic seat in a blue state. But it’s part of a national trend of younger candidates taking on longtime members as voters channel frustration at a Democratic Party that has little leverage in Congress in the minority.
Calls for generational change from Democrats got louder following catastrophic losses in the 2024 elections.
Unlike other House primaries in New York and Colorado or even Connecticut’s gubernatorial primary, the race for the 1st District wasn’t run as much on ideological grounds from Bronin and the other challengers but more on the push for new — and younger — leaders in Congress.
Bronin, West Hartford Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune sought to make the case that Larson hasn’t done enough to counter Trump.
Larson pushed back on that characterization, arguing that experience is needed to take on Trump and he’ll be well-positioned to do more with seniority on committees. He said he would have been poised to take the gavel of the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, the signature issue of his career and one he put a spotlight on throughout the campaign, if Democrats take back the House.
A former high school history teacher, Larson has had a lengthy career in Connecticut politics that predates his time in Congress. He served in the state Senate, eventually serving as president pro tempore. About a decade into his congressional career, he was elevated to leadership ranks as the chair of the House Democratic Caucus as Democrats worked to pass the Affordable Care Act.
Overall, there was little daylight between the four candidates on some of the biggest policy fronts. They all had similar policy messaging on abolishing ICE, pushing for Medicare for All, and wanting immigration reform that includes establishing a pathway to citizenship for immigrants.
But some of the central themes of the race revolved around campaign fundraising and debate over labor records between Larson and Bronin.
The congressman spent most of the campaign focused on Trump and Bronin, his main opponent. He went after Bronin’s fundraising from billionaires and those with ties to private equity, seeking to tag him as a “corporate Democrat.”
For his part, Bronin said he wouldn’t accept corporate PAC money and highlighted that the congressman got about half of his campaign donations from political action committees affiliated with corporations, unions and other industries.
Those themes were reflected in a deluge of TV ads, mailers and text messages from the Bronin and Larson campaigns and the outside groups supporting them.
Gilchrest and Fortune struggled to break through in the same ways, especially because they weren’t able to compete financially as the bulk of major donations and spending by outside groups flocked to Bronin and Larson. The two women bemoaned the heavy emphasis on spending in the race and the donations that went to Bronin and Larson from billionaires and wealthy networks.
Gilchrest narrowly qualified for the August primary after some of Larson’s delegates flipped to support her at the May nominating convention. Like she did in her first race in 2018 for state representative, she spent a lot of time canvassing in her campaign for Congress. Gilchrest relied on that strategy without the same funds 
Fortune, an estate attorney who was a first-time candidate for office, didn’t secure a spot on the primary ballot through the conventional route of the nominating convention. But she overcame the logistical challenge of qualifying for the primary by securing thousands of signatures through petition signatures.
The winner of the Democratic primary is the heavy favorite in November’s general election. Of the five U.S. House seats in Connecticut, the 1st District is the bluest.

Dr. Amy Chai, a GOP candidate for the 1st District, stands outside a polling place in Bloomfield on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Ginny Monk / CT Mirror

Dr. Amy Chai, the GOP nominee in the 1st District, spent Tuesday out at the polls, telling voters about her campaign. She said she’s heard from Democrats who aren’t happy with their choices. She was previously an independent but “realized she couldn’t win” unless she was affiliated with a major party.
“My motto is listen more, hate less,” Chai said. If elected, she wants to focus on the prevention of mental illness and addiction. She believes politics is making mental health disorders worse.
The 1st District primary was the only one for Democrats on the federal side. Republicans, meanwhile, held two primaries in the 4th District and the 5th District. But Democrats are strongly favored, especially since the party in power historically faces headwinds in a midterm election.

title: Rhett Marques wins Republican nomination in Alabama 2nd Congressional District
description: Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, won the Alabama Republican nomination for Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District Tuesday night, defeating five others in a winner-take-all special primary election. As of 8:41 p.m., Marques had about 15,468 votes, about 50% of the total with about 62% of ballots counted in unofficial returns. Hampton Harris, a business owner a[...]
text:
Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, giving a victory speech after winning a special primary election for Alabama's 2nd Congressional District on Aug. 11, 2026, in Enterprise, Alabama. Marques Tuesday won the Republican nomination for the seat, defeating five other candidates. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, won the Alabama Republican nomination for Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District Tuesday night, defeating five others in a winner-take-all special primary election.
As of 8:41 p.m., Marques had about 15,468 votes, about 50% of the total with about 62% of ballots counted in unofficial returns. Hampton Harris, a business owner and attorney, had 6,270 (20.4%). David Matthews, a former Trump appointee, had 5,584 (18.2%). 
Marques will face incumbent U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in the general election, who was the only Democratic candidate to qualify in the race. 
The election will take place under a map drawn by the Alabama Legislature in 2023 in response to a federal court ruling in a case known as Allen v. Milligan. A three-judge panel that heard Milligan ruled that a 2021 Alabama congressional map violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by not giving Black Alabama voters a chance to elect their preferred representatives. 
The courts later ruled that the 2023 map drawn by the Legislature also violated the VRA and drew new maps for the state, including a new 2nd Congressional District with a Black Voting Age Population (BVAP) of 48.7%. Figures was elected from the district in 2024. 
But in April, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Louisiana v. Callais that plaintiffs challenging legislative maps under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as the Milligan plaintiffs had, needed to show intentional discrimination, a significantly higher bar. The Supreme Court in June reversed its earlier Milligan decision and allowed Alabama to hold elections under the 2023 map.  The map cuts the BVAP in the 2nd Congressional District from 48.7% to 39.9%, and is expected to give the district a Republican lean.
Marques campaigned on his endorsement from Trump and his “conservative legislative record” in the Alabama Legislature since his election in 2018. He often touted his votes supporting Alabama’s near-total abortion ban, multiple tax cuts and a 2026 law that extends the death penalty to child sexual assault.
Marques thanked voters, his staff, President Donald Trump, and U.S. Sen. Katie Britt during a victory speech Tuesday night to a crowd of about 100 in Enterprise. He said Republicans need to maintain control of the U.S. House of Representatives to prevent the progressive wing of the Democratic party from taking control.
“This is not just about flipping a district. This about about craziness and common sense,” he said. “Basically they are communists who are trying to control their party and they’re letting them, and that’s scary … Do you really want Alabama to look like New York and California?”
Marques’ Republican opponents criticized the state representative for his 2018 vote to increase the state gas tax. Figures said in a statement Tuesday night that Marques’ support of the war in Iran will increase fuel prices more.
“The choice in this race is simple; I have worked for the people of Alabama because that is who we should be working for. My opponent would be just another rubber stamp on the same policies that are making life more expensive for the people right here in Alabama,” Figures said.


8:47 pmThis story was updated at 8:47 p.m. to include comments from Marques' victory speech.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah’s intense, dangerous fire season could be its most expensive
description: Utah has burned through an estimated $33 million to fight raging wildfires this year, putting the state on track to outspend last year’s record total.
text:
A firefighter looks over a burned area from the Rocky Canyon Fire near Henefer, Utah, in a photo shared by fire officials on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Samuel P Barlow Jr via Utah Fire Info)Utah has burned through an estimated $33 million to fight raging wildfires this year, putting the state on track to outspend last year’s record total. 
Inflation is partly to blame. But the rising cost also reflects the sheer size of this year’s fires, their encroachment on communities and the intense heat, drought and wind making them more resistant to containment, said Wade Snyder, deputy state fire management officer with the Division of Forestry, Fire & State Lands.  
Then there’s the fact that it’s only August, and firefighters often battle fires into September.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’re not out of the woods yet,” Snyder said Monday. He said the estimated $33 million spent so far may grow by another third. He also cautioned that the numbers are preliminary and the  exact costs won’t be sorted out for some time. 
So far this year, more than 532,000 acres have burned across the state, making it Utah’s second-biggest wildfire year on record. In 2007, the season topped out at about 629,200 acres. 
This year has been a perfect storm. Record-low snowpack, warm winter temperatures and stubborn drought primed forests to burn hot and fast, state officials said. They were alarmed when a forest fire was smoldering in the Uinta Mountains in March, noting slopes there are usually covered in snow that early in the year.  
Gov. Spencer Cox has noted Utah’s been saving up for big years, building up its wildfire fund to more than $120 million. He and other state officials are floating the idea of freeing up other sources of state funding. 
Members of Engine 213 from Idaho mop up the Cottonwood Fire near Beaver, Utah, in a photo shared by the U.S. Forest Service on June 26, 2026. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Forest Service)
Utah Rep. Carl Albrecht, chair of the House Natural Resources Committee, told Fox 13 he’s been speaking with legislative leaders about opening up “rainy day” funds for firefighting, flood mitigation and aiding in community recovery.
The federal government picks up most of the state’s firefighting costs. Updated totals from the Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands put last year’s overall firefighting cost at roughly $240 million, with the state’s share at $36 million, Snyder said. 
Already this summer, federal funding is on the way, including to offset costs of battling the Cottonwood Fire near Beaver and the Cherry Fire in Juab and Tooele counties. On Monday, the Federal Emergency Management Agency announced it approved Utah’s request for aid in battling the Rocky Canyon Fire in Morgan and Summit Counties, which was burning Tuesday at more than 14,000 acres and was 23% contained after forcing evacuations in Henefer. 
While FEMA didn’t say how much money it anticipates sending, the agency pledged to cover 75% of firefighting costs it deems eligible, noting individual homes and business owners don’t qualify. 
The Widemouth 2 Fire burns near Fillmore, Utah, in a photo shared by fire officials on Aug. 3, 2026. (Photo courtesy of inter-agency fire officials via InciWeb)
And under an agreement signed by Cox and the U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz last week, the state and feds will both chip in more than $9 million to help with the aftermath of the Cottonwood Fire that torched more than 97,000 acres east of Beaver in July. Utah’s share will come from the state’s wildfire fund, according to the governor’s office. 
And that’s to say nothing of the human cost. Two pilots died in a helicopter crash last week, while fighting the Widemouth 2 Fire in southern Utah. In an earlier tragedy in June, three members of a “helitack” crew died when they were trapped in a burnover incident on the Utah-Colorado border, and a fourth later died of the burn injuries. A surviving crew member was hospitalized. 
“There’s a lot of people grieving right now,” Snyder said. “When we have a loss, it impacts us all.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Darline Graham advances to runoff in special GOP primary. It’s unclear who she’ll face.
description: COLUMBIA — A month after the death of Lindsey Graham, his younger sister advanced to a runoff for the chance to succeed him in the U.S. Senate for the next six years. Sen. Darline Graham led the 10-candidate field with about 33% of the votes when The Associated Press called it. Her lead held as […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fulfill her brother Lindsey Graham's term that ends in January, makes her pitch to voters at the U.S. Senate Stump Stop held at River Bluff High School in Lexington, South Carolina, on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette) COLUMBIA — A month after the death of Lindsey Graham, his younger sister advanced to a runoff for the chance to succeed him in the U.S. Senate for the next six years.
Sen. Darline Graham led the 10-candidate field with about 33% of the votes when The Associated Press called it. Her lead held as vote-counting continued.
It’s not yet clear who will join her on the Aug. 25 ballot. U.S. Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman remained in a tight race for second place.
In South Carolina, a primary runoff is required if no candidate gets more than 50% of the votes.
It’s been a whirlwind month.
The unexpected death July 11 of South Carolina’s senior senator triggered a tight timeline in state law to replace him on November ballots. Candidates began filing for the contest a week before his funeral services in Washington, D.C., and Columbia.
Darline Graham, who was frequently by her brother’s side but never a candidate herself, accepted Gov. Henry McMaster’s appointment to fulfill the term that expires in January. She was expected to be an honorary placeholder — until President Donald Trump shook up the field pre-filing by urging the newly sworn-in senator to run.
But his surprise “complete and total endorsement” of someone without a political record of her own didn’t stop Republicans from jumping into South Carolina’s first open U.S. Senate race in 22 years. Candidates with years of experience in the Statehouse and Capitol Hill criticized her as unproven and unknown.
“I didn’t inherit a record. I earned it,” Fry said during the state GOP debate last week.
Graham countered that she has experience, just not as a politician. For the last seven years, she’s led the state Commission for the Blind.
On Monday, Trump doubled down on his endorsement, saying it’s what Lindsey Graham would’ve wanted.
“Darline’s gotten off to a great start,” he said during a call-in rally. He pointed to her votes enabling Todd Blanche to be sworn in Monday as U.S. attorney general as well as passage of sanctions against Russia as championed by her brother.
“She’s sort of a natural,” Trump said.
His tele-rally occurred hours after Joint Base Charleston was officially renamed in Lindsey Graham’s honor. Officials participating in the ceremonial unveiling in North Charleston included Sen. Darline Graham, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a South Carolina native, and McMaster.
Critics of Graham’s candidacy — and Trump’s decision — called it a case of political nepotism, saying South Carolinians don’t elect dynasties. But Graham is not the first South Carolina woman elected to fill a deceased family member’s seat.
She is, however, the first sister. The other women were widows. Lindsey Graham never married.
In the 20th century, four South Carolina women, all Democrats, were elected to finish serving their husband’s term in the U.S. House following his death. None, however, sought election to the next full term. Nationwide, 47 women have been elected or appointed to fill congressional vacancies created by the deaths of their husbands: eight to the U.S. Senate and 39 to the U. S. House, according to the Center for American Women and Politics.
 
This is a developing story. Check back for details.

title: Trump administration sues CT over in-state tuition for undocumented students
description: This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday filed a lawsuit against Connecticut over state laws that provide in-state tuition and financial assistance to immigrant students lacking permanent legal status. In its complain[...]
text:
The State Coat of Arms of Connecticut featuring the Latin motto that translates to 'He who transplanted still sustains' is mounted on a brick exterior at the main campus of the University of Connecticut in Storrs. (The George F. Landegger Collection of Connecticut Photographs in the Carol M. Highsmith's America, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday filed a lawsuit against Connecticut over state laws that provide in-state tuition and financial assistance to immigrant students lacking permanent legal status.
In its complaint, the DOJ argued that Connecticut’s laws unfairly give benefits such as lower tuition and scholarships to students without legal status while denying the same benefits to U.S. citizens who live outside the state. The DOJ also argued that the laws violate federal statutes and encourage illegal immigration to the U.S.
“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”
In response to the lawsuit, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who voted for the in-state tuition law in 2011 as a state legislator, said he would defend the state’s policies.
“Note to Trump — stay out of Connecticut,” Tong said in a statement. “Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams. Donald Trump doesn’t run UConn or any of our state colleges, and we’re not about to let him start.”
Gov. Lamont also defended the state’s policies, saying in a statement, “kids who grow up in Connecticut and graduate from Connecticut public schools should be able to afford to go to college here, including those who have applied for legal status.”
“We are making Connecticut the land of opportunity and education, and we will not accept his attempts to turn back the clock on progress,” Lamont said.
Connecticut first provided in-state tuition benefits to undocumented students under the 2011 state law, which required them to have attended high school in Connecticut for four years and earned a diploma. The state later reduced the high school attendance requirement to two years in 2015.
In 2018, Connecticut passed another law allowing students without permanent legal status to apply for and receive institutional aid at public colleges and universities.
The lawsuit also challenges other state laws involving financial aid at Connecticut State Community College, Roberta B. Willis need-based grants, and the state’s student loan reimbursement program.
The Trump administration has filed similar lawsuits challenging higher-education benefits in 16 other states.
